There are areas of ulceration and granulation tissue, along with early facial nerve weakness. Which of the following best describes the underlying process and its management?
options: Accumulation of desquamated keratin due to abnormal, outward epithelial migration of the EAC, managed conservatively with topical antibiotics alone
Accumulation of desquamated keratin due to failure of the normal outward (self-cleaning) epithelial migration of the EAC, managed by removal of the keratin mass by instrumentation
Cholesteatoma of the middle ear extending into the EAC, managed by modified radical mastoidectomy
Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas infection, managed with 6 weeks of antibiotics and debridement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Accumulation of desquamated keratin due to failure of the normal outward (self-cleaning) epithelial migration of the EAC, managed by removal of the keratin mass by instrumentation

| Feature | Keratosis obturans

| ------- | ------------------

| Mechanism | Failure of normal outward epithelial migration of EAC → keratin accumulates in a laminar, "onion-skin" arrangement

| C/F | Severe otalgia

| O/E | White keratin mass with wax in deep meatus, widening of EAC, ulceration/granulations, facial nerve palsy possible

| Management | Removal of keratin mass by instrumentation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old scuba diver presents with sudden onset vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss in the right ear after rapidly surfacing from a deep dive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perilymphatic fistula

Perilymphatic fistula occurs due to rupture of the oval or round window membrane, leading to leakage of perilymph from the inner ear into the middle ear.

Common causes:

• Barotrauma (scuba diving, flying)
• Sudden pressure changes
• Head injury
• Forceful Valsalva

Clinical features:

• Sudden sensorineural hearing loss
• Vertigo after pressure change
• Tinnitus
• Aural fullness
• Symptoms worsen with straining or pressure changes

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old teacher complains of hoarseness, vocal fatigue, and a weak voice, especially after prolonged speaking. Laryngoscopic examination reveals keyhole appearance of the glottis during phonation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phonasthenia

Phonasthenia is a functional voice disorder seen commonly in professional voice users (teachers, singers) characterized by vocal fatigue, hoarseness, weak voice, and throat discomfort without structural laryngeal pathology. On laryngoscopy, it shows a “keyhole” or spindle-shaped glottic gap during phonation due to incomplete closure of the vocal cords from vocal strain and misuse.

It must be differentiated from:

• Puberphonia: high-pitched voice in adolescent males
• Functional/hysteric aphonia: whispering voice with normal cough and sudden onset, usually psychogenic

Management: Voice therapy, vocal hygiene, and speech therapy are mainstay.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 36-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department after sudden onset of shortness of breath and difficulty swallowing. He has visited the emergency department several times before due to food and skin allergies. The patient is unconscious on arrival. Examination shows excessive accessory respiratory muscle use and edematous swelling of the face, lips, and tongue. There is also scattered urticaria over the upper body. Attempts at intubation are unsuccessful due to massive soft tissue edema involving the pharynx. A decision is made to perform an emergency cricothyrotomy. The incisions made during this procedure will most likely pass through which of the following structures?
options: Superficial cervical fascia and cricothyroid membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superficial cervical fascia and cricothyroid membrane

Emergency cricothyrotomy is performed to establish a rapid airway when endotracheal intubation is not possible (e.g., severe anaphylaxis with upper airway edema).

Skin → superficial cervical fascia (including platysma) → cricothyroid membrane → airway.

• Cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage
• Most superficial and avascular entry into airway
• Preferred site for emergency surgical airway

Why not tracheostomy in emergency:

• Takes longer
• More bleeding risk
• Thyroid isthmus and major vessels present
• Cricothyrotomy is faster and safer in acute airway obstruction

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 38-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of tinnitus and progressive hearing loss. Each episode is followed by a sudden attack of vertigo, after which the hearing improves dramatically. There is no history of ear discharge or trauma. Which of the following best describes this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lermoyez syndrome

Lermoyez syndrome is a rare variant of Ménière’s disease characterized by fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus that improve suddenly after an attack of vertigo.

• Hearing improves after vertigo → Lermoyez syndrome (reverse Ménière’s)
• Hearing worsens after vertigo → Ménière’s disease
• Vertigo without hearing loss → Vestibular neuronitis
• Positional vertigo lasting seconds → BPPV

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 38-year-old patient presents with sudden onset unilateral hearing loss noticed on waking up, associated with mild tinnitus but no vertigo. Otoscopic examination is normal. Tuning fork tests suggest sensorineural hearing loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Wait and watch for spontaneous recovery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate systemic corticosteroids

Idiopathic Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and early treatment to maximize hearing recovery.

• Definition:

o    ≥ 30 dB sensorineural hearing loss over ≥3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours
• Clinical features:

o    Sudden unilateral hearing loss (often on waking)

o    May have tinnitus ± vertigo

o    Normal otoscopic findings
• Management principle:

o    Immediate corticosteroids (systemic ± intratympanic)

o    Best outcomes when started within 72 hours
• Prognostic factors:

o    Early treatment → better recovery

o    Severe loss or delayed therapy → poor prognosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the office for "noisy breathing”, especially when he is lying on his back. The noise seems to improve when the patient is held upright or during "tummy time." He does not appear to have laboured breathing and has never turned blue. Which of the following would confirm the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy

• Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of congenital stridor in infants. It is a functional/dynamic problem.
• Here, floppy supraglottic structures (arytenoids and epiglottis) collapse inward during inspiration.
• Clinically characterized by noisy breathing that worsens in supine position and improves when prone or upright.

✅ Why Option C is correct

• Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy: helps in direct visualisation of epiglottis while the baby is breathing
• It confirms the diagnosis immediately.

Other options:

Option A. Chest radiography:

• Chest x-ray is a static imaging. It is useful for diagnosis of lung parenchymal disorders like pneumonia.
• But cannot visualise the inspiratory collapse of epiglottis (as seen on fiberoptic laryngoscope)

Option B. CT scan of the neck:

• CT is a static imaging. It is useful for diagnosis of structural disorders like neck masses, tumours.
• But cannot visualise the inspiratory collapse of epiglottis (as seen on fiberoptic laryngoscope)
• Plus, radiation in a 4-month-old? NO.

Option D. Fluoroscopic barium swallow:

• Barium swallow is used to assess swallowing dysfunctions.
• It does NOT assess the supraglottic airway during breathing.

Positional inspiratory stridor in an infant that improves upright → think laryngomalacia → confirm with flexible laryngoscopy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 42 year old man undergoes superficial parotidectomy for a pleomorphic adenoma located in the superficial lobe of parotid. During the operation, the surgeon identifies the facial nerve trunk emerging from stylomastoid foramen and uses it as a landmark to separate the superficial and deep lobe of the gland. What is the name of the fascial plane and what are its components?
options: Masseteric plane - Retromandibular vein, Facial nerve, Internal carotid artery.
McGreor’s plane - Retromandibular vein, Mandibular nerve, External carotid artery.
Patey’s plane - Retromandibular vein, Facial nerve, External carotid artery.
Fisch’s plane - Retromandibular vein, Mandibular nerve, External carotid artery.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patey’s plane - Retromandibular vein, Facial nerve, External carotid artery.

During parotid surgery, especially superficial parotidectomy, safe identification and preservation of the facial nerve is essential because the facial nerve divides the parotid gland into superficial and deep lobes. After identifying the facial nerve trunk at the stylomastoid foramen, surgeons dissect along a key anatomic fascial plane used as a landmark to separate glandular tissue.

This plane is called Patey’s plane, and it contains the classic “triad”:

• Facial nerve
• Retromandibular vein
• External carotid artery

Understanding this plane is crucial because:

• It guides safe dissection between superficial and deep lobes
• Helps prevent facial nerve injury
• Provides orientation to major vascular structures within the parotid

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 44-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of a neck lump. Serum TSH level is normal. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy reveals papillary thyroid cancer. A total thyroidectomy is performed. During an attempt to ligate the inferior thyroid artery, a nervous structure in close proximity is inadvertently damaged. Which of the following was most likely injured during the surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recurrent laryngeal nerve

During thyroidectomy, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery, making it highly susceptible to injury during ligation of this vessel.

• Motor supply to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.

Effects of injury:

• Unilateral injury → hoarseness
• Bilateral injury → airway obstruction, stridor
• Vocal cord paralysis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old man undergoes surgery for a tumor at the roof of the nasopharynx. During dissection near the sinus of Morgagni, a structure is injured. Postoperatively, he develops difficulty equalizing middle ear pressure and recurrent episodes of serous otitis media, with a normal gag reflex and normal voice. Which structure is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tensor veli palatini

The sinus of Morgagni is a gap between the base of the skull and the upper border of the superior constrictor muscle, through which several structures pass to reach the nasopharynx/Eustachian tube region.

Contents of the sinus of Morgagni (mnemonic: TAALA):

• Tensor veli palatini
• Ascending palatine artery
• Ascending pharyngeal artery
• Levator veli palatini
• Auditory (Eustachian) tube

Functional significance:

• The tensor veli palatini is the key muscle responsible for actively opening the Eustachian tube during swallowing and yawning (via its attachment to the tube's cartilaginous wall), which equalizes middle ear pressure and allows mucociliary drainage.
• Injury to this muscle causes Eustachian tube dysfunction, leading to negative middle ear pressure, fluid accumulation, and recurrent serous otitis media.

Why the other options are wrong:

• A. Levator veli palatini: Elevates the soft palate during swallowing (velopharyngeal closure) but plays a comparatively passive/minor role in actively opening the Eustachian tube; its injury causes palatal/speech issues (nasal regurgitation, hypernasal speech) more than ETD.
• C. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Would affect the gag reflex and posterior tongue sensation/taste — explicitly stated as normal here.
• D. Internal laryngeal nerve: Supplies laryngeal sensation above the vocal cords; injury would cause aspiration risk or laryngeal sensory loss, not middle ear symptoms, and voice is stated as normal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient has recurrent episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Despite treatment with salt restriction, diuretics, vestibular sedatives, and betahistine, the patient continues to have intractable vertigo. Audiometry shows that hearing is still useful. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transtympanic steroid injection

In Ménière’s disease with intractable vertigo despite maximal medical therapy, the next step depends on hearing status. When hearing is still serviceable, the preferred next management is intratympanic (transtympanic) steroid injection, which reduces vertigo, preserves hearing, and is minimally invasive.

❌ Total labyrinthectomy

• Destroys hearing.
• Only done when hearing is already non-functional.

❌ Vestibular nerve section

• More invasive. Reserved for refractory cases but after less invasive measures.

❌ Cochlear implant

• For profound hearing loss — not this scenario.

Management ladder in Ménière’s disease:

1. Lifestyle + medical therapy → salt restriction, diuretics, betahistine
2. Persistent vertigo with useful hearing → intratympanic steroid
3. Persistent vertigo with poor hearing → intratympanic gentamicin (chemical labyrinthectomy)
4.

Refractory cases:

5.

Useful hearing → vestibular nerve section

6. Non-serviceable hearing → labyrinthectomy

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with ear pain, tinnitus, a feeling of ear fullness, and headache. Otoscopic examination is normal. Symptoms worsen on chewing. The patient has loss of posterior teeth. Which of the following best explains this condition?
options: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction due to loss of vertical dimension (Costen’s syndrome)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Temporomandibular joint dysfunction due to loss of vertical dimension (Costen’s syndrome)

Costen’s syndrome refers to temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction caused by loss of vertical dimension, usually due to loss of posterior teeth, leading to referred otologic symptoms.

Clinical features:

• Ear pain with normal otoscopy
• Tinnitus
• Ear fullness
• Headache
• Pain worsens on chewing
• Often associated with missing molars/posterior teeth

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with long-standing nasal obstruction, post-nasal drip, and facial heaviness for several months. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses is performed to differentiate chronic sinusitis from acute sinusitis. Which of the following CT findings is most specific for chronic sinusitis?
options: Frothy secretions in the sinus cavity
Bony sclerosis of the sinus walls
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bony sclerosis of the sinus walls

• Bony sclerosis (thickening) of sinus walls on CT is the most specific radiological feature of chronic sinusitis, indicating long-standing inflammation and osteitis of the sinus walls.
• Chronic sinusitis = long-standing inflammation.
• When inflammation persists for months or years, the sinus walls respond by: Thickening ,sclerosing, Becoming denser (reactive bone change) This is called osteitis.
• Bone changes = chronic process. Bone doesn’t remodel in acute disease.

❌ Air–fluid level: Classic for acute sinusitis.

❌ Frothy secretions: Seen in acute infection.

❌ Diffuse mucosal edema: Seen in both acute and chronic — not specific.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to an intermittent ear discharge over the last 2 years. She has also noticed decreased hearing in the right ear recently. Otoscopy shows a small perforation in the right tympanic membrane and a pearly mass behind the membrane. Conduction hearing loss is noted in the right ear. The remainder of the ear, nose, and throat examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's aural mass?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Squamous cell debris

A cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinizing squamous epithelium and squamous debris within the middle ear that leads to chronic ear discharge and conductive hearing loss.

• Retraction pocket or perforation of tympanic membrane
• Causes bone erosion (ossicles, mastoid)

Clinical features:

• Chronic intermittent foul-smelling otorrhea
• Conductive hearing loss
• Pearly white mass behind tympanic membrane
• Possible complications: facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, brain abscess

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman presents with unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance for 8 months. Pure tone audiometry shows a moderate sensorineural hearing loss, but her speech discrimination score is disproportionately poor relative to the degree of pure tone loss. Acoustic reflex testing shows reflex decay, and CT temporal bone shows mild widening of the internal auditory canal on the affected side. Which investigation should be performed next to confirm the diagnosis, and what finding would you expect on it?
options: CT temporal bone with contrast — homogeneously enhancing bony lesion
MRI with gadolinium contrast — well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing CPA mass
PET scan — increased FDG uptake in the internal auditory canal
BERA alone is sufficient — no further imaging required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MRI with gadolinium contrast — well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing CPA mass

The clinical picture here is a classic retrocochlear (as opposed to cochlear) pattern of hearing loss, which should raise suspicion for vestibular schwannoma even before imaging:

• Speech discrimination score (SDS) disproportionately worse than pure tone thresholds — a hallmark of retrocochlear pathology (in cochlear lesions, SDS roughly correlates with pure tone loss).
• Acoustic reflex decay — abnormal adaptation of the reflex over time, another retrocochlear sign (tested via the Metz recruitment/decay test).
• CT showing IAC widening — a supportive but not definitive finding; CT can suggest bony canal erosion/widening from a slow-growing tumor, but it lacks the soft-tissue resolution to characterize the lesion itself and can miss small intracanalicular tumors.

Despite all these suggestive findings, contrast-enhanced MRI remains the gold standard — it can detect tumors just a few millimeters in size, characterizes the classic "ice cream cone" appearance (intracanalicular "cone" extending into a CPA "scoop" of ice cream), and confirms intense homogeneous enhancement with gadolinium.

Why the others are wrong?

• A. CT temporal bone with contrast: Can show a CPA mass but is inferior to MRI for small/intracanalicular lesions and soft tissue characterization; not the gold standard.
• C. PET scan: Not used for routine vestibular schwannoma diagnosis; expensive, low spatial resolution for small posterior fossa lesions, and typically reserved for oncologic staging/recurrence workup in select cases.
• D. BERA (auditory brainstem response) alone: Useful as a screening test (prolonged wave I–V interpeak latency is suggestive), but cannot confirm diagnosis or provide anatomic localization — MRI is still required for definitive diagnosis.

Exam trap:

The stem loads you with retrocochlear audiological clues (poor SDS, reflex decay) and a CT finding (IAC widening) to tempt you into picking CT as "sufficient" — but the answer is still MRI with contrast, since it remains the definitive, most sensitive test regardless of supportive findings elsewhere.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with Congenital cholesteatoma. According to Levenson's criteria, which factor is not used to diagnose this condition?
options: Whitish mass behind a normal tympanic membrane
Intact pars flaccida and pars tensa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Family history of Congenital Cholesteatoma

Levenson’s diagnostic criteria for congenital cholesteatoma are used to differentiate it from acquired cholesteatoma.

Diagnosis requires:

• Pearl-like whitish mass behind an intact, normal tympanic membrane
• Intact pars flaccida and pars tensa
• No history of tympanic membrane perforation, otorrhea, or ear surgery
• Exclusion of conditions such as canal atresia

Family history is NOT part of Levenson’s criteria — congenital cholesteatoma is typically sporadic, not inherited.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, dysphagia, and neck stiffness. On examination, there is a unilateral bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall. Despite initial management, the child rapidly deteriorates and develops chest pain and signs of mediastinitis. Which of the following anatomical pathways most likely explains the spread of infection?
options: Retropharyngeal space extending up to T4
Prevertebral space extending up to T4
Danger space extending from skull base to diaphragm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Danger space extending from skull base to diaphragm

Deep neck space infections spread along fascial planes—understanding these spaces helps predict complications and guide management.

• Retropharyngeal space:

• Extends from base of skull → T4
• Infection presents as unilateral posterior pharyngeal wall bulge
• Common in children (retropharyngeal lymph nodes)

• Danger space (between alar & prevertebral fascia):

• Extends from base of skull → diaphragm
• Allows rapid spread to mediastinum → mediastinitis (life-threatening)

• Prevertebral space:

• Extends to T4
• Produces diffuse midline swelling

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50 year old man presents with slow growing parotid mass for 8 months. The patient recently starts having difficulty closing the left eye. FNAC shows pleomorphic adenoma with atypia. Which of the following is the best treatment for this extent of tumor?
options: Superficial parotidectomy with resection of facial nerve and immediate cable grafting.
Total parotidectomy with resection of facial nerve and immediate cable grafting.
Radiotherapy done as there is no use of surgical intervention due to the widespread tumor extension.
Total conservation parotidectomy preserving the facial nerve as it may regenerate and become functional again after a few days of rest.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total parotidectomy with resection of facial nerve and immediate cable grafting.

A long-standing, slow-growing parotid mass with new-onset facial nerve dysfunction (difficulty closing the eye) is highly suspicious for malignant transformation or primary parotid malignancy. Although pleomorphic adenoma is benign, the presence of atypia on FNAC plus facial nerve palsy suggests carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma or another invasive malignancy with perineural involvement.

In malignant parotid tumors:

• Surgery is the mainstay.
• The goal is complete oncologic clearance (R0 resection).
• If the facial nerve is involved or non-functional preoperatively, it should be resected en bloc with the tumor, followed by immediate reconstruction (cable grafting) to restore facial continuity.

Because malignancy may involve both superficial and deep lobes, and facial nerve involvement indicates extensive disease, the preferred surgery is Total parotidectomy with facial nerve resection and immediate cable grafting

Other options are incorrect because:

• Superficial parotidectomy is inadequate for suspected malignant/invasive disease.
• Radiotherapy alone is not definitive primary treatment for resectable parotid malignancy.
• Nerve preservation is inappropriate when there is preoperative palsy, as it implies tumor infiltration—waiting for “nerve rest” will not restore function.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with dysphagia and a sensation of a lump in the throat. On examination, a mass is noted on the posterior pharyngeal wall. Which anatomical structure primarily forms the inner layer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pharyngobasilar Fascia

The pharyngeal wall is composed of distinct layers from inside to outside.

Layers of pharynx (inner → outer)

1. Mucosa
2. Submucosa
3. Pharyngobasilar fascia → inner fibrous layer (forms inner structural framework)
4. Muscular layer (constrictors and longitudinal muscles)
5. Buccopharyngeal fascia → outer fascial covering

Other options

A. Investing fascia → neck fascia

B. Buccopharyngeal fascia → outer covering of pharynx

C. Prevertebral fascia → posterior boundary of retropharyngeal space

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with sudden onset hearing loss in one ear after using cotton buds daily. Otoscopic examination reveals a hard, dark mass completely occluding the external auditory canal. He has no pain or discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Removal with ear probe without preparation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cerumenolytic drops followed by syringing

Impacted cerumen is a common cause of reversible conductive hearing loss and should be managed using a safe, stepwise approach.

• Etiology: Often due to self-cleaning attempts (cotton buds) pushing wax deeper
• Symptoms: Hearing loss, ear fullness, tinnitus (usually painless)

Management principle:

1.   Soften wax first → cerumenolytics (oil, glycerin, hydrogen peroxide)

2.  Then remove → syringing or manual extraction

Precautions:

• Use body-temperature water to avoid vertigo
• Avoid syringing in:

• Perforated tympanic membrane
• Active infection

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old male presents with dizziness and involuntary eye movements. Examination reveals non-fatiguable nystagmus that changes direction with gaze and is not suppressed by visual fixation. There are no significant auditory symptoms. What is the most likely cause of his nystagmus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brainstem stroke

Features of central vertigo (brainstem or cerebellar lesion) must be distinguished from peripheral vestibular disorders.

Central nystagmus characteristics:

• Non-fatigable
• Direction-changing with gaze
• Not suppressed by visual fixation
• May be vertical or multidirectional
• Usually no auditory symptoms
• Often associated with neurological deficits

Peripheral nystagmus characteristics (BPPV, Ménière, vestibular neuritis):

• Fatigable
• Unidirectional
• Suppressed by visual fixation
• Often associated with tinnitus or hearing loss
• Severe vertigo but fewer CNS signs

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient is diagnosed with glottic carcinoma involving the right side of the vocal cord. The tumor extends to the supraglottis with impaired vocal cord mobility. What is the most appropriate primary treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vertical hemilaryngectomy

Vertical hemilaryngectomy is the preferred primary treatment for selected unilateral glottic cancers with extension to supraglottis and impaired vocal cord mobility, provided the disease remains confined to one side without cartilage invasion or distant spread.

Treatment selection in glottic carcinoma depends on stage and cord mobility:

• Early T1–T2 with mobile cord: Radiotherapy or endoscopic laser excision
• Unilateral disease with impaired mobility (T2–early T3): Vertical hemilaryngectomy
• Bilateral involvement, cartilage invasion, or advanced T3–T4: Total laryngectomy

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient with sensorineural hearing loss undergoes hearing tests. The examiner performs the Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) Test and the Schwabach Test. What are the expected findings of the duration of both tests?
options: ABC - Shorter, Schwabach - Same as Examiner
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Both are Shorter

Tuning fork tests comparing bone conduction duration help distinguish type of hearing loss.

| Test | Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SNHL) | Conductive Hearing Loss (CHL)

| ---- | --------------------------------- | -----------------------------

| Absolute Bone Conduction (ABC) | Shortened | Normal or relatively prolonged

| Schwabach Test | Shortened (patient < examiner) | Prolonged (patient > examiner)

| Reason | Cochlear/nerve defect → ↓ perception | Bone conduction preserved, air conduction reduced

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with acute onset vertigo without hearing loss. On examination, she has unsteady gait and horizontal nystagmus. Audiometry is normal. Vestibular testing reveals: • Absent cervical VEMP (cVEMP) on the right side • Normal ocular VEMP (oVEMP) bilaterally Which of the following is the most likely site of lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right inferior vestibular nerve

Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potentials (VEMP) are used to localize vestibular pathway lesions by differentiating superior vs inferior vestibular nerve involvement.

• cVEMP assesses:

o    Saccule → Inferior vestibular nerve → SCM muscle

o    Absent cVEMP → Inferior vestibular nerve lesion
• oVEMP assesses:

o    Utricle → Superior vestibular nerve → ocular muscles

o    Normal oVEMP → Superior vestibular nerve intact
• Clinical localization principle:

o    Absent cVEMP + normal oVEMP = Inferior vestibular nerve involvement

o    Absent oVEMP + preserved cVEMP = Superior vestibular nerve involvement

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman presents to the ENT clinic with complaints of vertigo. Along with vertigo, she reports diplopia (double vision) and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and is noted to have nystagmus on examination. There is no associated hearing loss. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Central vestibular disorder

• The combination of vertigo with diplopia, dysphagia, and nystagmus — without hearing loss — points to involvement of the brainstem/cerebellum rather than the inner ear, since these additional cranial nerve and long-tract signs (extraocular muscles, lower cranial nerves for swallowing) indicate a central cause.
• Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière's disease) typically present with isolated vertigo ± hearing loss/tinnitus, but do NOT cause diplopia or dysphagia, since the inner ear pathology doesn't affect brainstem cranial nerve nuclei.
• Ocular vertigo results from a mismatch between visual, vestibular (labyrinthine), and somatosensory inputs that normally coordinate to maintain balance — it isn't associated with cranial nerve deficits like dysphagia.
• Psychogenic vertigo is considered in the context of anxiety or emotional stress, and characteristically lacks objective findings such as nystagmus or hearing loss.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 58-year-old man comes to the OPD due to muffled hearing and difficulty understanding speech over the past several weeks. Medical history includes hypertension, coronary artery disease, ischemic cardiomyopathy, and chronic kidney disease. He has had repeated hospitalizations for acute heart failure decompensation and was recently treated for acute prostatitis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Otoscopic examination shows no abnormalities. Audiometry reveals symmetric high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Furosemide

According to the given scenario, likely that the patient was treated with such a drug during hospitalisation and treatment of CHF that led to SNHL.

Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) can cause ototoxicity, leading to bilateral symmetric high-frequency SNHL, especially in patients with renal failure or those receiving high IV doses.

• Inhibit Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ transporter in stria vascularis
• Disrupt endolymph production and cochlear hair cell function
• Results in reversible or sometimes permanent SNHL

Drug comparison:

• Aspirin → tinnitus, reversible hearing loss
• Ciprofloxacin → rarely ototoxic
• Sacubitril-valsartan → no ototoxicity
• Furosemide → classic cause of ototoxic SNHL.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of increasing swelling in his left cheek and recurrent oral ulcers for 1 year. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. Examination shows firm, nontender swelling above the angle of jaw. USG guided biopsy shows adenoid cystic carcinoma. A left sided total parotidectomy is performed. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
options: Hyperesthesia of the left ear lobe
Impaired taste of the posterior 1/3 of the tongue
Flushing of the right cheek while eating
Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead

The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland and divides into its branches inside it (classic “pes anserinus”). So when you remove the gland (especially total parotidectomy), you can injure:

• Temporal branch: loss of forehead wrinkling, eyebrow droop
• Zygomatic branch: inability to close eye
• Buccal branch: weak upper lip movement
• Marginal mandibular: asymmetric smile
• Cervical: platysma weakness

Other Options:

A) Hyperesthesia of the left ear lobe: Parotid surgery actually risks loss of sensation (hypoesthesia) of the ear lobe due to injury of the great auricular nerve(C2–C3). Hyperesthesia (increased sensation) isn’t the classic complication.

B) Impaired taste of posterior 1/3 of tongue: Posterior 1/3 taste = CN IX (glossopharyngeal).That’s not running through the parotid like CN VII does.

C) Flushing of the right cheek while eating: That’s Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating/flushing) — due to aberrant reinnervation of sweat glands by parasympathetic fibers after parotidectomy.

Two issues:

1. It would occur on the same side as surgery (left), not right.
2. Also, the question says “greatest risk” — facial nerve injury is the big one in total parotidectomy.

✅ D) Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead because wrinkling the forehead = frontal branch of the facial nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with ear discomfort and reduced hearing for 2 days following an upper respiratory tract infection. Otoscopy shows a retracted tympanic membrane with an air-fluid level behind it, without marked fever or severe systemic symptoms. What is the most likely underlying cause?
options: Barotrauma due to rapid pressure changes
Increased secretory activity of the middle-ear mucosa
Biofilm formation in the middle ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eustachian tube dysfunction

The child has otitis media with effusion (OME), also called serous otitis media or glue ear.

Following a common cold, inflammation and edema obstruct the Eustachian tube, preventing proper ventilation of the middle ear. Absorption of trapped air creates negative pressure, causing:

• Retraction of the tympanic membrane
• Transudation of fluid into the middle ear
• Conductive hearing loss
• A visible air-fluid level or bubbles behind the tympanic membrane

Children are particularly susceptible because their Eustachian tubes are shorter, more horizontal, and functionally immature.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. Barotrauma follows air travel, diving, or sudden pressure changes.
• B. Increased mucosal secretion contributes to effusion but is secondary to impaired Eustachian tube ventilation.
• C. Biofilms may contribute to chronic or recurrent middle-ear disease but are not the primary mechanism in this acute post-viral presentation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is admitted with high fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The child was recently treated for acute otitis media. Lumbar puncture shows a predominance of polymorphs, protein level is raised, sugars reduced and chlorides diminished. Otoscopic examination reveals bulging of the tympanic membrane. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention to manage the underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringotomy

In a child with acute bacterial meningitis secondary to acute otitis media, the most important immediate step is drainage of the middle ear infection. Myringotomy is the treatment of choice because it:

• Provides immediate drainage of infected middle ear pus
• Reduces bacterial load and intracranial spread
• Allows culture of middle ear pus for targeted antibiotics
• Relieves pressure from bulging tympanic membrane

Radical/modified radical mastoidectomy → indicated only if mastoiditis, abscess, or complications persist despite myringotomy + antibiotics

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with a midline swelling over the nasal bridge since birth. The swelling is soft, non-tender, and increases in size when the child cries or strains. There is no transillumination. On performing a clinical maneuver, the swelling becomes more prominent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Encephalocele

Fürstenberg test is used to identify intracranial communication in congenital midline nasal masses.

Key points:

• Positive Fürstenberg test (swelling increases with crying/straining):

• Indicates connection with intracranial cavity
• Most suggestive of encephalocele

• Negative Fürstenberg test:

• No intracranial communication
• Seen in nasal glioma and dermoid cyst

• Clinical importance:

• Do NOT biopsy or aspirate a suspected encephalocele due to risk of CSF leak and meningitis
• Imaging (CT/MRI) is mandatory before intervention

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with a midline swelling over the nasal bridge, present since birth. The swelling is soft, non-tender, and increases in size when the child cries or strains. It does not transilluminate. On performing a clinical maneuver, the swelling becomes more prominent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Encephalocele

The clinical maneuver described is the Fürstenberg test — compressing the internal jugular veins (or having the child cry/strain/perform Valsalva) increases intracranial venous pressure, which is transmitted to any mass in direct communication with the intracranial cavity, causing it to enlarge or become tenser.

Key points:

• Positive Fürstenberg test → mass communicates with the intracranial/subarachnoid space → most consistent with encephalocele.
• Negative Fürstenberg test → no intracranial communication → favors dermoid cyst or nasal glioma.

Why the other options are wrong:

• A. Dermoid cyst: Midline, but classically shows a punctum with a hair tuft; Fürstenberg negative (no CSF connection).
• B. Nasal glioma: Firm, non-compressible mass; also Fürstenberg negative, since its intracranial stalk typically involutes.
• D. Hemangioma: Vascular lesion with a proliferative-involuting course, often with a color change; unrelated to intracranial communication.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with congenital severe sensorineural hearing loss. Imaging shows a normal bony labyrinth, but histopathology reveals degeneration of the organ of Corti and saccule, with preservation of the utricle and semicircular canals. Which of the following inner ear malformations best explains this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scheibe aplasia

Scheibe aplasia (cochleosaccular dysplasia) is the most common congenital membranous labyrinth malformation causing severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

Key differentiating points among inner ear malformations:

• Scheibe aplasia: Membranous defect of cochlea + saccule (most common; severe SNHL)
• Mondini dysplasia: Incomplete cochlear development (1.5 turns) with bony abnormality
• Michel aplasia: Complete absence of inner ear (most severe)
• Alexander dysplasia: Basal turn cochlear degeneration → high-frequency hearing loss

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with unilateral microtia and external auditory canal atresia. Hearing assessment shows conductive hearing loss in the affected ear, with normal hearing in the contralateral ear. What is the most appropriate next step to optimize speech and auditory development?
options: Delay all intervention until auricular reconstruction at adolescence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone conduction hearing device (BAHA) placement

In microtia/anotia with EAC atresia, the inner ear (cochlea) is typically normal, and the hearing loss is purely conductive, arising from the absent/malformed external canal and middle ear structures. The guiding principle is: restore hearing early, correct cosmesis later.

Key learning points:

• Early auditory rehabilitation is critical for speech-language acquisition, cognitive development, and social development — delays here have lasting impact.
• A bone conduction device (BAHA on a softband in young children, or bone-anchored implant later) bypasses the atretic canal and middle ear entirely, transmitting sound directly via bone conduction to the normally functioning cochlea.

Recommended management timeline:

• Early childhood (as soon as diagnosed): Bone conduction hearing device (softband BAHA) — non-surgical, reversible, and immediately restores functional hearing.
• \~6–10 years: Auricular reconstruction (staged costal cartilage grafting or prosthesis).
• Atresiaplasty (canal reconstruction): Reserved for select cases with favorable anatomy on imaging (e.g., good middle ear pneumatization on CT), and typically deferred until after auricular reconstruction to avoid compromising the reconstructed ear's blood supply/framework.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Delay all intervention until auricular reconstruction at adolescence: Delaying all intervention risks permanent speech/language delay; auditory input in early childhood is time-sensitive.
• B. Immediate surgical canal reconstruction (atresiaplasty): Immediate atresiaplasty is not first-line — it's technically demanding in a young child, carries risks to nearby structures (facial nerve, TMJ), and is usually deferred and selectively offered later.
• D. Cochlear implantation: Cochlear implantation is for sensorineural hearing loss; this child has a conductive loss with a presumably normal cochlea, so it's not indicated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with unilateral microtia with external auditory canal atresia. Hearing assessment reveals conductive hearing loss on the affected side, while the opposite ear is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management to ensure optimal speech and auditory development?
options: Delay all intervention until auricular reconstruction at adolescence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone conduction hearing device (BAHA) placement

Management of microtia/anotia with external auditory canal atresia is guided by the principle of early auditory rehabilitation before cosmetic correction.

Key learning points:

• Hearing loss is typically conductive → inner ear function is usually normal
• Early hearing restoration is critical for:

• Speech and language development
• Cognitive and social development

Management sequence:

• Early childhood:

• Bone conduction hearing devices (e.g., BAHA/soft band) → bypass external/middle ear

• Later (≈6–10 years):

• Auricular reconstruction
• ± Canal reconstruction (atresiaplasty) in selected cases

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the neck undergoes radical neck dissection. Which of the following structures is typically spared during this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digastric muscle

Classical Radical Neck Dissection:

Removes:

• All cervical lymph nodes (levels I–V)
• Sternocleidomastoid muscle
• Internal jugular vein
• Spinal accessory nerve
• Submandibular gland ± tail of parotid

Structures usually preserved unless directly invaded:

• Digastric muscle
• Carotid artery
• Vagus nerve
• Hypoglossal nerve

Modified Radical Neck Dissection Preserves one or more of:

• Spinal accessory nerve
• SCM
• IJV

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of disorientation and slurred speech. He has a 10-year history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. His blood pressure is 210/110 mmHg, and pulse is 90/min. Once the patient is stabilized, an MRI of the brain is performed, which shows an infarct of the left precentral gyrus involving the region that supplies the facial nerve. Given the MRI findings, which of the following neurological findings would most be expected?
options: Loss of taste in the posterior third of the right half of the tongue
Flattening of the right nasolabial fold
Decreased lacrimation of the left eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Flattening of the right nasolabial fold

A lesion in the left precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) affecting the facial area causes a contralateral upper motor neuron (UMN) facial palsy.

• Facial nucleus has bilateral cortical input for upper face
• Lower face receives contralateral cortical input only
• UMN lesion → weakness of contralateral lower face with forehead sparing

Expected finding:

• Right lower facial weakness
• Flattening of right nasolabial fold
• Forehead wrinkling preserved
• Eye closure preserved

Why other options are wrong:

A. Taste loss in posterior 1/3 of right half of tongue → glossopharyngeal nerve

C. Decreased lacrimation of left eye/D. Hyperacusis of left ear → LMN facial nerve lesion

• Cortical stroke causes UMN, not LMN features

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension presents with massive posterior epistaxis. Initial management — including Trotter's method, cauterization, and anterior and posterior nasal packing — has failed. Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) was performed, but bleeding persists. What is the next best step in management?
options: Maxillary artery ligation via Caldwell-Luc approach
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maxillary artery ligation via Caldwell-Luc approach

Management of intractable posterior epistaxis follows a stepwise escalation from distal to proximal vascular control:

1. Conservative measures: Trotter's method (postural + pressure), cauterization
2. Nasal packing: Anterior, then posterior (or combined) packing
3. Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL): First-line surgical option, targeting the terminal branch supplying the posterior/lateral nasal wall
4. Maxillary artery ligation (transantral, via Caldwell-Luc approach) — if SPA ligation fails, more proximal control of the same vascular territory is obtained by ligating the internal maxillary artery before it gives off the sphenopalatine branch
5. External carotid artery ligation — reserved as a last resort if maxillary artery ligation also fails, providing even more proximal control

Why the other options are wrong:

• A. Anterior ethmoidal artery ligation: Relevant for anterior/superior epistaxis (ethmoidal artery territory), not posterior bleeds from the sphenopalatine distribution.
• B. External carotid artery ligation: A valid next step, but only after maxillary artery ligation has also failed — it's further down the escalation ladder, not the immediate next step.
• D. Repeat anterior packing: Already failed once; repeating a failed conservative measure is not appropriate when surgical ligation is already underway.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension presents with massive posterior epistaxis. Initial management including Trotter’s method, cauterization, anterior and posterior nasal packing has failed. Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation was performed, but bleeding persists. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
options: Maxillary artery ligation via Caldwell-Luc approach
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maxillary artery ligation via Caldwell-Luc approach

Management of refractory epistaxis follows a stepwise escalation from local control to proximal arterial ligation.

• After failure of anterior + posterior nasal packing, the first surgical step is:

• Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL)

• If bleeding persists after SPA ligation:

• Proceed to maxillary artery ligation (more proximal control)

• Further escalation:

• External carotid artery ligation

• Anterior ethmoidal artery ligation:

• Reserved for anterior epistaxis, not posterior bleeds

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with hearing issues. During the examination, the audiologist performs the Bing Test and Gelle’s Test to assess the type of hearing loss. What would be indicative of conductive hearing loss in the Bing and Gelle tests?
options: Bing: No change; Gelle: No change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bing: No change; Gelle: No change

Bing and Gelle tests are tuning fork tests used to differentiate conductive hearing loss (CHL) from normal or sensorineural hearing loss.

Bing Test

• Based on occlusion effect
• Normal/SNHL: Sound becomes louder when ear canal is occluded (positive Bing)
• Conductive loss: Already has occlusion effect → no change in loudness (negative Bing)

Gelle’s Test

• Assesses stapes mobility by applying pressure in external canal
• Normal/SNHL: Increased pressure reduces sound perception (positive Gelle)
• Conductive loss (e.g., otosclerosis, ossicular fixation): Stapes already fixed → no change in sound (negative Gelle)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with acute-onset headache accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and a spinning sensation. She first noticed these symptoms the previous day upon waking, and they have persisted without improvement since. She denies ear pain, hearing loss, fever, or chills. She was recently started on hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril for hypertension, and has a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and pulse is 86/min. With the patient lying still, there is pure rotatory nystagmus, but no limb weakness or sensory deficits. On ambulation, her symptoms worsen and she veers/falls toward the left. Fingerstick glucose is 145 mg/dL, and CBC and electrolytes are unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Noncontrast CT scan of the head
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Noncontrast CT scan of the head

• Although this presentation might initially resemble peripheral vertigo (vestibular neuritis) with pure rotatory nystagmus and gait imbalance, several red flags point toward a possible central (posterior circulation) cause: significant vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia), an associated severe headache, and symptoms that are continuous and unimproving for over 24 hours rather than brief/positional.
• In a patient with vascular risk factors and acute, persistent vertigo with headache, the priority is to rule out a cerebellar or brainstem stroke/hemorrhage before attributing symptoms to a benign peripheral cause — an initial noncontrast CT is done emergently to exclude hemorrhage, even though MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is more sensitive for early posterior fossa ischemic stroke.

Why the others are wrong?

• A. Ambulatory ECG monitoring: Would be considered if a cardioembolic arrhythmia (e.g., atrial fibrillation) were suspected as a source of stroke — but that's a secondary step after neuroimaging.
• B. Discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide: Would be relevant if this were orthostatic hypotension or electrolyte disturbance — but her BP is normal and electrolytes are unremarkable.
• D. Reassurance with meclizine: Would be appropriate for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) — but BPPV causes brief, positional episodes (seconds), not a continuous, unrelenting vertigo lasting over a day, and would not typically present with headache.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction, facial swelling, and proptosis. Imaging reveals a malignancy in the sinonasal region. According to Lederman’s classification, which of the following tumor locations is categorized as mesostructural?
options: Extension to the respiratory part of the nasal cavity
Extending to sphenoid sinus and the orbit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extension to the respiratory part of the nasal cavity

Lederman classification divides maxillary/sinonasal tumors based on anatomical spread into suprastructure, mesostructure, and infrastructure, which helps predict prognosis and surgical planning.

| Category | Anatomical Involvement | Structures Included | Prognosis

| -------- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | ---------

| Suprastructure | Superior extension | Orbit, ethmoid sinus, frontal sinus, sphenoid sinus, cribriform plate, skull base | Worst prognosis

| Mesostructure | Central/respiratory part | Respiratory part of nasal cavity, turbinates, medial wall of maxilla | Intermediate prognosis

| Infrastructure | Inferior extension | Floor of maxillary sinus, hard palate, alveolar process, upper teeth | Best prognosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with a long history of using chewing tobacco comes to the office for follow up of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the oral cavity. A month ago, the patient was diagnosed with SCC of the left lateral tongue. He underwent resection, the surgical specimen showed clear margins, and he started additional treatment. The patient recently noticed a second ulcerative lesion on the right lateral tongue. Biopsy is performed and it also shows SCC. The second tumor most likely arose from which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Field cancerization

• Long history of chewing tobacco
• First SCC on left lateral tongue
• Resection with clear margins
• Now develops second SCC on right lateral tongue

Mechanism of field cancerization: Chronic exposure to carcinogens (like tobacco) causes:

• Multiple independent premalignant areas
• Separate tumors arising in different locations

So the entire oral mucosa becomes a “field” of genetically altered cells.

This explains why patients with head & neck SCC often develop multiple synchronous tumors or new primary tumors months/years later, even after clean margins. This is exactly what happened here.

Other Options:

Option A. Chemotherapy-induced malignancy:

• Chemo-induced second cancers usually take years to develop
• (And this patient was just treated)
• Hence, not the answer.

Option C. Hematogenous spread: If this were metastasis:

• It would show same tumor spreading
• Typically to lung, bone, liver
• Not a new ulcerative lesion on the opposite tongue

Hence, this is a new primary lesion, not metastasis.

Option D. Immunologic privilege: Seen in areas like eye, testis and brain. Not relevant here.

Hints in questions like these:

• Heavy smoker or tobacco chewer
• Multiple head & neck SCCs
• Separate lesions

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with persistent foul-smelling otorrhea from the right ear. Otoscopic examination reveals a small perforation in the pars flaccida with surrounding retraction. There is no history of acute pain or fever. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Prolonged topical antibiotics with nasal decongestants
Intravenous antibiotics followed by delayed reassessment
Type I tympanoplasty after infection control
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tympanomastoid exploration

Pars flaccida perforation with foul-smelling otorrhea and retraction is highly suggestive of atticoantral (unsafe) chronic suppurative otitis media, often associated with cholesteatoma.

• Atticoantral disease = bone-eroding cholesteatoma
• Risk of intracranial complications (meningitis, brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis)
• Medical therapy alone is not definitive
• Tympanomastoid exploration (mastoidectomy) for removal of cholesteatoma and disease clearance is the most appropriate management.

Why other options are wrong

A. Prolonged topical antibiotics with nasal decongestants: only temporary control; cholesteatoma persists

B. IV antibiotics followed by delayed reassessment: not primary treatment without acute complication

C. Type I tympanoplasty after infection control: for safe (tubotympanic) CSOM, not unsafe disease

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 74-year-old woman comes to the office due to several days of right ear pain. This morning she had 2 episodes of dizziness and almost fell. The patient is currently taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection. She has had no subjective fever, vision loss, or headaches. Temperature is 37⁰C (98.6⁰F), blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. Ear examination reveals several erythematous vesicles in the right external auditory canal with no drainage. The tympanic membrane is visible and intact. There is mild right-sided facial droop. The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Varicella zoster virus

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is caused by reactivation of varicella zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve.

Classic triad:

• Painful vesicular rash in external auditory canal/pinna
• Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy
• Possible vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss

Management:

• Acyclovir/valacyclovir
• Corticosteroids
• Eye protection

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle aged female came to the OPD with the complaint of a slowly growing, painless firm mass in her right parotid region for over 2 years. She notes recent rapid enlargement over the last 1-2 months. An ultrasound is done for the same and that reveals a heterogenous hypoechoic lesion in the superficial lobe. A subsequent FNAC reveals the presence of epithelial and myxochondroid stromal elements. She is counselled about the risks associated with this tumor. Which of the following is the most concerning complication if treated inadequately?
options: Early facial nerve paralysis due to perineural infiltration
High grade transformation into adenocarcinoma with early nodal metastasis
Recurrence due to the presence of pseudopodia that causes tumor spill during surgery
Multiloculated cystic spaces with oncocytic epithelium causing high bilateral recurrence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Recurrence due to the presence of pseudopodia that causes tumor spill during surgery

This patient has pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) of the parotid:

• Slow-growing painless parotid mass
• FNAC: epithelial + myxochondroid stromal elements (classic)

Most concerning complication if inadequately treated is Recurrence due to pseudopodia and tumor spillage during surgery. Therefore, Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation should be done. Avoid simple enucleation.

Why other options are wrong

A. Early facial nerve ~~palsy~~ paralysis due to perineural infiltration → suggests malignancy

B. High-grade transformation into adenocarcinoma with early nodal metastasis → rare (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), long-term risk

D. Multiloculated cystic spaces with oncocytic epithelium causing high bilateral recurrence → Warthin tumor

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged woman develops hoarseness following a total thyroidectomy. On laryngoscopic examination, there is complete vocal cord palsy on left side. What is the best management in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Speech therapy, medialization of cord

Unilateral vocal cord paralysis following thyroidectomy is most commonly due to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and leads to hoarseness due to a paramedian, immobile vocal cord.

Best management: Speech therapy + medialization of vocal cord

• Injection laryngoplasty or thyroplasty
• Improves glottic closure and voice quality
• Prevents aspiration

Why not others:

• Tracheostomy → only for bilateral paralysis with airway compromise
• Lateralization → done in bilateral paralysis to improve airway
• Gutzmann maneuver → used in functional voice disorders

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A newborn undergoes transient evoked otoacoustic emission (TEOAE) screening within 48 hours of birth. The result is absent bilaterally. According to the neonatal hearing screening protocol, what is the next best step?
options: Clean the external auditory canal and repeat TEOAE after 7–10 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clean the external auditory canal and repeat TEOAE after 7–10 days

In newborn hearing screening, an absent TEOAE within the first 48 hours is often due to transient external or middle ear factors such as vernix, debris, or middle ear fluid rather than true sensorineural hearing loss.

Next best step: Clean the external auditory canal and repeat TEOAE after 7–10 days before proceeding to definitive testing.

❌ Refer directly for BERA – Too early. You repeat screening first.

❌ Diagnose congenital SNHL – Way too premature.

❌ Start hearing aids – Absolutely not without confirmatory testing.

Screening protocol logic:

• Initial failed OAE → repeat screening after clearing canal/debris
• Persistent failure → perform BERA (ABR) for confirmation
• Do not diagnose congenital SNHL or start hearing aids until confirmatory testing

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient develops recurrent peritonsillar abscess despite adequate drainage and antibiotics. What is the preferred timing of definitive tonsillectomy?
options: Six weeks after resolution of infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Six weeks after resolution of infection

• Interval tonsillectomy is performed 4–6 weeks after the acute episode resolves.
• Immediate ("hot") tonsillectomy is rarely performed because of increased operative difficulty and bleeding risk.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient has unilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss (left ear). Tuning fork tests are performed. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Rinne test will be positive in the affected ear 2. Weber test will lateralize to the right ear 3. False negative Rinne test may occur in this patient 4. Masking of the opposite ear may be required to interpret Rinne correctly 5. Schwabach test will be prolonged in the affected ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Tuning fork tests can be misleading in severe unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) due to cross hearing, making recognition of pitfalls essential.

Key learning points:

• Rinne test in SNHL:

• Usually positive (AC > BC)
• But may appear false negative in severe unilateral SNHL

• Mechanism of false negative Rinne:

• Bone conduction from the affected ear is perceived by the normal ear via skull transmission

• Weber test:

• Lateralizes to the better (normal) ear in SNHL

• Schwabach test:

• Shortened in SNHL

• Masking:

• Required to prevent cross hearing and misinterpretation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with bilateral hearing loss with worsened right ear hearing loss. Based on the findings the surgeon recommends stapedectomy as a final resort to the problem. What would be the findings of tuning fork tests based on which the doctor has recommended stapedectomy?
options: Rinne’s test positive, Weber’s test lateralized to left ear
Rinne’s test positive, Weber’s test lateralized to right ear
Rinne’s test negative, Weber’s test lateralized to left ear
Rinne’s test negative, Weber’s test lateralized to right ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rinne’s test negative, Weber’s test lateralized to right ear

Stapedectomy is performed in otosclerosis, which causes conductive hearing loss due to stapes footplate fixation.

Tuning fork findings in conductive hearing loss (otosclerosis):

• Rinne test: Negative (BC > AC) in affected ear
• Weber test: Lateralizes to affected ear (conductive loss)

In this case:

• Bilateral hearing loss, worse in right ear
• Conductive pattern → Weber lateralizes to right (worse ear)
• Rinne negative in affected ear

→ Suggests otosclerosis requiring stapedectomy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of the sudden vertigo when his head is in one particular position. The physician performs a maneuver to relieve the patient's symptoms. Arrange the steps of that procedure in the proper sequence: a. Affected ear is facing up at 90° rotation b. Head turned 45° to the affected side and head in hanging position c. Head turned forward and chin brought down to 20° d. Whole body and head rotated to a lateral recumbent position e. Sitting position with head turned to unaffected side by 45°
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. b, a, d, e, c

The described maneuver is the Epley maneuver, used to treat posterior canal BPPV, the most common cause of positional vertigo. BPPV occurs due to displaced otoliths (canaliths) in the posterior semicircular canal. The Epley maneuver sequentially repositions these particles back into the utricle using gravity.

Correct sequence:

b. Head turned 45° to affected side and placed in hanging position (Dix-Hallpike position)

a. Rotate head 90° so affected ear faces up

d. Rotate whole body to lateral recumbent position

e. Bring patient to sitting with head turned to unaffected side

c. Head brought forward (chin down)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of loss of wrinkles on forehead, inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I/L Facial LMN

Lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy causes ipsilateral paralysis of the entire face, including the forehead and eye closure. LMN facial nerve palsy features:

• Loss of forehead wrinkles
• Inability to close eye
• Drooling of saliva
• Deviation of mouth to opposite side
• Entire ipsilateral face affected (upper + lower face)

UMN vs LMN facial palsy:

• UMN lesion: Forehead spared (bilateral cortical supply)
• LMN lesion: Forehead involved (complete ipsilateral paralysis)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with vertigo and imbalance. Evaluation reveals dysfunction of a structure that detects linear acceleration and head tilt, with otoliths identified overlying its sensory epithelium. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Macula of utricle and saccule

The vestibular system is functionally divided by the type of motion each structure detects:

• Macula of utricle and saccule — detects linear acceleration and head tilt (gravity). The sensory epithelium is overlain by the otolithic membrane, embedded with otoliths (otoconia) — calcium carbonate crystals whose inertia-driven displacement deflects hair cell stereocilia in response to linear movement or gravity.
• Crista ampullaris (semicircular canals) — detects angular/rotational movement; it lacks otoliths, instead using the gelatinous cupula deflected by endolymph flow.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Crista ampullaris of semicircular canals: Detects rotation, not linear acceleration; no otoliths present.
• C. Organ of Corti: Auditory structure (hearing), unrelated to vestibular/balance function.
• D. Stria vascularis: Produces endolymph and maintains the endocochlear potential; also an auditory (cochlear), not vestibular, structure.

High-yield line:

• Otoliths + linear/gravity sensing → macula (utricle/saccule).
• No otoliths + rotational sensing → crista ampullaris.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with vertigo associated with horizontal nystagmus. The slow component is towards the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right purulent labyrinthitis

The direction of the slow phase of nystagmus indicates the side of the lesion, while the fast phase (named direction of nystagmus) beats toward the more active labyrinth.

• Destructive lesions (e.g., purulent labyrinthitis) → affected labyrinth becomes hypoactive
• Brain perceives opposite side dominance → fast phase toward normal side
• Therefore, slow phase toward affected side

In this case:

• Slow component toward right → lesion on right side
• Purulent labyrinthitis = destructive lesion → nystagmus to opposite side → Consistent with right purulent labyrinthitis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a lesion involving the right lateral lemniscus presents with hearing difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely clinical finding?
options: Complete hearing loss in the right ear
Complete hearing loss in the left ear
Partial hearing loss in both ears
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Partial hearing loss in both ears

The central auditory pathway is bilaterally represented from the level of the cochlear nuclei onward:

• Cochlea → Cochlear nuclei → bilateral crossing (trapezoid body) → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex
• Because decussation occurs early (predominantly at the trapezoid body, with contributions continuing at multiple levels), each cochlear nucleus projects to both the ipsilateral and contralateral lateral lemniscus/superior olivary complex. This means each ear's signal is represented in both hemispheres beyond the brainstem entry point.

Clinical significance:

• Peripheral lesions (cochlea, auditory nerve, cochlear nucleus itself) → unilateral, often complete hearing loss, since these are pre-decussation and represent only one ear.
• Central lesions (lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body, auditory cortex) → partial, bilateral hearing loss — true "cortical deafness" or complete central deafness is rare and requires bilateral lesions.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Complete hearing loss in the right ear, B. Complete hearing loss in the left ear: Complete unilateral deafness implies a peripheral (pre-crossing) lesion — cochlea, auditory nerve, or cochlear nucleus — not a lateral lemniscus lesion.
• D. No significant hearing deficit: A lesion at this level does produce a measurable deficit, just not complete or purely unilateral.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media reports that their hearing improves when the ear is discharging compared to when it is dry. Which phenomenon best explains this observation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Round window shielding effect

In chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), some patients report better hearing when ear discharge is present than when the ear is dry called as Round window shielding effect

•

Normally, sound transmission depends on pressure difference between oval and round windows

•

When discharge/pus fills middle ear:

o It may cover (shield) the round window

o Prevents dissipation of sound waves through round window

o Improves effective transmission to cochlea

• Result → temporary improvement in hearing during discharge

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with left side vestibular neuritis had a positive head impulse test. What does it indicate?
options: On rotating head to left, right saccade is seen
On rotating head toward right, left saccade is seen
On rotating head toward right, right saccade is seen
On rotating to the left, left saccade is seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. On rotating head to left, right saccade is seen

The Head Impulse Test (HIT) evaluates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and helps identify peripheral vestibular dysfunction.

- When the head is rapidly turned toward the affected side, a defective vestibular system fails to maintain gaze fixation, causing the eyes to move with the head.

- A corrective (catch-up) saccade then occurs toward the opposite side to refixate on the target.

In left vestibular neuritis:

• Left labyrinth is hypoactive
• When head is turned toward left (affected side) → VOR fails
• Eyes move with head
• Corrective saccade toward right to refocus → Positive HIT

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with long-standing Ménière’s disease suddenly collapses to the ground without loss of consciousness and without warning vertigo. He is able to get up immediately after the fall. What is the most likely explanation for this episode?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tumarkin otolithic crisis

•

Tumarkin otolithic crisis (drop attack) is a complication of long-standing Ménière’s disease characterized by sudden falls without warning, vertigo, or loss of consciousness, with immediate recovery.

•

Sudden stimulation or dysfunction of the otolithic organs (utricle/saccule) due to endolymphatic hydrops → abrupt loss of postural control → patient suddenly collapses.

Differentiation:

• Vertebrobasilar insufficiency → LOC or neurological deficits
• Tulio phenomenon → vertigo induced by loud sound
• Lermoyez syndrome → hearing improves after vertigo

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A person presents with a tongue ulcer persisting for 3 months. Upon examination, a lesion measuring 3.5 cm x 2.5 cm is observed, accompanied by a 12 mm depth of invasion on biopsy. No lymph node enlargement is detected. According to the 8th AJCC guidelines, what stage does this lesion correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage III

In the AJCC 8th edition TNM staging for oral cavity cancers, depth of invasion (DOI) is a critical factor in determining T stage, not just surface size.

T staging (oral tongue SCC):

• T1: ≤2 cm and DOI ≤5 mm
• T2: ≤2 cm with DOI 5–10 mm OR 2–4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm
• T3: >4 cm OR DOI >10 mm
• T4: Invasion of adjacent structures

In this case:

• Tumor size: 3.5 cm (would suggest T2)
• DOI: 12 mm (>10 mm) → upgrades to T3
• No nodes, no metastasis → N0 M0

Stage grouping (simplified)

• Stage I: T1 N0
• Stage II: T2 N0
• Stage III: T3 N0 or T1–T3 with N1
• Stage IVA: T4a or N2
• Stage IVB: T4b or N3
• Stage IVC: Any T, any N with distant metastasis

Thus: T3N0M0 = Stage III

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A woman develops wheezing after taking aspirin for a headache. Which statement is true about this condition?
options: Positive skin test for inhaled allergens
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Associated with ethmoid polyps

Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), also called Samter’s triad, is characterized by:

1. Asthma

2. Aspirin/NSAID sensitivity

3. Ethmoidal nasal polyps

What’s going on physiologically?

This is not IgE mediated.

❌ A type of extrinsic asthma:

• Extrinsic asthma is IgE-mediated allergy.
• Aspirin asthma is non-IgE mediated.

❌ Raised serum IgE levels: Not an IgE allergy.

❌ Positive skin test for inhaled allergens: Not allergy based.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A woman presents with a history of sudden spontaneous lacrimation upon salivation. The lesion behind this pathology is located at?
options: Facial nerve proximal to geniculate ganglion
Facial nerve at the vertical segment of ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Facial nerve proximal to geniculate ganglion

Crocodile tears syndrome (Bogorad syndrome) is characterized by lacrimation during eating due to aberrant regeneration of facial nerve fibers.

Site of lesion: Must be proximal to geniculate ganglion because:

• Greater petrosal nerve (lacrimal secretomotor) arises here
• Aberrant regeneration occurs before separation of lacrimal and salivary pathways

Why other options are incorrect:

• Chorda tympani lesion → affects salivation/taste only
• Stylomastoid foramen lesion → motor only (no parasympathetic)
• Vertical segment lesion → distal to lacrimal fibers

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young girl with chronic ear discharge presents with pain on eye movements and vertigo. She undergoes mastoidectomy, but postoperatively there is no relief — purulent ear discharge continues, and she subsequently develops sensorineural hearing loss. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute petrositis

Acute petrositis is a complication of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) in which infection spreads from the middle ear/mastoid to the petrous apex of the temporal bone — a site that mastoidectomy alone does not adequately drain, explaining why symptoms and discharge persist despite surgery.

This classically produces Gradenigo syndrome, a triad of:

1. Persistent otorrhea — ongoing middle ear infection
2. Retro-orbital/ocular pain on eye movement — from irritation of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) as it runs along the petrous apex (Dorello's canal region)
3. Diplopia from abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy — CN VI is also closely related to the petrous apex at Dorello's canal

Mapping to this case:

• Chronic ear discharge → underlying CSOM
• Pain on ocular movement → trigeminal nerve irritation at the petrous apex
• Persistent discharge despite mastoidectomy → infection has extended beyond the mastoid into the deeper petrous apex, which standard mastoidectomy doesn't address
• Vertigo + sensorineural hearing loss → spread of infection to the adjacent inner ear (labyrinth)

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Suppurative labyrinthitis: Would explain vertigo and SNHL, but doesn't account for the pain on ocular movement (no CN V/VI involvement) or the failure of mastoidectomy to relieve symptoms.
• C. Serous labyrinthitis: A milder, non-purulent inner ear irritation (typically from toxin diffusion rather than direct bacterial invasion); doesn't explain the ocular pain, and SNHL is usually absent or reversible, not established as here.
• D. Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis: Presents with spiking fever, "picket-fence" temperature pattern, and signs of raised ICP/septic emboli, not this specific ocular pain + vertigo + SNHL constellation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: According to Fisch's classification of glomus tumors, tumors with intracranial invasion measuring less than 2 cm are classified under which type?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type D1

Fisch classification is used to stage temporal bone paragangliomas (glomus tumors) based on extent of local and intracranial spread.

• Type A: Limited to middle ear (glomus tympanicum)
• Type B: Tympanomastoid involvement
