• Type C: Infralabyrinthine/apical involvement with carotid canal erosion
• Type D: Intracranial extension

• Type D1: Intracranial extension < 2 cm
• Type D2: Intracranial extension > 2 cm

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are correctly matched congenital pinna anomalies, except:
options: Mozart ear – Fusion of helix and antihelix
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wildermuth ear – Large pinna

Congenital anomalies of the pinna are classified based on size, shape, and developmental defects of auricular cartilage.

Correct associations:

• Microtia: Abnormally small or rudimentary pinna
• Bat ear (prominent ear): Underdeveloped/absent antihelix → protruding ear
• Mozart ear: Fusion of helix and antihelix (loss of normal folds)
• Wildermuth ear: Wildermuth's ear (or auricle) is a congenital ear deformity characterized by a backward-turned helix (upper outer rim) and a prominent antihelix (inner ridge).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following contribute to the formation of the nasal septum, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior nasal concha

The nasal septum forms the medial wall of the nasal cavity and is composed of both bony and cartilaginous components. Components of nasal septum:

• Perpendicular plate of ethmoid → superior bony part
• Vomer → posteroinferior bony part
• Septal cartilage → anterior cartilaginous part
• Contributions from nasal crest of maxilla & palatine (minor support)

Not part of septum:

• Inferior nasal concha → separate bone forming the lateral wall of nasal cavity (inferior turbinate)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An 82-year-old woman with Alzheimer dementia is brought to the OPD for evaluation of new-onset drooling. The patient lives in a nursing home and the staff noticed that she has been having liquid drip out of the right side of her mouth when they feed her. She has also been very tearful over the past 2 weeks, particularly at night when she wakes up crying and clutching her ear. The patient has type 2 diabetes mellites that requires insulin and multiple medications. Her last hemoglobin A1c was 8.5%. Temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination of the right ear canal shows granulation tissue with a surrounding white drainage in the floor of the canal. The tympanic membrane is clear and mobile to pneumatic otoscopy. There is facial asymmetry with some downward deviation of the right corner of the mouth. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

• This is Malignant otitis externa and m/c/c is pseudomonas aeroigenosa.
• This is invasive infection of external auditory canal → skull base osteomyelitis
• Classic risk factors: Elderly, Diabetic, Immunocompromised

Classical findings:

• Granulation tissue at the floor of the ear canal
• Severe pain out of proportion
• Cranial nerve involvement (drooling → facial nerve)

Other options:

Option A. Aspergillus niger:

• Causes otomycosis.
• Black fungal debris, Itching
• Not skull base infection / Not cranial nerve deficits.

Option B. Herpes zoster:

• Facial paralysis + vesicles
• No vesicles mentioned here.

Option D. Rhizopus:

• Causes mucormycosis
• Seen in uncontrolled diabetes but affects sinuses and orbit.
• Does Not cause isolated ear canal granulation tissue.
• Hence not the answer.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An ENT surgeon has difficulty locating the mastoid antrum due to the presence of Korner's septum. Which of the following sutures is persistent in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Petrosquamous suture

Körner’s septum (petrosquamous lamina) is a bony plate that may persist in the temporal bone and can obscure access to the mastoid antrum during mastoid surgery.

Clinical significance:

• Can make mastoid antrum difficult to locate
• Risk of incomplete mastoidectomy
• Important surgical landmark in otologic surgery

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: During a physiology demonstration, students are asked why the ossicular chain amplifies sound transmission. The lever advantage of the ossicular chain is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1.3:1

The handle of the malleus is approximately 1.3 times longer than the long process of the incus, producing the ossicular lever ratio of 1.3:1.

The middle ear provides an overall impedance-matching mechanism between air (low impedance) and the fluid-filled inner ear (high impedance), achieved through two separate mechanisms that are often mixed up:

1. Lever action of the ossicles (malleus-incus lever arm ratio) — contributes an amplification of \~1.3:1
2. Area ratio between the tympanic membrane and stapes footplate (the TM is much larger than the oval window) — contributes an amplification of \~17:1 (sometimes quoted as \~14–20:1 depending on the source, since the effective vibrating area of the TM vs. the total TM area is calculated differently)

Combined, these two mechanisms give a total amplification of \~22:1 (1.3 × 17 ≈ 22), which corresponds to roughly a 25–30 dB gain in sound pressure — this is what overcomes the impedance mismatch between air and inner ear fluid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: During diagnostic nasal endoscopy, the endoscope is advanced along a specific pathway that allows visualization of the medial surface of the middle turbinate, sphenoethmoidal recess, and the medial wall of the middle meatus. Which endoscopic path is being used in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Second endoscopic path

Second Endoscopic Path

• The endoscope is passed medial to the middle turbinate and directed posteriorly and superiorly.

Structures visualized:

1. Posterior part / medial surface of middle turbinate
2. Sphenoethmoidal recess → opening of sphenoid sinus (key clue)
3. Superior turbinate and superior meatus
4. Openings of posterior ethmoidal cells

Correlation with the Question

The question mentions:

• Medial surface of middle turbinate
• Sphenoethmoidal recess (decisive feature)
• Medial wall of middle meatus

These structures are classically examined in the SECOND PASS according to Dhingra.

• First pass: Inferior meatus → NLD
• Second pass: Sphenoethmoidal recess, superior meatus, sphenoid sinus, posterior ethmoidal cells
• Third pass: Middle meatus – uncinate process, bulla ethmoidalis, hiatus semilunaris

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the causes of sensorineural hearing loss: 1. Acoustic neuroma 2. Presbycusis 3. Meniere’s disease 4. Superior semicircular dehiscence syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from pathology of the cochlea, auditory nerve, or central auditory pathways.

Causes of SNHL:

• Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): Retrocochlear SNHL due to VIII nerve compression
• Presbycusis: Age-related degeneration of cochlear hair cells → bilateral high-frequency SNHL
• Ménière’s disease: Endolymphatic hydrops causing fluctuating SNHL

Not a cause of SNHL: Superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD):

• Causes conductive or mixed hearing loss
• Due to “third window effect” in inner ear
• Presents with autophony, sound-induced vertigo

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the correct plane of Frankfurt horizontal plane:
options: Inferior border of infraorbital rim and superior border of external auditory canal
Superior border of infraorbital rim and superior border of external auditory canal
Inferior border of infraorbital rim and inferior border of external auditory canal
Superior border of infraorbital rim and inferior border of external auditory canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior border of infraorbital rim and superior border of external auditory canal

The Frankfurt horizontal plane is an important anthropometric reference plane used in ENT, dentistry, maxillofacial surgery, and radiology to standardize head position. It is a line joining:

• Inferior orbital margin (orbitale)
• Superior border of external auditory canal (porion)

This plane should be parallel to the ground when the head is in anatomical position.

Clinical uses:

• Standard head positioning in cephalometry
• Planning orthognathic and facial surgeries
• Radiographic skull measurements
• Anthropometric facial analysis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Gelle test is positive in otosclerosis 2. RLN and ILN are connected by Galen’s Anastmosis 3. Cricothyroid is an extrinsic laryngeal ligament 4. Otoplasty may be done after 5-6 years of age.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 4

Statement 1. Gelle test positive in otosclerosis – False

• In otosclerosis → stapes fixation → Gelle test negative
• Positive Gelle = normal ossicular mobility

Statement 2. RLN and ILN connected by Galen’s anastomosis – True

• Anastomosis between recurrent laryngeal nerve and internal laryngeal nerve
• Provides sensory–motor interconnections in larynx

Statement 3. Cricothyroid is extrinsic ligament – False

• Cricothyroid is an intrinsic laryngeal ligament
• Hyo-epiglottic, thyrohyoid, cricotracheal are extrinsic membranes

Statement 4. Otoplasty after 5–6 years of age – True

• Pinna reaches \~85–90% adult size by 5–6 years
• Safe and appropriate age for correction of prominent ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Ideal time to do electroneurography studies in a patient with facial nerve injury will be 1 week to 3 weeks following injury. 2. Tonsillolingual sulcus is the ENT surgeon’s graveyard. 3. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate function of inner hair cells 4. The Chevallet and Jarjaway fractures are important describing vertical and horizontal fractures of the nasal septum respectively.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

1. Electroneurography (ENoG) timing in facial nerve injury will be 1-3 weeks following injury: True

• Best performed 1–3 weeks after facial nerve injury
• Allows Wallerian degeneration to occur for accurate assessment
• Used in Bell’s palsy, trauma, and prognostication

2. Tonsillolingual sulcus is the “surgeon’s graveyard”: True

• Risk of severe hemorrhage during tonsillectomy
• Contains tonsillar branch of facial artery

3. Outer hair cells: True

• Arranged in 3–4 rows
• Modulate and enhance inner hair cell function and sensitivity

4. Chevallet & Jarjavay fractures: True

• Describe vertical and horizontal nasal septal fractures respectively
• Important in septal trauma assessment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the incorrect pair of branch and parent nerve:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infratrochlear- Maxillary Nerve

Correct nerve–branch relationships:

• Frontal nerve (V1) → supraorbital, supratrochlear
• Nasociliary nerve (V1) → anterior ethmoidal, posterior ethmoidal, long ciliary, infratrochlear
• Maxillary nerve (V2) → infraorbital, zygomatic, superior alveolar nerves

Incorrect pair:

• Infratrochlear nerve is a branch of nasociliary nerve (V1), NOT maxillary nerve (V2)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Match the following conditions with their most commonly affected sinuses: 1. Osteoma 2. Fibrous Dysplasia 3. Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps a. Maxillary sinus b. Ethmoid sinus c. Frontal sinus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-c, 2-a, 3-b

| Condition | Most Commonly Affected Sinus | Reason / Key Point

| --------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------

| Osteoma | Frontal sinus | Most common benign tumor of paranasal sinuses; often incidental on imaging

| Fibrous dysplasia | Maxillary sinus | Causes bony expansion with “ground-glass” appearance

| Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps | Ethmoid sinus | Ethmoids are primary site for polyp formation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Nystagmus to the opposite side of the lesion occurs in: 1. Purulent labyrinthitis 2. Trauma to labyrinth 3. Serous labyrinthitis 4. Hypoactive labyrinth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 4

Direction of nystagmus in labyrinthine disorders depends on whether the labyrinth is irritative (hyperactive) or destructive (hypoactive).

• Irritative lesions (hyperactive labyrinth) → nystagmus towards same side
• Destructive lesions (hypoactive labyrinth) → nystagmus towards opposite side

Opposite-side nystagmus occurs in destructive lesions:

• Purulent labyrinthitis → destroys labyrinth → opposite side
• Labyrinthine trauma → loss of function → opposite side
• Hypoactive labyrinth → reduced vestibular tone → opposite side

Serous labyrinthitis: Irritative stage so Nystagmus usually towards affected ear (same side)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: On otoscopic examination, retraction of the pars tensa of the tympanic membrane is noted. According to the Sade classification, which of the following findings corresponds to Grade 3 retraction?
options: Retracted tympanic membrane touching the long process of incus
Tympanic membrane touching the promontory and not moving on Siegelization
Tympanic membrane touching the promontory but moving on Siegelization
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tympanic membrane touching the promontory but moving on Siegelization

The Sade classification is used to grade pars tensa tympanic membrane retraction based on severity and mobility.

Grades

• Grade 1: Mild retraction of TM
• Grade 2: TM touches long process of incus/stapes
• Grade 3: TM touches promontory but remains mobile on Siegelization
• Grade 4: TM adherent to promontory and immobile (adhesive otitis media)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Regarding the facial recess and related middle ear anatomy, which of the following statements are correct? 1. The facial recess is bounded medially by the facial nerve 2. The chorda tympani forms the medial boundary of the facial recess 3. The facial recess is used as a surgical approach in cochlear implantation 4. The fossa incudis forms the superior boundary of the facial recess
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3, 4

The facial recess is a key surgical landmark in middle ear anatomy, and understanding its boundaries and relations is essential for safe otologic procedures.

Key learning points:

•

Boundaries:

• Medial → Facial nerve
• Lateral → Chorda tympani
• Superior → Fossa incudis

•

Functional importance:

• Provides a safe access route to the middle ear cavity
• Used in posterior tympanotomy and cochlear implantation

•

Clinical significance:

• Close proximity to facial nerve → high risk of injury
• Misidentification of boundaries can lead to facial palsy

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Regarding the impedance matching (transformer function) of the middle ear, which of the following statements are correct? 1. The areal (hydraulic) ratio between tympanic membrane and stapes footplate is approximately 17:1 2. The ossicular lever ratio is approximately 2:1 3. The total transformer ratio of the middle ear is about 22 4. The curved membrane (catenary) effect contributes to additional amplification of sound 5. Loss of phase difference due to simultaneous exposure of oval and round windows leads to maximum conductive hearing loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3, 4, 5

The middle ear functions as an impedance-matching transformer, converting low-energy sound waves in air into higher-energy vibrations suitable for the fluid-filled inner ear.

Key mechanisms of amplification:

• Areal (hydraulic) ratio:

• Tympanic membrane vs stapes footplate ≈ 17:1 → major contributor

• Ossicular lever action (malleus–incus):

• ≈ 1.3:1

• Curved membrane (catenary) effect:

• Provides additional amplification (\~2×)

Net effect:

• Total amplification ≈ 22 times

Phase difference concept:

• Oval and round windows normally move out of phase → prevents sound cancellation
• Loss of phase difference (e.g., both windows exposed) → maximum conductive hearing loss

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Sequentially arrange the following structures that are involved in the production & conduction of otoacoustic emissions. 1. Outer hair cells 2. Basilar membrane 3. Oval window 4. Perilymph 5. Ossicles 6. Tympanic membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-2-4-3-5-6

Otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) are sounds generated by the outer hair cells of the cochlea and transmitted in reverse through the middle ear to the external auditory canal.

Sequence of production and conduction:

1. Outer hair cells (1) generate mechanical vibrations
2. Vibrations transmitted to basilar membrane (2)
3. Passed into perilymph (4) of inner ear
4. Transmitted via oval window (3)
5. Through ossicles (5)
6. To tympanic membrane (6) → then detected in external ear canal

Correct order: 1 → 2 → 4 → 3 → 5 → 6

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The narrowest part of the external auditory canal (isthmus) is located at which of the following positions?
options: At the junction of cartilaginous and bony canal
In the cartilaginous part of the canal
Approximately 5–7 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane in the bony canal
At the lateral opening of the external auditory canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Approximately 5–7 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane in the bony canal

The isthmus is the narrowest part of the external auditory canal (EAC) and is located in the bony canal approximately 5–7 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane.

• Outer 1/3: cartilaginous canal (with hair, glands)
• Inner 2/3: bony canal
• Narrowest point (isthmus): bony canal near tympanic membrane

Clinical significance:

• Common site for impaction of foreign bodies and wax
• Area where instrumentation is most painful due to thin skin tightly adherent to periosteum
• Important landmark during otoscopy and ear procedures (syringing, endoscopy, microsuction)
• Avoid deep instrumentation beyond this point to prevent tympanic membrane injury

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The presence of which structure is responsible for infants to be able to breathe simultaneously while suckling milk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High larynx

Infants can breathe and suckle simultaneously because of a highly placed larynx in the neck. Anatomical basis:

• In infants, the larynx lies at C2–C3 level (higher than adults)
• Epiglottis lies close to the soft palate
• Creates a near-separate airway and food passage
• Allows milk to pass laterally while airway remains patent

Changes with age:

• With growth, larynx descends to C4–C6 level
• Separation between airway and food passage increases
• Adults cannot breathe and swallow simultaneously

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Ventilation of the paranasal sinuses occurs predominantly during which phase of respiration and by what mechanism?
options: Expiration by eddy currents in the nasal cavity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Expiration by eddy currents in the nasal cavity

Ventilation of the paranasal sinuses occurs mainly during expiration, facilitated by eddy currents (turbulent airflow) in the nasal cavity that drive air into and out of the sinus ostia.

Physiological basis:

• During inspiration → airflow is relatively laminar and directed posteriorly, with minimal entry into sinus ostia
• During expiration → turbulent airflow creates eddy currents around sinus openings,These eddies push air into and out of the sinus ostia.This allows sinus aeration and gas exchange.

❌ Inspiration by laminar airflow

• Laminar flow doesn’t effectively ventilate sinuses.

❌ Inspiration by diffusion across mucosa

• Gas exchange via diffusion is minimal and not the primary mechanism.

❌ Expiration by mucociliary activity

• Mucociliary clearance moves mucus, not air.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the improper pairing between the anatomical limits of lymph nodes and the Level of lymph nodes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Level 5: Cricoid to suprasternal notch

Cervical lymph node levels and their anatomical boundaries

• Level I: Submental & submandibular region
• Level II: Skull base → hyoid bone
• Level III: Hyoid → cricoid cartilage
• Level IV: Cricoid → clavicle
• Level V: Posterior triangle nodes (skull base → clavicle along SCM posterior border)
• Level VI: Central compartment (hyoid → suprasternal notch)

Level V is not limited from cricoid to suprasternal notch. It extends from skull base to clavicle in posterior triangle.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What type of epithelium lines the vocal cords, and what is the space between them called?
options: Non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium; Rima vestibularis
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; Rima glottidis
Non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium; Rima glottidis
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; Rima vestibularis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium; Rima glottidis

True vocal cords are lined by non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium to withstand friction and vibration during phonation. In contrast, Most of larynx is lined by pseudo stratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium

Space between true vocal cords is Called rima glottidis.

• Narrowest part of laryngeal airway in adults
• Extends between the two true vocal cords and arytenoids

Space between false vocal cords is called rima vestibuli.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of the phase difference between the oval and round windows in sound transmission?
options: It amplifies sound waves by 10 dB
It prevents the cancellation of sound waves, allowing perilymph movement
It ensures simultaneous vibration of the oval and round windows
It decreases sound transmission efficiency, reducing hearing sensitivity by 4 dB
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It prevents the cancellation of sound waves, allowing perilymph movement

Effective cochlear sound transmission requires a phase difference between the oval window and round window.

Mechanism

• Stapes footplate movement at oval window pushes perilymph into scala vestibuli
• For fluid movement to occur, pressure must be released at round window
• Thus, oval and round windows move out of phase
• This prevents pressure buildup and allows perilymph displacement → basilar membrane vibration → hearing

If both windows moved in the same phase, perilymph would not move effectively and sound transmission would be poor due to wave cancellation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is least likely to be mistaken for nasal polyps on clinical examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhinoscleroma

• Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection (caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) that typically presents as a firm, non-ulcerative, nodular mass with nasal obstruction — its distinct clinical and histological features (Mikulicz cells, Russell bodies) make it less likely to be confused with the smooth, pale, boggy appearance of nasal polyps.
• Concha bullosa (pneumatized middle turbinate) can mimic a polyp on anterior rhinoscopy since it appears as a smooth, rounded mass in the nasal cavity.
• Meningoencephalocele and glioma are congenital masses that can present as unilateral nasal masses in children, often misdiagnosed as polyps — a critical distinction since biopsy of these is contraindicated due to risk of CSF leak/meningitis.

High-yield point:

• Always suspect meningoencephalocele/glioma in a child with a unilateral "nasal polyp" — a positive Furstenberg sign (mass enlarges with crying/jugular compression) and CT/MRI prior to any biopsy are essential to avoid catastrophic complications.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following incisions is most appropriate when ligating the anterior ethmoidal artery to control anterior epistaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lynch-Howarth incision

The anterior ethmoidal artery is a key arterial supply to the anterior nasal septum and lateral wall. When severe anterior epistaxis is uncontrolled by packing or cautery, surgical ligation may be required.

Best surgical approach: Lynch–Howarth incision

• Medial orbital incision along the anterior lacrimal crest
• Provides access to anterior ethmoidal artery at frontoethmoidal suture line
• Used for ligation/cauterization to control refractory epistaxis

Why other options are incorrect

B. Sublabial incision: used for maxillary sinus/Caldwell-Luc

C. Gullwing incision: eyelid reconstructive procedures

D. Weber-Ferguson incision: maxillary tumor access

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a characteristic of the inactive phase of otosclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Excessive osteoclast activity

Otosclerosis has two histopathological phases: Active (otospongiosis) and inactive (sclerotic) phase.

Inactive (sclerotic) phase features

• Dense, sclerotic, mineralized bone
• Minimal bone remodeling
• Hypocellular, avascular bone
• Replacement of earlier spongy bone with hard sclerotic bone

Excessive osteoclast activity is NOT seen in the inactive phase as it is a feature of the active otospongiotic phase, where bone resorption and vascular spongy bone formation occur.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following middle ear structures is the most reliable landmark for identifying the first genu of the facial nerve during otologic surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Processus cochleariformis

The processus cochleariformis is the most reliable surgical landmark for identifying the first genu (geniculate ganglion region) of the facial nerve during middle ear surgery.

• The tympanic segment of the facial nerve runs just superior to the processus cochleariformis.
• The processus cochleariformis acts as a pulley for the tensor tympani tendon and consistently marks the turn (first genu) of the facial nerve.

Other landmarks (less reliable):

• Oval window → related to stapes
• Pyramidal eminence → marks stapedius tendon
• Round window niche → posteroinferior landmark
• Sinus tympani → posterior recess near facial nerve but variable

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following properties of the eustachian tube predisposes to higher incidence of acute otitis media in children than adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wider and shorter tube

Proper functioning of the Eustachian tube is essential for middle ear ventilation, pressure equalization, and clearance of secretions.

In children, the anatomical characteristics (short, wide, horizontal tube, Less rigid) lead to:

• Inefficient middle ear drainage
• Easy reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions during crying, feeding, or URTI
• Negative middle ear pressure —> leading to fluid accumulation

This predisposes to:

• Recurrent acute otitis media
• Otitis media with effusion (glue ear)
• Conductive hearing loss affecting speech development

Other Options:

Option A. More angulated at isthmus – children actually have a more horizontal tube, not more angled.

Option B. Rigid cartilage – pediatric tube is actually more compliant, not rigid.

Option C. Dense elastin in cartilage – not the key predisposing factor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the venous drainage of the nose is false?
options: The venous networks parallel the arterial supply in their distribution
The fronto-median area drains to the facial vein, while the orbito-palpebral area drains to the ophthalmic vein
The facial vein originates as the angular vein, which is formed by the confluence of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins
Infections in the upper lip and nose can potentially spread to the cavernous sinus due to a valveless venous connection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The venous networks parallel the arterial supply in their distribution

Venous drainage of the nose is clinically important because of its connection to intracranial venous sinuses.

• Nasal veins do NOT strictly parallel arterial supply → statement is false
• Fronto-median area drains into facial vein
• Orbito-palpebral area drains into ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus
• Facial vein begins as angular vein (union of supratrochlear + supraorbital veins)
• Veins of face and nose are valveless so infections can spread from upper lip, nose and medial canthus can spread retrograde via angular → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true? 1. Sinus tympani is most common site of residual cholesteatoma 2. Canal wall down procedure has a higher risk of residual disease 3. Prussack space is the most common site for recurrent disease 4. Trautmann's triangle gives access to middle ear cavity.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1

Key concepts:

Statement 1. Sinus tympani —is the most common site of residual cholesteatoma (True)

• Deep recess posterior to oval window
• Difficult to visualize and access surgically
• Most frequent site for residual disease after surgery

Statement 2. Canal wall down (CWD) has higher risk of residual disease (False)

• CWD provides better exposure
• Lower residual/recurrent rates than canal wall up
• Easier postoperative surveillance

Statement 3. Prussack space is the most common site for recurrent disease (False)

• Most common site for primary acquired cholesteatoma
• Recurrent disease more often due to retraction pockets or inadequate clearance, not specifically Prussack space

Statement 4. Trautmann’s triangle gives access to middle ear cavity (False)

• Trautmann’s triangle provides access to posterior cranial fossa
• Not middle ear cavity

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the caloric test is correct?
options: The test evaluates the function of the posterior semicircular canal by inducing convection currents within the perilymph
Irrigation with cold water (30°C) induces nystagmus with the fast phase directed toward the same (ipsilateral) side
The 30° head elevation during the test is performed to bring the lateral semicircular canal into a vertical plane, maximizing convection currents
Warm water irrigation (44°C) produces endolymph convection currents that mimic a hypoactive labyrinth, causing nystagmus toward the opposite side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The 30° head elevation during the test is performed to bring the lateral semicircular canal into a vertical plane, maximizing convection currents

| Parameter | Detail

| --------- | ------

| Canal tested | Lateral (horizontal) SCC — each labyrinth tested separately

| Head position | 30° elevation — orients the lateral SCC into the true vertical plane, maximizing thermally-induced endolymph convection currents

| Stimulus | Bithermal water: 30°C (cold, body temp −7°C) and 44°C (warm, body temp +7°C), pumped into EAC

| Cold water (30°C) | Mimics a hypoactive labyrinth → nystagmus fast phase to the OPPOSITE side

| Warm water (44°C) | Mimics a hyperactive labyrinth → nystagmus fast phase to the SAME side

| Mnemonic | COWS — Cold Opposite, Warm Same

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which type of sphenoid sinus pneumatization is contraindicated in endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Conchal

Conchal Pneumatization involves minimal air space and dense trabecular bone, making surgical access to the sella turcica extremely difficult.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with a congenital deformity of the external ear. What is the ideal age for performing otoplasty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-6 years

Otoplasty (pinnaplasty) is ideally performed at 5–6 years of age, when:

• The external ear has reached approximately 85–90% of its adult size, allowing durable correction.
• The auricular cartilage is still soft and pliable, making surgical reshaping easier.
•

The procedure is completed before school age, helping reduce psychological distress, teasing, and bullying related to prominent or malformed ears.

•

Common indication: Prominent ears (bat ears), congenital auricular deformities (when adequate cartilage is present).

• Goal: Improve ear shape and symmetry while minimizing psychosocial impact.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient undergoes parotid gland surgery and subsequently develops loss of cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible and the lower part of the external ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
options: Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Great auricular nerve

The great auricular nerve (C2–C3), a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, ascends superficially across the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible, parotid region, mastoid process, and the lower part of the auricle (external ear). Because it runs superficially over the parotid gland, it is commonly injured during parotidectomy, resulting in postoperative numbness over these areas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Marginal mandibular nerve: A motor branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) supplying muscles of the lower lip (depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis). Injury causes asymmetry of the lower lip, not sensory loss.
• B. Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve: A motor branch supplying muscles of facial expression in the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi, etc.). Injury causes facial weakness, not cutaneous sensory loss.
• C. Auriculotemporal nerve: A sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplying the anterior auricle, external acoustic meatus, temporal region, and TMJ. It does not supply the angle of the mandible or lower ear. It also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland and is involved in Frey syndrome after parotid surgery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Mark the correct statement/s about Inner and Outer hair cells. 1. Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses. 2. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate function of inner hair cells. 3. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of tectorial membrane. 4. Inner hair cells are in single row and modulate function of outer hair cells. 5. Outer and inner hair cells are present in the ratio 3:1.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 5 are correct

Understanding the structure and function of inner and outer hair cells in the organ of Corti is essential for interpreting hearing physiology.

OHC : IHC = \~3 : 1

Inner Hair Cells (IHC):

• Arranged in single row
• Primary sensory receptors
• Transmit auditory impulses to brain via afferent fibers

Outer Hair Cells (OHC):

• Arranged in 3–4 rows
• Function: modulation and amplification of sound
• Show electromotility (prestin protein) → enhance basilar membrane vibration
• Help in fine-tuning frequency and sensitivity

Incorrect statements explained:

• Statement 3: OHC do not primarily move the tectorial membrane; they amplify basilar membrane motion
• Statement 4: IHC do NOT modulate OHC; rather OHC modulate IHC function

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding from the ear following a fall. What is the investigation of choice in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT temporal bone

In a patient with ear bleeding following trauma, the investigation of choice is CT temporal bone, as it is the best modality to detect temporal bone fractures.

·  CT temporal bone (HRCT) provides detailed visualization of:

o    Bony structures of ear (external, middle, inner ear)

o    Fracture lines (longitudinal/transverse)

o    Ossicular disruption, facial canal involvement

·  Helps classify fractures and identify complications such as:

o    CSF leak

o    Facial nerve injury

o    Hearing loss

Why not other options:

·   MRI brain: Better for soft tissue and intracranial complications, not first-line for fractures

·   CBP: Irrelevant

·   X-ray skull: Low sensitivity, largely obsolete

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presented with left facial weakness. Routine lab workup was normal. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticosteroids

A patient with acute onset unilateral facial weakness and normal investigations is most likely having Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy).

First-line management:

·         Corticosteroids (within 72 hours) → reduce nerve inflammation and edema

·         Significantly improve recovery outcomes

·         Inflammation of facial nerve (CN VII) within facial canal

·         Leads to compression → demyelination → weakness of facial muscles

Clinical features:

·         Unilateral facial paralysis

·         Inability to close eye (lagophthalmos)

·         Loss of forehead wrinkling (LMN lesion)

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Acyclovir: May be added in severe cases, but not first-line alone

·         Antibiotics: No role (non-bacterial)

·         Physiotherapy: Adjunct, not initial primary treatment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Facial nerve

Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy causes ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis, leading to:

• Inability to close eye → orbicularis oculi paralysis
• Drooling of saliva → loss of buccinator tone
• Deviation of angle of mouth to opposite side → unopposed normal side
• Loss of forehead wrinkling (LMN lesion)

Functions of facial nerve:

• Motor: Muscles of facial expression
• Parasympathetic: Lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands
• Sensory: Taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue

Why not others:

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Mastication, facial sensation (not facial expression)
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Eye movements, ptosis
• Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX): Taste posterior 1/3, swallowing

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with weakness of the lower half of the face on the right side, while forehead wrinkling is preserved. The lesion is most likely located in which of the following?
options: Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve
Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve

An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face with preservation of forehead movements. This occurs because the upper facial muscles (forehead) receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation, whereas the lower facial muscles receive only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Therefore, a unilateral UMN lesion affects only the contralateral lower face.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve: Produces ipsilateral paralysis of the entire half of the face, including inability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile (e.g., Bell’s palsy).
• C. Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Supplies the muscles of mastication and facial sensation; it does not cause facial expression weakness.
• D. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII): Supplies the tongue muscles; injury causes tongue deviation toward the affected side, not facial weakness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of the classical triad of Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proptosis

Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome is a rare neuro-mucocutaneous disorder characterized by the classical triad of recurrent orofacial edema, recurrent facial nerve (LMN) palsy, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata). The diagnosis is clinical, although not all three features are present in every patient.

• Proptosis is not a component of the classical triad of Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome.

Why not the other options?

• B. Orofacial edema ✓: Recurrent, painless swelling of the lips (especially the upper lip) is the most common manifestation.
• C. Fissured tongue ✓: Also known as lingua plicata or scrotal tongue.
• D. Recurrent facial paralysis ✓: Typically a recurrent lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, resembling Bell’s palsy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most favourable prognostic parameter in Bell’s palsy?
options: Incomplete paralysis in the first week
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incomplete paralysis in the first week

Bell’s palsy is an acute idiopathic lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, thought to result from reactivation of Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) causing inflammation and edema of the facial nerve within the facial canal.

The most important prognostic factor is the severity of facial weakness at presentation. Patients with incomplete facial paralysis have an excellent prognosis, with the majority achieving complete recovery.

Why not the other options?

• B. Mild CSF lymphocytosis: CSF examination is not routinely performed in Bell’s palsy and has no prognostic significance.
• C. Denervation on EMG after 10 days: Indicates significant axonal degeneration and is associated with a poor prognosis.
• D. Pain behind the ear: Common early symptom but does not predict recovery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presented with history of dysphagia, halitosis and aspiration pneumonia. A barium swallow was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zenker’s diverticulum

The given image shows the collection of contrast in a pouch-like structure, which favours the diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum.

Zenker’s diverticulum is a pulsion-type pseudodiverticulum. It occurs due to the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian’s triangle. Killian’s triangle represents a weak muscular space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle - the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus. This phenomenon may lead to the creation of a sac with a narrow neck that can trap liquid and food. The distended sac may compress the cervical oesophagus.

Clinical presentation:

The entrapment of liquid and/or food within the diverticulum may result in:

* Globus sensation

* Dysphagia

* Halitosis

* Regurgitation

* Aspiration pneumonia

Diagnosis is by Barium swallow studies and video laryngoscopy.

Pearl PF1662: Zenker’s Diverticulum

Zenker's diverticulum occurs due to herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian's triangle, which is a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor - (thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus) in the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is usually seen in elderly patients (>60 years).

Characteristics of Zenker's diverticulum:

* Hypopharyngeal

* False diverticula - doesn't have a muscle coat

* Acquired

* Pulsion diverticulum

Pathophysiology: Impaired relaxation and spasm of the cricopharyngeus muscle after swallowing can result in increased pressure within the distal pharynx, and cause the diverticulum.Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

The investigation of choice is barium swallow (lateral X-ray).

It is treated with:

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with carcinoma in pyriform Fossa. On laryngoscopy, the lesion is around 5cm and the right vocal folds are not mobile. There is no lymph Node involvement and no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging for the malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3N0M0

The patient has carcinoma hypopharynx as it is a tumor in the pyriform fossa and his staging of the disease is T3N0M0 as he has no nodal mets or involvement of vocal cords.

Staging of carcinoma hypopharynx:

1)Tumour

T1:

* Tumor involves only in one part of the hypopharynx

* is less than <2 cms

T2:

* Tumor involves more than one part of the hypopharynx

* has grown into a nearby area

*  > 2cm but < 4 cm across

* not affected the vocal cords

T3:

* Tumor is > 4 cm across

* Tumor is affecting the movement of the vocal cords

* Tumor has grown into the esophagus

T4a:

* The tumor has grown into thyroid or cricoid cartilage/ hyoid bone/ thyroid gland/nearby muscle or fat.

T4b:

* Tumor grows into Prevertebral Space

* Superior Mediastinum

* Encases carotid artery

2)Nodal staging:

* NX -cannot be assessed

* N0 No regional lymph node metastasis

* N1 Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, <3 cm

* N2a Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, >3cm but < 6 cm

* N2b Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, <6 cm

* N2c Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, < 6 cm

* N3 Metastasis in a lymph node > 6 cm

3)Systemic metastasis

* M0- no metastasis

* M1- metastasis present

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with hoarseness of Voice. On examination an ulcero-proliferative Mass is seen on Right Vocal Cord, Cord was however mobile. There is no lymph node involvement and no metastasis. Which of the following is the best treatment modality for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radiotherapy

The patient with superficial exophytic lesions will be advised for radiotherapy.

Cases that do well with radiotherapy:

* Cancer of the vocal cord without impairment of its mobility

* Superficial exophytic lesions

Radiotherapy does not give good results in:

* Lesions with fixed cords

* Subglottic extension

* Cartilage invasion

* Nodal metastases

These lesions require surgery. Cartilage invasion is a contraindication to radiotherapy.

Laryngeal carcinoma is more common in males.

Laryngeal cancer

* Male: Female ratio is 10:1

* Risk factors: Smoking tobacco and alcohol

* 90-95% are squamous

* Most common site: Glottis followed by supraglottis and subglottis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young adult presents with a deformed nose after falling from a ladder. The CT scan shows a displaced nasal fracture. What is the ideal time to reduce the fracture in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-7 days following injury

The ideal time for reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema from the injury has subsided.

The presence of edema interferes with the accurate reduction of the fracture. In most cases, the deformity is due to edema. So, ice packs and head elevation are advised initially after injury. After 3-5 days, the edema would subside and the underlying deformity will be apparent on clinical assessment.

After 2 weeks it is difficult to reduce since the process of callus formation and the bony and fibrous union would have started.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound when compressing the swelling. As the X-ray neck was inconclusive a CT neck was taken which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given CT image along with the examination finding of Bryce sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocoele:

* Air-filled cavity within the larynx developing in the saccule.

* The patient presents with a neck swelling that is soft and compressible.

* Bryce sign: on compressing the swelling, there is a gurgling sound.

It is seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to raised transglottic air pressure. It presents with hoarseness, cough, and if large, causes obstruction of the airway.

Types of laryngocoele are:

* Internal - confined within the larynx and presents as distension of false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External - the distended saccule herniates through the thyroid membrane and presents in the neck. It presents as a reducible swelling in the neck, increasing in size on coughing or performing Valsalva manoeuvres.

* Mixed - both external and internal compounds are seen

Diagnosis is done by indirect laryngoscopy, soft tissue AP and lateral views of the neck x-ray with Valsalva. CT scan helps to find out the extent of the lesion. External type is managed by surgical excision through an external neck incision. Internal type is managed by marsupialization and endoscopic carbon dioxide laser resection.

Other options:

Option A: Zenker diverticulum or pharyngeal pouch is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian’s triangle represents a weak space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the Esophagus and Trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: A tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Bony septal perforation occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Syphilis

Syphilis involves the perforation of the bony and cartilaginous parts.

Lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy cause perforation only in the cartilaginous part.

Septal perforation can be caused by:

* Trauma

* Pathological:

* Septal abscess

* Nasal myiasis

* Rhinolith

* Chronic granulomatous disease

* Wegner's granulomatous disease

* Drug-related:

* Chronic use of steroid spray

* Cocaine abuse

* Arsenic/ chromium

* Idiopathic

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Gold standard investigation before Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT scan

The gold standard investigation before FESS is a CT scan to rule out other pathologies and for confirmation of diagnosis. CT scan is better than MRI for visualizing bones and their anatomy.

Even while doing surgery, decisions on whether to open the mastoid antrum are based on CT findings and intraoperative findings. FESS is done for failed medical management of rhinosinusitis.

Other indications of FESS:

* Chronic bacterial sinusitis that is unresponsive to adequate medical treatment.

* Recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis

* Polypoid rhinosinusitis (diffuse nasal polyposis)

* Fungal sinusitis with a fungal ball or nasal polypi

* Antrochoanal polyp

* Mucocele of frontoethmoid or sphenoid sinus

* Control of epistaxis by endoscopic cautery.

* Removal of foreign body from the nose or sinus

* Endoscopic septoplasty

Advanced nasal endoscopic techniques

* Removal of benign tumors, e.g. inverted papillomas or angiofibromas.

* Orbital abscess or cellulitis management.

* Dacryocystorhinostomy

* Repair of CSF leak

* Pituitary surgery

* Optic nerve decompression

* Orbital decompression for Graves’ disease

* Control of posterior epistaxis (endoscopic clipping of sphenopalatine artery)

* Choanal atresia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the endoscopic image of nasopharynx.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fossa of Rossenmuller

The structure marked in the image is the Fossa of Rossenmuller.

Fossa of Rossenmuller is the most common site for carcinoma in the nasopharynx.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma usually originates from the nasopharynx in the fossa of Rossenmuller. It presents with the following symptoms:

* Nasal- Nasal obstruction due to blockage of the choana or the nasal cavity, denasal speech, nasal discharge, epistaxis.

* Otologic- Obstruction of the eustachian tube leads to unilateral conductive hearing loss, serous or suppurative otitis media.

* Ophthalmologic- These symptoms occur due to the involvement of cranial nerves.

* Squint and diplopia- involvement of cranial nerve VI.

* Facial pain and reduced corneal reflex- cranial nerve V.

* Exophthalmos and blindness- cranial nerve II.

* Cervical node metastasis- Usually between the angle of the jaw and the mastoid.

* Distant metastasis- to bone, liver, lung, etc.

The treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

* Radiotherapy for stages I and II.

* Radiotherapy + chemotherapy for stages III and IV.

* Radical neck dissection can be done in case of recurrent or residual disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which condition is the reservoir sign seen along with mastoid tenderness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute mastoiditis

Reservoir sign along with the tenderness of the mastoid is seen in acute mastoiditis.

Reservoir sign is seen in acute mastoiditis/coalescent Mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

Mastoiditis is a complication of otitis media.

Other signs of acute mastoiditis:

The light-house effect is seen is acute mastoiditis. It is described as a pulsatile mucopurulent or purulent discharge, coming through a central pin-hole perforation of pars tensa. It suggests a reservoir of infection in the mastoid and middle ear.

Note: In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose is also called reservoir sign.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The most common site of obstruction by a nasal polyp from the maxillary sinus is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle meatus

The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus at the lower part of the infundibulum, in its medial wall and thus a nasal polyp will obstruct the middle meatus.

Infundibulum is the space limited medially by the uncinate process and frontal process of the maxilla, and laterally by the lamina papyracea.

Pearl PF1078: Structures opening into meatuses of nose

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which is the false statement among the following for the condition given in the picture?
options: Retention cyst of major salivary glands
Most common site is lower lip
Retention cyst of minor salivary glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retention cyst of major salivary glands

The image shows a mucocele of the lower lip and it is a retention cyst of the minor salivary glands of the lip.

Mucocele:

* The most common site of mucocele in the oral cavity is the lower lip.

* It is a retention cyst of the minor salivary glands of the lip.

* The lesions appear as a soft and cystic mass of bluish color.

* Treatment is surgical excision.

Note:

If the ducts of any salivary gland become obstructed they can develop a retention cyst. If such cysts occur due to the obstruction in the sublingual salivary gland, it is called a ranula. A ranula usually presents as a large, tense, bluish swelling on the floor of the mouth to one side on the midline.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy who is a football player comes to the casualty with complaints of epistaxis while playing football on the ground. There is no history of trauma or falls. He gives a history of recurrent spontaneous nasal bleeding, unilateral nasal obstruction and denasal speech. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is shown below. What is this sign known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Holman Miller sign

The given CT scan showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus is called the Holman Miller sign or Antral sign.

The given clinical picture along with a CT scan showing the Holman Miller sign is suggestive of the diagnosis of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. It most commonly arises from the sphenopalatine foramen. From here the tumour grows into the:

* Nasal cavity

* Nasopharynx

* Pterygopalatine fossa

* Pterygomaxillary fossa

* Infratemporal fossa

Other options:

Aquino sign is the blanching of the tumour mass in a glomus tumour when the ipsilateral carotid artery is compressed manually.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum.

Given below is CT showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus - Antral sign or Holman Miller sign

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presented with a history of discomfort while swallowing food. She has no history of fever, sore throat, or smoking but has a history of Marfan's syndrome in her father. On examination of the oral cavity, there is unilateral swelling of the tonsils along with pulsation. What is the most likely cause of the swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm

The history of Marfan's syndrome( autosomal dominant disease) along with the pulsation of the tonsils is suggestive of an extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm.

Even though the tonsils are supplied by the external carotid artery branches an internal carotid artery aneurysm can push the tonsil medially which gives the pulsation. The external carotid artery is more superficial in its course and would not lead to the medial displacement of the tonsils.

The internal carotid artery which gives no branches in the cervical region can cause kinks, elbowing, etc which leads to aneurysms when it lies close to the pharynx. In children, the tonsillo-carotid distance increases with growth to a maximum value of 25 mm.

Note: A common differential in a unilateral swelling of the tonsil is Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) which requires incision and drainage as the treatment. Hence aneurysms need to be ruled out before the procedure as trauma to the internal carotid artery can be devastating since it supplies the brain too.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her mother with complaints of mouth breathing. She has a flat, expressionless long face with an open mouth. On examination, a high-arched palate and crowded upper teeth are noted. The X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adenoid hypertrophy

The clinical scenario along with the x-ray which shows enlarged adenoids suggests the diagnosis of adenoid hypertrophy.

Clinical features:

* Nasal obstruction is the most common symptom. This leads to mouth breathing. Nasal obstruction also interferes with feeding or suckling in a child. As respiration and feeding cannot take place simultaneously, a child with adenoid enlargement fails to thrive.

* Nasal discharge, sinusitis, and epistaxis.

* Bilateral conductive hearing loss and serous otitis media due to eustachian tube obstruction.

* Rhinolalia clausa - hyponasal voice.

* Adenoid facies - elongated face with a dull expression, pinched up nose, absent nasolabial crease, open mouth, prominent and crowded upper teeth.

* Sleep apnoea - chronic cases lead to hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction. This consequently leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

* Aprosexia - lack of concentration.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old male diagnosed with carcinoma of the larynx is scheduled for treatment and has undergone the procedure shown in the image below. At what level is the incision made for this procedure?
options: At the level of the 2nd tracheal ring
At the level of the 1st tracheal ring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. At the level of the 1st tracheal ring

The clinical scenario describes a 50-year-old male with carcinoma of the larynx undergoing a tracheostomy, as shown in the image. The incision is made at the level of the first tracheal ring, above the isthmus, in a patient with laryngeal carcinoma, and this procedure is referred to as a high tracheostomy.

Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy. It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea. High tracheostomy is performed above the level of the thyroid isthmus (the Isthmus lies against the II, III, and IV tracheal rings). The only indication for high tracheostomy is carcinoma of the larynx.

It provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
It uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood.

Indications of tracheostomy:

* Respiratory obstruction due to infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria).

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures.

* Neoplasms.

* Foreign bodies or edema.

* Retained secretionsInability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles.

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions.

* Painful cough.

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Steps of Tracheostomy:

* Incision: Make a vertical incision in the midline from the cricoid cartilage to above the sternal notch. For a better cosmetic outcome for elective procedures, a 5 cm transverse incision two fingers' breadth above the sternal notch can be used.

* Dissection: Dissect tissues in the midline. Displace or ligate any dilated veins encountered to control bleeding.

* Muscle separation: Separate and retract the strap muscles of the neck laterally to expose underlying structures.

* Thyroid isthmus management: Displace the thyroid isthmus upwards or divide and ligate it with sutures.

* Local anaesthesia: Inject a few drops of 4% lignocaine into the trachea to suppress coughing.

* Tracheal incision: Fix the trachea with a hook and make a vertical incision between the third and fourth tracheal rings(Option D), converting it into a circular opening. Avoid dividing the first tracheal ring to prevent perichondritis and stenosis.

* Inserting the tube: Insert a tracheostomy tube of appropriate size into the tracheal opening and secure it with tapes.

* Avoid tight suturing: Avoid tightly suturing or packing the skin incision to prevent subcutaneous emphysema.

* Dressing: Place a gauze dressing between the skin and the flange of the tracheostomy tube around the stoma to absorb secretions, provide a barrier against infection, and allow air to escape, promoting proper healing.

Pearl PF1486: Types of Tracheostomy

High tracheostomy

* Done through the 1st tracheal ring

* An opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland

* Done in case of malignancy of the larynx

* Increased risk of perichondritis and subglottic stenosis

Mid tracheostomy

* Done through the 2nd - 3rd rings

* Most commonly done tracheostomy

* Isthmus has to be retracted or divided

Low tracheostomy

* Done through the 4th - 5th tracheal ring

* Done below the isthmus

* Done when the airway is blocked at an upper airway level

* Risk of injuring the great vessels of the neck

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70 year old male presents with neck nodes. Examination of left ear reveals a dull tympanic membrane, deafness and tinnitus. On tympanogram, a Type B curve is obtained. Most probable diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Points in favour:

* 70yr old with neck nodes pointing towards malignancy (can be either due to infection but no other signs of infection given plus the age points more towards malignancy).

* On examination ear shows dull tympanic membrane and audiometry shows curve B which means  fluid is present in left ear ruling out option d (Sensorineuronal hearing loss).

* Type B tympanogram seen in serous otitis media. Presence of unilateral serous otitis media in an adult should raise the suspicion of a nasopharngeal growth.

* Age of the patient (most common age 5th -7th decade).

* sex of the patient (most common in males).

Other options:

Option a: On examination either cholesteotoma granulation or perforation will be seen.

Option b: On examination, otoscopy shows a red reflex through intact tympanic membrane. “Rising sun” appearance is seen when tumour arises from the floor of middle ear.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

* Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is also called Guangdong tumor.

* Commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmüller.

* Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Presenting symptoms and signs of nasopharyngeal cancer in order of frequency are:

* Cervical lymphadenopathy (most common) (60–90%)

* Hearing loss

* Nasal obstruction

* Epistaxis

* Cranial nerve palsies -Cranial nerves V and VI are the most commonly involved among all the cranial nerves. (V more than VI)

* Headache

* Earache

* Neck pain

* Weight loss

Nasopharyngeal cancer can cause:

* Conductive deafness (eustachian tube block)

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal/facial neuralgia (involvement of CN V) and

* Palatal paralysis (CN X)

This is collectively called Trotter’s triad.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone.

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child is brought to you with complaints of noisy breathing. On examination, you notice inspiratory stridor in the child and laryngeal examination is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laryngomalacia

This child with inspiratory stridor and Omega-shaped epiglottis has laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in newborns. It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. On examination, the omega-shaped epiglottis is seen.

Factors increasing Stridor in laryngomalacia:

* Supine Position

* Sleep

* Agitation

* URI (Upper Respiratory tract Infection)

Stridor is increased on crying but subsides on placing the child in a prone position; crying is normal.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. It may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both.

* Inspiratory stridor is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

Treatment is mainly conservative. Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction. In cases of severe laryngomalacia, supraglottoplasty is done.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A housewife presents with complaints of a blocked nose, loss of smell, and dry, greenish crusty nasal discharge. On examination, nasal cavities appear roomy and turbinates are atrophied. Which of the following surgeries can be done on this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Young’s operation

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of atrophic rhinitis. Young’s and modified Young’s operations are done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

In Young’s operation, both the nostrils are closed completely just within the nasal vestibule by raising flaps. They are opened after 6 months or later when the mucosa may revert to normal and crusting will be reduced.

Modified Young’s operation aims at partially closing the nostrils.

Other options:

Options A and C: Submucous resection and septoplasty are done for deviated nasal septum.

Option D: Vidian neurectomy is done for vasomotor rhinitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with the following lesion on his face. He has a history of acne rosacea. The condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhinophyma

The image above shows an exophytic, pink, lobulated mass over the nose with superficial vascular dilation suggesting a diagnosis of phymatous rosacea or rhinophyma

Phymatous rosacea is a subtype of acne rosacea characterized by thickened skin and prominent follicular openings. There is marked nasal distortion with an increase in size and a bulbous tip. Rhinophyma is the most common type of phymatous rosacea.

Rhinophyma (potato tumour/elephantiasis of the nose) is due to hypertrophy of the sebaceous gland. It is associated with long-standing cases of acne rosacea.  It is mostly seen in middle-aged men involving the tip of the nose causing unsightly appearance and obstruction to breathing and vision.

Treatment of rhinophyma

* First-line

* Topical skin‐peeling agent if there are large occluded follicles

* Electrocautery or laser for telangiectases

* Second-line - Low‐dose isotretinoin therapy

* Third line - Ablation of phymatous tissue with carbon dioxide laser • Surgical remodelling of the nose.

Other options:

Option B: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by gram-negative bacillus Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It presents with chronic granulomatous inflammation of the nasal cavity, causing nasal obstruction, discharge, crusting, and eventual nasal deformity.

Option C: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. It presents with painless, friable, polypoidal masses in the nasal cavity, often causing nasal obstruction and bleeding.

Option D: Scleroderma causes rashes on the face but has no association with long-standing acne rosacea. It is characterized by skin thickening, tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and internal organ involvement such as the lungs, heart, and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following organisms can cause croup except ___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rhinovirus

Croup can be caused by parainfluenza types 1, 2,3, RSV(Respiratory syncytial virus), and influenza viruses and it cannot be caused by Rhinovirus.

Croup, or laryngotracheobronchitis, is a viral infection affecting the upper airway, primarily in children aged 6 months to 3 years. It causes inflammation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, leading to characteristic symptoms such as:

* Barking cough (seal-like cough)

* Inspiratory stridor

* Hoarseness

* Respiratory distress in severe cases

The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus. While other viruses like influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus can also cause croup, parainfluenza is the predominant cause

On X-ray: Steeple/ Church top/ Pencil top sign (obstruction in subglottis) is seen as below:

Management:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction.

* Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.

* Dexamethasone is indicated in all grades of croup.

* Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %).

* Antibiotics are not indicated in croup.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Dohlman’s procedure is for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zenker’s diverticulum

Dohlman’s  procedure is done for Zenker’s diverticulum.

A transoral endoscopic approach (Dohlman's procedure) -using staplers, laser, or coagulation through an endoscope that ablate the septum between the diverticulum and the cervical esophagus, can be used for diverticula between 2 and 5 cm in size.

The treatment is either endoscopic or open surgery.For diverticula 3 cm or smaller in size, surgical repair is superior and thus preferred to endoscopic repair.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Laryngeal crepitus is absent in all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parapharyngeal abscess

Laryngeal crepitus is absent in all of the following except parapharyngeal abscess.

Moving the larynx back and forth while pressing it against the spine demonstrates laryngeal crepitus. When absent, it is a clinical sign of a mass in the retrolaryngeal space or hypopharynx, probably due to a laryngeal trauma or malignancy. It is absent in cases where the larynx is fixed suggesting posterior extension of malignancy into the prevertebral fascia.

In parapharyngeal abscess, the maximal swelling is behind the posterior faucial pillar and there may be little or no oedema of the soft palate. This condition is usually unilateral and occurs on one side of the neck.

Any condition behind the cricoid e.g. postcricoid malignancy or in front of the vertebra e.g. prevertebral or retropharyngeal abscess (hypo pharyngeal abscess) will lead to absent laryngeal crepitus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The following sign is seen in a patient presenting with rhinorrhea following a skull base fracture. Identify the sign.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Double Target Sign

The given image shows the Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign seen in CSF rhinorrhoea and suggests basal skull fracture due to trauma in this case.

Double target sign is seen patients with CSF rhinorrhea. The nasal discharge in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood. When this discharge is collected on a filter paper, it shows a double target sign with a central red spot and a peripheral lighter halo.

The following features help in differentiating CSF rhinorrhoea from nasal secretions:

Features
CSF Fluid
Nasal Secretions
