Note: Nasal discharge stiffens the handkerchief because of the presence of mucus.

A basilar skull fracture occurs due to direct impact behind the ear or crush injuries of the head and present with the following features:

* Hemotympanum

* Battle sign: bruising behind the ear

* Racoon eyes

* CSF rhinorrhoea

Pearl PF1086: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: Reservoir sign is also seen in acute mastoiditis/ coalescent mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What clinical test is depicted in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cottle’s test

The image representing a clinical test where the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly is Cottle’s test.

This test is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve in patients with a deviated nasal septum. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive and indicates an abnormality of the vestibular component of the nasal valve on that side.

Option A: Epley’s maneuver is used in the treatment of BPPV.

Option B: Heimlich manoeuvre is used in the treatment of accidental inhalation of foreign body.

Procedure: Stand behind the person and place your arms around his lower chest and give four abdominal thrusts. The residual air in the lungs can dislodge the foreign body providing some airway.

Option D: Trotter’s method is used in the treatment of epistaxis. In Trotter’s method, the patient is made to sit, leaning a little forward over a basin to spit any blood. He should pinch the nose firmly for 5 to 10 mins and breathe quietly from the mouth.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Labyrinthitis

In the above options, labyrinthitis is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss while all others are causes of conductive hearing loss.

Causes of sensorineural hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Anomalies of the inner ear or the hearing apparatus due to prenatal or perinatal factors

* Acquired

* Labyrinthitis—viral, bacterial, or spirochaetal

* Trauma to labyrinth or VIIIth nerve

* Noise-induced hearing loss

* Ototoxic drugs

* Presbycusis

* Ménière’s disease

* Acoustic neuroma

* Systemic disorders-diabetes, autoimmune disorders, multiple sclerosis

Causes of conductive hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Meatal atresia

* Fixation of stapes footplate/malleus head

* Ossicular discontinuity

* Congenital cholesteatoma

* Acquired

* External ear

* Obstruction in the ear canal-wax, foreign body, furuncle

* Middle ear

* Perforation of tympanic membrane

* Fluid in the middle ear-acute otitis media, serous otitis media

* Tumors in the middle ear

* Disruption of ossicles-chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma

* Fixation of ossicles-otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis, adhesive otitis media

* Eustachian tube blockage-retracted tympanic membrane, serous otitis media

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry)?
options: It can be used for screening of hearing loss.
It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway and can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

* The recording is made from brain stem potentials

* Click stimulus is used

* Responses are not frequency specific

* Can be performed in awake and restless patients

* Responses begin after 1 -10 milliseconds after stimuli

* Suitable for even younger children

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

Auditory brainstem response:

* Used to elicit brainstem responses to auditory stimulation by clicks or tone bursts.

* Non-invasive technique to find the integrity of central auditory pathways through the eighth nerve, pons and midbrain.

TYPE
SITE OF ORIGIN

Wave I
Distal part of CN VIII

Wave II
Proximal part of CN VIII near the brainstem.

Wave III
Cochlear nucleus

Wave IV
Superior olivary complex

Wave V
Lateral lemniscus

Wave VI and VII
Inferior colliculus

Pearl PF1553: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)

It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway.

Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms.

* Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave III – cochlear nucleus

* Wave IV – superior olivary complex

* Wave V – lateral lemniscus

* Wave VI – inferior colliculus

* Wave VII - medial geniculate body

Findings:

* Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal

* Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent

* Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms.

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The most probable diagnosis is Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Adolescent male presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx points towards angiofibroma. The consistency of the tumor is firm but the digital palpation should never be done until at the time of operation, because of the risk of profuse bleeding.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head with contrast enhancement is now the investigation of choice. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus often called antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomonic of angiofibroma.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice though radiotherapy and chemotherapy monotherapy or in combination have also been used.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to you with complaints of difficulty in hearing in the right ear which is slowly progressive. She also has tinnitus which is pulsatile in nature. On examination, a reddish mass was seen behind the tympanic membrane and an audible bruit is heard over the mastoid when auscultation with a stethoscope. Her Rinnie test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glomus tumour

The given clinical picture of a woman with progressive conductive hearing loss, tinnitus , reddis mass behind the tympanic membrane and audible bruit heard over the mastoid suggests a diagnosis of a ‘glomus tumor’.

Glomus tumor:

The cell of origin in the glomus tumor is paraganglionic cells (not perivascular cells). These cells are derived from the neural crest. They are paragangliomas of the glomus bodies found in the mastoid.

Glomus tumor is the most common benign neoplasm of the middle ear.

It is of 2 types:

* Glomus jugulare: Origin is from the dome of the jugular bulb causing neurological signs of IXth to XIIth cranial nerve involvement.

* Glomus tympanicum: Promontory in the  middle eari s the source of Glomus tympanicum. It produces auditory symptoms and occasionally facial paralysis.

The rule of 10 is seen in the glomus tumor. It comprises of

* 10% familial

* 10% multicentric

* 10% functional

It is 5 times more common in women. Common presenting features include:

* Progressive conductive hearing loss

* Tinnitus in glomus tumors is pulsatile, of swishing character, synchronous with a pulse, and can be temporarily stopped by carotid pressure.

* Audible bruit heard over the mastoid with a stethoscope in all stages

Investigations would include:

* Phelp's sign-on CECT scan helps to distinguish glomus tympanicum from the glomus jugulare tumor by identification of caroticojugular spine which is eroded in the latter.

* MRI gives the soft tissue extent of the tumor.

* Four vessel angiography is necessary when the CT head shows the involvement of a jugular bulb, carotid artery, or intradural extension.

* A biopsy is never done since it’s a highly vascular tumor.

The below-given image shows a triangular red-colored glomus tumor behind the tympanic membrane in the middle ear.

Pearl PF1487: Signs in Glomus Tumors

Sign

Seen on

What is seen

Rising sun

Otoscopy

Tumor arising from floor

Brown sign

Otoscopy

On increasing the ear canal pressure, tumor pulsates and then blanches

Phelp sign

CT

Loss of carotico-jugular crest

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy fell from the bed and developed swelling in the nose and difficulty in breathing. Examination revealed smooth rounded swellings on either side of the septum, through both the nares. On palpation, it was soft and fluctuant. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incision and drainage

This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.

Septal hematoma is caused due to collection of blood in between the perichondrium or periosteum and the cartilage of the nasal septum. It may be caused due to trauma, septal surgery, or spontaneously as in bleeding disorders.

Clinically, patients may present with bilateral nasal obstruction, pain, pressure over the nasal bridge, or a frontal headache. On examination, bilateral hematomas will be seen as purplish or reddish smooth swelling on either side of the septum. Palpation will reveal a soft, fluctuant swelling.

All septal hematomas must be drained to prevent the formation of septal abscess or organization of the hematoma by fibrosis leading to a permanently thickened septum. Drainage of the hematoma should be done either through aspiration with a wide gauge needle or through an incision made over the mucosa at the point of greatest fluctuation. It must be followed by nasal packing. Patients should thereafter be started on systemic antibiotics.

Given below are a clinical image and a illustrated image of septal hematoma.

Pearl PF1620: Septal Haematoma

* Septal hematoma is a collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum

* Causes: Trauma, septal surgery and bleeding disorders

* Clinical features: Bilateral nasal obstruction (most common presenting feature), frontal headache

* Treatment:

* Aspiration of small hematomas

* Incision and drainage of large hematomas followed by nasal packing

* Systemic antibiotics to prevent abscess formation

* Complications: Septal abscess, depression of dorsum, permanently thickened septum

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with ear wax and was subjected to syringing to remove the wax. She developed a syncopal episode while doing the procedure when the tip of the syringe touched the ear canal. Which of the nerves is responsible for this episode of syncope?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arnold's nerve

The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.

When the vagus nerve is stimulated, a parasympathetic response occurs leading to braycardia and decreased blood flow into the brain which causes syncope.

Nerve supply of External auditory canal:

* Anterior wall and roof- the auriculotemporal branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) (Option A).

* Posterior wall and floor - the auricular branch of Vagus (Arnold's nerve). Cough response while cleaning the ear canal is mediated by the vagus which also supplies the larynx.

* Posterior wall also receives sensory supply by the facial nerve (CN VII).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A school-going child presents with a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, mouth breathing, and impaired hearing. On examination, a high arched palate is noted. What is the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical picture is suggestive of adenoid hypertrophy. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

Indications of adenoidectomy:

* Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome, or speech abnormalities, i.e. (rhinolalia clausa)

* Recurrent rhinosinusitis

* Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid hyperplasia

* Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia

* Dental malocclusion. Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent their recurrence after orthodontic treatment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A worried mother brought her 6-year-old unimmunized child to the ER with complaints of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Examination reveals a bull-neck appearance and a pseudomembrane over the tonsils that bleeds when removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diphtheria

The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria.

Diphtheria is caused by the bacteria Corynebacterium diphtheriae which spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites.

Respiratory tract diphtheria is characterized by a thick, adherent pseudomembrane (grey or white) on one/both tonsils and adjacent pharynx. Underlying soft tissue oedema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance.

Patients with laryngeal diphtheria are at risk for suffocation because of local soft-tissue oedema and airway obstruction by the diphtheritic membrane.

Management includes antitoxin therapy as a single empirical dose of 20,000-100,000 units and antibiotics. Penicillin G/ Benzylpenicillin is the drug of choice for diphtheria. However, in case of an allergy to the same, Erythromycin is used. Other antibiotics used are clindamycin, rifampin, and tetracycline.

A greyish-white membrane forms over the tonsils in the oropharynx and spreads to the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils onto the soft palate and is dirty grey. It is adherent, and its removal leaves a bleeding surface. In the larynx, the diphtheritic membrane may cause airway obstruction.

Cervical lymph nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric, become enlarged and tender, sometimes presenting a bull-neck appearance. The patient is ill and toxaemic, but fever seldom rises above 38°C.

D/D for membrane over tonsil:

* Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms

* Diphtheria

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Vincent’s angina

* Leukaemia

* Candida

* Agranulocytosis

* Malignancy

* Aphthous ulcer

* Traumatic ulcer

Other options :

Option A: Infectious mononucleosis most commonly presents in adolescents with initial symptoms of fever, sore throat, fatigue, myalgia, and malaise. Pharyngitis is often the most prominent sign, with the enlargement of the tonsils and an exudate resembling that of streptococcal pharyngitis. It can be associated with tender, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

Option B: In acute membranous tonsillitis, exudates from the crypts coalesce to form a membrane on the surface of the tonsil that is easily wiped away without any bleeding.

Option D: Oral candidiasis/Oral thrush associated with candida albicans presents as white plaque-like lesions with cheesy exudate on an erythematous mucosa. They are typically painful and can be easily brushed off.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young lady presented to the ENT OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. Rinne test and fistula test were positive. She had refused treatment then and currently came with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. On examination, the fistula test was negative. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. False negative

The given clinical scenario indicates severe sensorineural hearing loss as a consequence of untreated suppurative labyrinthitis and Rinne's test is a false negative in this case.

Initially, the patient had a positive fistula test, which implies that the labyrinth is still functioning. Rinne's test is positive which could be due to normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss.

Currently, the patient has a negative fistula test which implies that the labyrinth is dead. This is an example of severe sensorineural hearing loss and here, Rinne test is a false negative.

If intermittent pressure applied to the external ear produces vertigo and nystagmus, it is a positive fistula test. The pressure changes in the external ear are transmitted to the labyrinth. This is suggestive of abnormal communication between the middle ear and the inner ear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the Battle sign?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mastoid ecchymosis

Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the petrous temporal bone.

An image showing Battle sign is shown below:

Pearl PF0033: Signs of base of skull fracture

Signs of Base of Skull Fracture

* Bilateral periorbital haematoma (raccoon eyes)

* Battle’s sign (bruising over mastoid)

* CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea

* Haemotympanum or bleeding from ear

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is part of trotter's triad, seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
options: Conductive hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, Contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Conductive hearing loss, Contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conductive hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis

Trotter’s triad seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma consists of conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, and palatal paralysis.

Trotter’s triad consists of the following:

* Conductive hearing loss due to Eustachian tube obstruction.

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia due to involvement of the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) which presents as facial pain.

* Palatal paralysis, due to involvement of the vagus nerve(CN X) which presents as palatal asymmetry.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true with respect to the Little's area?
options: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum.
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

The correct statement among the following is Option A, Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area.

Little's area:

Little’s area, situated at the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum is the most common site of epistaxis in children and young adults. 90% of bleeds arise from Little's area, where the Kiesselbach plexus is situated on the nasal septum.

Factors that increase the risk of epistaxis in children when compared to adults, include the habit of nose picking and increased friability of mucosa due to frequent upper respiratory tract infections.

Kiesselbach’s plexus:

Four arteries anastomose at the anterior inferior part of the nasal septum (Little's area) to form a vascular plexus called Kiesselbach’s plexus.

* Anterior ethmoidal

* Septal branch of the superior labial

* Septal branch of sphenopalatine

* Septal branch of the greater palatine

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the left posterior choanae. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Surgical excision

The most probable diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and the most appropriate step in its management is surgical excision.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma(JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumour seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Patients usually present with, profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis (most common presentation). A mass may be present in either the postnatal space, resulting in progressive nasal obstruction, or nasopharynx, where it may obstruct both choanae. The mass is firm in consistency, but digital palpation of the same should not be done. If the mass obstructs the eustachian tube, conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion may be observed. Proptosis, swelling of the cheeks, broadening of the nasal bridge, and involvement of 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves may occur.

JNA can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and carotid angiography. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space is a characteristic CT finding of JNA. This is known as the Holman-Miller sign or antral sign, as shown in the image below.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice though radiotherapy and chemotherapy monotherapy or in combination have also been used. Radiotherapy(Option C) is considered for recurrent inaccessible tumours. Chemotherapy with doxorubicin, vincristine, and dacarbazine is used in the case of very aggressive recurrent tumours and residual tumours. Hormonal therapy can be used as a primary or adjunctive treatment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old was brought to the emergency department with difficulty swallowing for the last few hours. The X-ray is given below. Which is the next best step to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophagoscopy

The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the given x-rays are suggestive of a foreign body lodged in the esophagus, most likely a coin/disc battery.

The given x-rays are anteroposterior and lateral views of the chest and neck. Coins, disk batteries, and small toy items are commonly ingested by children.

The flat surface of a coin in the esophagus is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) i.e; they are oriented in the coronal plane. The edge is seen on the lateral view. While coins in the trachea lie in the sagittal plane, those in the oesophagus typically lie in the coronal plane.

Presenting symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory distress is seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall.

Imaging with PA and lateral views of the chest and abdomen should be done.

Treatment includes the removal of the foreign body by esophagoscopy.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35- year old woman presented to the clinic with the symptoms of hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Further examination reveals conductive hearing loss with Rinne test negative. A reddish mass is seen behind the tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glomus tumor

This clinical scenario is suggestive of a glomus tumor.

Glomus tumor is the most common benign middle ear neoplasm. It is seen frequently in middle-aged females. The tumor consists of paraganglionic cells from the neural crest. Glomus tumor is an extremely vascular benign tumor.

There are two types of glomus tumors: glomus jugulare and glomus tympanicum. Glomus jugulare arises from the dome of the jugular bulb and invades the hypotympanum. Glomus tympanicum arises from the promontory of the middle ear.

Clinical features include conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus- earliest symptoms. Otoscopy examination shows a red reflex through an intact tympanic membrane as a "rising sun" appearance since the tumor arises from the floor of the middle ear. Paralysis of the 9th to 12th cranial nerves can also occur. An audible bruit over the mastoid is heard on auscultation in all the stages of the tumor.

Other options:

Option A: Acute otitis media presents with throbbing earache and a red and bulging tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks on examination. Tuning fork tests reveal a conductive type of hearing loss.

Option B: Chronic otitis media presents with mucoid or mucopurulent ear discharge, the conductive type of hearing loss, and central perforation of the tympanic membrane. Middle ear mucosa can be seen through the perforation.

Option D: Serous otitis media presents with hearing loss, delayed and defective speech, and mild earaches associated with upper respiratory tract infections. Otoscopy reveals a dull, opaque, and retracted tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex, a thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus, fluid levels, and air bubbles behind the tympanic membrane.

What is seen

Otoscopy

Otoscopy

CT

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman takes aspirin for a headache, later she presented with wheezing and breathlessness. These symptoms are likely to be associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nasal polyp

This clinical vignette is suggestive of aspirin intolerance. It is most likely to be associated with nasal polyps.

In a patient with Samter's triad, aspirin should be avoided due to the risk of the development of aspirin intolerance.

Samter triad is a non-IgE mediated hypersensitivity reaction associated with the intake of aspirin or other cyclooxygenase inhibitors. Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of:

* Nasal polyposis

* Bronchial asthma

* Aspirin intolerance

Patients with Samter's triad will have persistent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, nasal polyps, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis. Asthma and aspirin intolerance develop later.

Acute asthma attacks usually occur 3 hours after intake of aspirin or NSAIDs. Severe rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, facial flushing, and periorbital edema are also seen. Aspirin-induced hypersensitivity reactions also may occur.

Patients should avoid aspirin and NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1. Treatment may involve aspirin desensitization and endoscopic sinus surgery.

Pearl PF1083: Ethmoidal polyps

* Main etiological factor is allergy

* Usually affects the middle-aged

* Site of origin: Lateral wall of the nose

* Clinical features: Nasal stuffiness, headache (due to sinusitis), sneezing, watery nasal discharge, anosmia/ hyposmia, mass protruding from the nasal cavity

* Findings:

* Anterior rhinoscopy: Multiple, bilateral polypi that are smooth, glistening, grape-like masses often pale in color

* They may be sessile or pedunculated, insensitive to probing and do not bleed on touch

* Investigation of choice: NCCT

* Treatment of choice: FESS

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the clinic by her mother with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringitis bullosa

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with hearing loss for the past 2-3 months and vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane is suggestive of myringitis bullosa.

Bullous myringitis (myringitis bullosa haemorrhagica) is the finding of vesicles in the superficial layer of the tympanic membrane without affecting the contents of the external or middle ear. If the middle ear becomes involved, this would be consistent with acute otitis media. It occurs due to infection by influenza virus or by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Bloody otorrhea can occur when a bulla rupture and is referred to as bullous hemorrhagic myringitis.

Option B: Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.

Option C: Acute otitis media is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache and hearing loss is seen in later stages. Otoscopy shows a red and bulging tympanic membrane.

Option D: Myringitis granulosa is characterized by granulations on the outer surface of the tympanic membrane. It is associated with long-standing foreign body, wax impaction, and external ear infection.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with unilateral nasal obstruction associated with watery nasal discharge and bleeding. A diagnosis of inverted papilloma is made. Which of the following is true about this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benign and invasive

Inverted papilloma is a benign and invasive tumor.

Inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor or transitional cell papilloma or Schneiderian papilloma) is a benign neoplasm of the non-olfactory mucosa of the nose (also called the Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses. The lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus is the most common site of origin.

The hyperplastic papillomatous tissue grows into the stroma. It is common in the 4th to 7th decades of life with a male preponderance. Clinical features are unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. It is almost always unilateral. It can invade sinuses or the orbit, resulting in proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.

An examination of the nose or endoscopy shows a polypoidal mass resembling simple nasal polyps. A computed tomography(CT) scan and/or magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) show the location and extent of the lesion.

MRI is used to differentiate associated secretions in the sinus from the actual tumor mass. A biopsy is essential for diagnosis.

Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice, done preferably via endoscopy. Malignancy has been observed in up to 15% of the cases.

Pearl PF1087: Inverted Papilloma

* Inverted papilloma is also known as transitional cell papilloma or Ringertz tumor or Schneiderian papilloma

* It is the most common benign tumor of the nasal cavity

* It is a premalignant condition with 10-15% chances of turning malignant

* Etiology: Human papilloma virus has been implicated in its etiology

* Origin: Arises from the lateral wall of the nose from the non-olfactory epithelium of nose

* Clinical features:

* More common in males

* The age group most commonly affected is 40-70 years

* Unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis are the main presenting symptoms

* It is a locally invasive tumor and can invade orbit and paranasal sinuses.

* Proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation can result from orbital invasion

* Findings:

* It is seen as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a simple nasal polyp

* Investigations: A biopsy is needed for diagnosis

* Treatment: Medial maxillectomy via lateral rhinotomy or midfacial degloving approach

* Radiotherapy can lead to malignancy

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with painful vesicles in the external auditory meatus and over the tympanic membrane. In addition to that, he also has facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis and which is the site that is affected?
options: Ramsay Hunt syndrome and basal ganglion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion

This clinical vignette is suggestive of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and the geniculate ganglion is affected.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome, also called herpes zoster oticus, is a late complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection that results in inflammation of the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

The causative agent, the varicella-zoster virus, is a double-stranded DNA virus. Clinical features are facial paralysis along with vesicular rash in the external auditory canal and pinna. Intense pain around the ear in addition to the vesicles also occurs. There may also be anesthesia of the face, giddiness, and hearing impairment due to the involvement of the Vth and VIIIth nerves.

Facial nerve palsy on the affected side, vesicles in the external acoustic meatus & auricle, and pain in the ear form the classic triad.

The illustration given below shows the clinical features seen in Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

The treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves antiviral medications like acyclovir or famciclovir, as well as corticosteroids like prednisone.

Melkersson syndrome presents with a triad of facial paralysis, swelling of the face and lips, and furrows in the tongue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with thick nasal discharge and headache. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the inferior turbinate with a mulberry appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypertrophic rhinitis

This clinical vignette is suggestive of hypertrophic rhinitis.

It is characterized by the thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucous glands, periosteum, and bone.

Recurrent nasal infections, chronic sinusitis, chronic irritation of nasal mucosa due to smoking, prolonged use of nasal drops, vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, and industrial irritants are some of the causes of hypertrophic rhinitis.

Clinical features are thick and sticky nasal discharge, headache, and transient anosmia. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the turbinates with underlying fibrosis. Mulberry hypertrophy is seen in hypertrophic rhinitis. Maximum changes are seen in the inferior turbinate.

Treatment includes cryosurgery of turbinates, linear cauterisation, submucosal diathermy, partial or total turbinectomy and lasers.

Pearl PF1339: Clinical Features of Atrophic Rhinitis

* More common in females

* Usually starts at puberty

* It is a bilateral condition

* Symptoms:

* Foul smell from the nose

* Nasal obstruction in spite of roomy chambers due to large crusts filling nasal cavity

* Epistaxis on removing of the crusts

* Anosmia due to degeneration of nerve elements (merciful anosmia)

* Signs:

* Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinates and septum

* After removal of crusts, nasal cavities appear roomy with atrophy of turbinates

* Nasal mucosa appears pale

Pearl PF1084: Antrochoanal Polyp

* Main etiological factors: Infection and allergy

* Usually affects children

* Site of origin: Mucosa of the maxillary antrum

* Clinical features:

* Usually single and unilateral

* Unilateral nasal obstruction which becomes bilateral when it grows posteriorly and obstructs opposite choana

* Mucoid nasal discharge

* Hyponasal voice

* Findings:

* Grows posteriorly and usually missed on anterior rhinoscopy

* Posterior rhinoscopy: Globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx

* Investigation of choice: Nasal endoscopy. Shows nasal polyps that are pale, gelatinous and pedunculated

* Treatment of choice: FESS

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocal nodule

This clinical scenario is suggestive of a vocal nodule.

Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes. It occurs at the mid-membranous portion of the vocal cords at the free edge. It is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus is subjected to maximum trauma. It presents as bilateral swellings in the vocal cords.

Vocal nodules occur due to vocal trauma when a person speaks in a loud voice for prolonged periods. They mostly affect teachers, actors, vendors, or pop singers.

Symptoms of vocal nodules are hoarseness, vocal fatigue, and pain in the neck on prolonged phonation.

Treatment includes educating the patient on proper use of voice. Surgery is reserved for patients who remain symptomatic despite voice therapy.

Option A: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting which results in hemorrhage and edema of the vocal cord.Affected individuals present with hoarseness of voice and diplophonia(double voice). Other factors associated with it are allergy and cigarette smoking. It presents as a benign swelling on the free edge of the vocal cord.

Option B: Vocal cysts are retention cysts due to blockage of seromucinous glands of the laryngeal mucosa. They occur in the false vocal cords.

Option D: Reinke's edema is the collection of fluid in Reinke's space. Affected individuals present with diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. Treatment involves the removal of gelatinous collection by a longitudinal incision on the vocal cord.

Pearl PF0616: Muscles of larynx

Remember 2 exceptions:

* All muscles are adductors, except PCA (an abductor)

* All muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, except cricothyroid (superior laryngeal nerve)

Action

Muscle

Opening of the inlet of larynx

Thyroepiglotticus

Closing of the inlet of larynx

Aryepiglotticus, Interarytenoids

Abductor of vocal cords

Posterior cricoarytenoid

Adductor of vocal cords

Lateral cricoarytenoid

Tensor of vocal cords

Cricothyroid

Relaxer of vocal cord

Thyroarytenoid

Vocalis

Safety muscle of larynx: Posterior cricoarytenoid

Safety muscle of tongue: Genioglossus

The muscle of whispering: Lateral cricoarytenoid

Vocalis is known as the modulator of larynx because, the anterior part of the vocalis muscle can tense the vocal cord, and its posterior part can relax the vocal cord.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female patient presented as shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Diabetic patients with local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resemble the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus Oryza.

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness, followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The image below shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis:

Risk factors:

* Diabetes (diabetic ketoacidosis).

* Immunocompromised individuals

Treatment of the infection includes 4 steps:

* Initiation of therapy (amphotericin B) as early as possible. Posaconazole can also be used in the management of this condition.

* Surgical debridement

* Reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors

* Treatment of underlying malignancy if present.

The image below shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis:

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of a black or greyish membranes in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.

Pearl PF0822: Classification of fungus based on morphology

Fungi are classified into 4 types based on their morphology:

* Yeast

* Yeast-like

* Molds

* Dimorphic fungi

Yeast:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding

* Oval to round forms

* Example: Cryptococcus, Saccharomyces.

Yeast like:

* Unicellular fungi

* Reproduces by budding or binary fission

* Spherical or oval forms

* Pseudohyphae may be seen.

* Example: Candida, Malassezia furfur.

Molds/filamentous fungi:

* Have hyphae which may be septate or aseptate

* Aseptate or coenocytic hyphae – Rhizopus, mucor, Lichtheimia.

* Septate hyphae – Penicillium, Dermatophytes, Aspergillus, fusarium.

Dimorphic fungi

* Filamentous forms in the culture at 220C – 250C and in the environment.

* Yeast form in the culture at 370C and in tissues.

* Examples – Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides immitis, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Talaromyces marneffei, Sporothrix schenckii.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the sinus marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maxillary sinus

The sinus marked in the non-contrast CT image is the maxillary sinus.

Paranasal sinuses are air-containing cavities in that are present in the bones of the skull. These paranasal sinuses have been divided into two groups:

Anterior group: It includes,

* Maxillary sinus(Antrum of highmore)

* Frontal sinus

* Anterior ethmoidal.

All of the above sinuses open in the middle meatus and their ostia lie anterior to basal lamella of middle turbinate.

Posterior group: It includes,

* Posterior ethmoidal sinuses: Opens in the superior meatus

* Sphenoid sinus: Opens in sphenoethmoidal recess.

Note:

Maxillary and Ethmoid sinuses( including both anterior and posterior ethmoidal sinuses) are present at birth. The frontal and the sphenoid sinuses are not present at birth.

The sinuses seen in Water's view is marked in the Xray below:

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the function of utricle and saccule?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Linear acceleration

The function of utricle and saccule is linear acceleration.

Utricle and saccule which contain sensory epithelium called macula that are stimulated by linear acceleration and deceleration or gravitational pull during the head tilts.

The ampullated end of each semicircular canal contains a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium called crista ampullaris that respond to angular acceleration and deceleration.

Hearing is mediated by the organ of Corti on the basilar membrane of the inner ear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with CSF otorrhea?
options: Traumatic rupture of the tympanic membrane
Fracture of the roof of the nose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Battle sign

A battle sign is seen in CSF otorrhea.

Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the temporal bone. CSF leak is associated with head trauma and fracture of the temporal bone. It can present as CSF otorrhea or CSF rhinorrhea or both.

Signs in basilar skull fractures:

* Hemotympanum: Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of basilar fracture.

* Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa.

* Retroauricular or mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign): Pooled blood behind the ears in the mastoid region is associated with fractures to the middle cranial fossa.

* CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: Double target sign, a double-ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen.

Spontaneous resolution is seen within 14 days. Perioperative fluorescein cisternography is used for identifying the site of leakage. Persistent CSF leaks and large tegmen defects are treated with surgery due to the risk of herniation of the meninges and the brain.

Pearl PF1086: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: Reservoir sign is also seen in acute mastoiditis/ coalescent mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to cause mucormycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broad spectrum antibiotics

Among the given options, the condition least likely to cause mucormycosis is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about laryngeal cancer stage T1b N0 M0?
options: Both vocal cords involved and fixed
Both vocal cords involved and mobile
One vocal cord involved and fixed
One vocal cord involved and mobile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Both vocal cords involved and mobile

In stage T1b N0 M0 laryngeal cancer, both the vocal cords are involved and are mobile.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms does a patient with Reinke's edema classically present with?
options: Dysphagia of liquids more than solids
Dysphagia of solids more than liquids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysphonia

Dysphonia is the classic symptom that a patient with Reinke's edema presents with.

Reinke’s edema is a bilateral symmetrical swelling of the membraneous part of vocal cords. It is most commonly seen in middle aged smokers. It is also known as diffuse vocal polyposis or smoker’s larynx.

The classical symptom seen in this condition is hoarseness of voice (dysphonia). Patients can also present with a low pitched monotonous voice.

On examination of the larynx, the vocal cords appear swollen and edematous with a pale translucent look.

Treatment mainly consists of microlaryngoscopic stripping of the vocal cords. It should be done in two stages, taking one cord at a time to prevent anterior glottic web formation.

Other options

Option A - Diplophonia (double pitch) occurs when the vocal folds produce two distinct pitches simultaneously, often from uneven vibration. This can also be seen in Reinke’s edema.

Options C and D - Dysphagia is not a symptom of Reinke’s edema as it is a laryngeal pathology. Dysphagia of liquids more than solids is commonly seen in achalasia cardia. Tumors of the esophagus show dysphagia for solids more than liquids.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient with hearing loss underwent an audiogram, which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otosclerosis

The above Pure tone audiogram is characteristic of Otosclerosis.

In the above audiogram,

* An air-bone gap is present.

* BC > AC

This is suggestive of Conductive Hearing loss. In the above options, only Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss. Carhart’s notch is the characteristic dip in the BC curve at 2000 Hz seen in otosclerosis. It disappears after successful stapes surgery.

PTA in Sensorineural hearing loss :

* Shows no Air Bone gap.

* Both BC and AC are in hearing loss range (>25 DB)

Other options:

* Meniere’s disease shows a low-frequency loss in the SNHL curve.

* Noise-induced hearing loss is SNHL and PTA shows characteristic Acoustic dip at 4000 Hz.

* Ototoxicity causes SNHL and shows high-frequency hearing loss in the SNHL curve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40 year old male patient presented with pain and hearing loss after trauma to his right ear. Otoscopy reveals the presence of blood clots along with irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane. What is the next step in management in this case?
options: Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics

In this case, the presence of blood clots and irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane suggests traumatic injury to the ear. The initial management involves keeping the ear dry to prevent infection and further damage.

When a patient presents with pain and hearing loss after trauma to the ear, it's important to manage the condition appropriately. Systemic analgesics can be prescribed to alleviate pain.

Other options:

* It's important to avoid introducing any foreign substances into the ear canal, such as ear drops or irrigation, as this can exacerbate the injury and increase the risk of infection.

* Aspirating and performing audiometry may be considered later in the management process, once the acute phase has resolved and the extent of damage needs further evaluation.

* Giving gentamicin and levofloxacin or other antibiotics is not indicated at this stage unless there are signs of infection, as prophylactic antibiotic use is generally not recommended due to the risk of promoting antibiotic resistance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50 year old male presents with pain in his right ear. He is diagnosed with right sided otitis media after investigations. He also adds that he recurrently gets these ear infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis in a 50 year old male with recurrent otitis media is most likely nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking. It commonly occurs in males in the 5th to 7th decade. The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with the following symptoms:

* Nasal - obstruction, discharge, rhinolalia clausa, epistaxis

* Ear - eustachian tube obstruction leading to conductive hearing loss or recurrent otitis media.

* Ophthalmoneurologic - all the cranial nerves (CN) may be involved.

* CN VI - squint and diplopia

* CN III, IV, VI, - ophthalmoplegia

* CN V - reduced corneal reflex

* CN II - exophthalmos

* CN IX, X, XI - jugular foramen syndrome

* Horner’s syndrome

* Cervical lymph node metastasis

* Distant metastasis to the bone, liver, and lung.

Examination of the ear shows a dull tympanic membrane and audiometry shows a Type B curve due to the presence of fluid in the middle ear. The presence of unilateral serous otitis media in an adult suggests nasopharyngeal growth.

Trotter's triad consists of ipsilateral conductive hearing loss (eustachian tube blockage), trigeminal neuralgia of the mandibular division, and palatal asymmetry due to the involvement of the CN X may be seen. This triad occurs in malignant tumors of the lateral nasopharyngeal wall due to extensive invasion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of spontaneous nasal bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is taken, which is shown below. Which of the following is not true regarding this patient's condition?
options: Biopsy is the investigation of choice
Blood supply is mostly from the external carotid artery.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biopsy is the investigation of choice

The given clinical picture along with a CT scan showing the Holman-Miller sign is suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma commonly arising from the sphenopalatine foramen. The statement "Biopsy is the investigation of choice" is incorrect because in this condition, biopsy is avoided due to the risk of bleeding.

It is a benign tumor, which commonly arises from the sphenopalatine foramen. From here, the tumor grows into the:

* Nasal cavity

* Nasopharynx

* Pterygopalatine fossa

* Pterygomaxillary fossa

* Infratemporal fossa

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males in the age group of 10-20 years. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity that is close to the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen. These patients have a hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the nasopharynx that forms angiofibroma when testosterone appears. Therefore, it is thought to be testosterone-dependent.

Angiofibroma can extend into the nasal cavity causing obstruction, epistaxis, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, cheek, orbits causing proptosis, frog-face deformity, and cranial cavity. The clinical features include:

* Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis- most common

* Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech- due to mass in the postnasal space

* Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion- due to obstruction of the eustachian tube

* Sessile, lobulated, or smooth mass in the nasopharynx

* Other clinical features include the broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling, involvement of IInd, IIIrd, IVth, and VIth cranial nerves

Diagnosis is based on the clinical picture. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is the investigation of choice that reveals anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (antral sign/Holman-Miller sign) which is pathognomonic of angiofibroma as shown below.

MRI can also be done that reveals soft tissue extensions. Carotid angiography is also done which shows the extent of the tumor with its vascularity. The feeding vessels mostly come from the external carotid artery. In large tumors with intracranial extension, vessels come from the internal carotid system also.

Given below is a CT image showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus - antral sign or Holman-Miller sign.

Staging of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

Stage
Spread

IA
Limited to the nose and/or nasopharynx

IB
Extension into ≥ one paranasal sinus

IIA
Minimal extension into the sphenopalatine foramen with minimal part of pterygopalatine fossa

IIB
Full occupation of pterygopalatine fossa with Holman-Miller sign, may with an erosion of orbital bones

IIC
Extension into the cheek, temporal fossa, or posterior to pterygoids through the pterygomaxillary fossa

IIIA
Erosion of skull base with minimal intracranial

IIIB
Erosion of skull base with extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

Treatment: Surgical approach is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery. Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was diagnosed with croup. Which of the following types of stridor will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inspiratory stridor

This child has croup, which would most likely be associated with inspiratory stridor.

In croup, the sudden onset of prominent inspiratory stridor is characteristic, although a softer expiratory stridor may also be present. As the severity increases, a biphasic stridor is heard along with visible suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions.

Croup, or laryngotracheobronchitis, is a viral infection affecting the upper airway, primarily in children aged 6 months to 6 years. The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus. While other viruses like influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus can also cause croup, parainfluenza is the predominant cause.

The severity of croup is determined by the Westley croup score.

* Mild croup – Stridor may be present when upset or crying but it is not present at rest. Barking cough, hoarse cry, and either no or only mild chest wall/subcostal retractions are seen.

* Moderate croup- Stridor is present at rest. Mild retractions are at least present. Children may have other symptoms or signs of respiratory distress. The child does not appear agitated.

* Severe croup – Stridor is present at rest. Retractions are severe that include indrawing of the sternum. The child may appear anxious, and agitated.

Hospitalization is done in a child for any of the following:

* progressive stridor,

* severe stridor at rest,

* respiratory distress,

* hypoxia,

* cyanosis,

* depressed mental status,

* poor oral intake

Treatment:

1. Racemic epinephrine nebulization - It causes narrowing of pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa. This lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and promotes the reabsorption of fluid from the interstitial space and thus reduces edema. The indications for the administration of nebulized epinephrine are:

* moderate to severe stridor at rest

* The possible need for intubation

* respiratory distress

* hypoxia

2. Oral dexamethasone - Indicated in all the grades of croup. Corticosteroids reduce laryngeal edema through their anti-inflammatory action. IM dexamethasone and nebulized budesonide have an equal clinical effect. Corticosteroids should not be administered to children with varicella or tuberculosis as they may worsen the disease.

3. A helium-oxygen mixture (heliox) may be considered for severe croup when intubation is being considered. Oxygen recommented for child with spo2 <92% i.e in hypoxia
Note: Antibiotics are not indicated.

The image below shows a steeple sign, seen in croup.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A male patient presents with nasal obstruction, foul-smelling nasal discharge, and loss of smell. Endoscopic findings are shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrophic rhinitis

The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and the endoscopic findings points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known. It is more common in females and starts around puberty.

Clinically patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, and merciful anosmia. Merciful anosmia is when the patient has marked anosmia and is unable to smell the foul odor coming from their nose.

On examination of the nose, greenish or greyish crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. The roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment:

* Nasal irrigation - using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate 1 part, sodium biborate 1 part, sodium chloride 2 parts in 280 mL of water.

* Local antibiotics - Kemicetine antiozena solution containing chloromycetin, estradiol, and vitamin D2.

* 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, systemic use of streptomycin, potassium iodide, placental extract.

* Surgical management:

* Young's operation: In this procedure, flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both the nostrils are completely closed and are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa may revert to normal and the crusting is reduced.

* Modified Young's operation: In this procedure, the nostrils are partially closed and thereby avoiding the discomfort of complete closure of the nostrils. The results are the same compared to Young's operation.

* Narrowing of the nasal cavity can be done by submucosal injection of Teflon paste, or by insertion of fat, cartilage, or Teflon strips under the mucoperiosteum.

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps. They present with a polypoid mass in the nose.

Option C: Allergic rhinitis is associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy and can cause chronic nasal obstruction. It is characterized by watery nasal discharge, sneezing, and itching in the nose.

Option D: Foreign body nose is commonly seen in children. The child presents with unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the findings as shown in the image below. What is the most likely voice abnormality that would be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhinolalia clausa

The image shown above is indicative of adenoid hypertrophy. Patients with this condition would present with rhinolalia clausa.

Adenoid hypertrophy occurs in response to allergens or infections. It is more common in children. Affected children typically present with symptoms of nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and rhinolalia clausa (loss of nasal tone of voice).

They may also experience aprosexia (inability to concentrate) leading to declining academic performance. These children have characteristic adenoid facies marked by a dull expression, open mouth, hitched-up upper lip, pinched-in nose, high arched palate, and crowded upper teeth.

Other options:

* Rhinolalia aperta is hypernasality seen in Velopharyngeal insufficiency etc.

* Muffled and thick speech, often called “hot potato voice” is seen in peritonsillar abscess or quinsy.

* Staccato voice is broken speech and is seen in multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. The fiberoptic laryngoscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocal nodule

The swollen area in the given image and the clinical scenario is suggestive of vocal nodules.

Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes. It is present at the junction of anterior one-third with the posterior two thirds. It is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus is subjected to maximum trauma.

Vocal nodules occur due to vocal trauma when person speaks in unnatural low tones for prolonged periods or at high intensities. They mostly affect teachers, actors, vendors or pop singers.

Nodule:

* Early stages soft, reddish and oedematous swellings

* Later stages - greyish or white in colour

Symptoms:

* Hoarseness

* Vocal fatigue

* Pain in the neck on prolonged phonation

Treatment:

* Educating the patient in proper use of voice.

* Surgery is required for large nodules or nodules of long standing in adults. They are excised with precision.

Other options:

Option A: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting which results in hemorrhage and edema of the vocal cord.Affected individuals present with hoarseness of voice and diplophonia(double voice). Other factors associated with it are allergy and cigarette smoking. It presents as a benign swelling on the free edge of the vocal cord.

Option B: Vocal cysts: These are retention cysts due to blockage of seromucinous glands of the laryngeal mucosa. They occur in the false vocal cords.

Option D: Reinke's edema is the collection of fluid in Reinke's space. Affected individuals present with diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. Treatment involves the removal of gelatinous collection by a longitudinal incision on the vocal cord.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea. Investigations revealed that his HbA1C is 10%. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease. Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

The treatment of malignant otitis external would include control of diabetes, ear toileting to remove the discharge, debris or granulation tissue, antibiotic therapy against Pseudomonas with fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, beta-lactam antibiotics with/without aminoglycosides.

If the patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the given instrument:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tracheo-esophageal prosthesis

The instrument shown above is a Blom-Singer prosthesis. Blom-Singer prosthesis and Panje prosthesis are types of tracheoesophageal prosthesis.

A tracheoesophageal prosthesis(TEP) involves a one-way valve that is inserted through a previously-created tracheoesophageal puncture. When the patient occludes the stoma, the exhaled air is shunted through the TEP into the oesophagus, where it induces vibration of the upper oesophagal sphincter, which is responsible for phonation. It generates the most intelligible, fluent, natural-sounding voice in contrast to other laryngeal speech methods.

Vocal rehabilitation after total laryngectomy is broadly divided into:

* Esophageal speech

* Artificial larynx

* Tracheo-oesophageal speech

Other options:

Transoral pneumatic device is an artificial larynx used in those who fail to learn oesophageal speech. The vibrations generated in a rubber diaphragm are carried by a plastic tube into the back of the oral cavity. Here the sound is converted into speech by modulators. It uses expired air from the tracheostome to vibrate the diaphragm.

Electrolarynx produces vibrations that are transmitted through the skin toward the throat. The sound generated is converted into low-pitch speech by the vocal tract—palate, tongue, and teeth. The advantages are that is easy and quick to learn, while the disadvantages are that the voice is monotonous and the constant occupation of one hand.

Mendelsohn maneuver is a form of a supraglottic swallow. It is done by voluntarily holding the larynx at its maximum height to prolong the duration of the cricopharyngeal opening. It has been used to treat patients with pharyngeal dysphagia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The audiogram of a patient who presented with a gradually progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo is given below. Which among the following would be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ménière's disease

The given audiogram is seen in Ménière's disease in its early stages. It shows an upsloping/ascending curve suggesting that the lower frequencies are affected first.

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, and sound-induced hearing loss have downsloping audiograms since the higher frequencies are affected first in these conditions.

Points to remember in PTA audiogram:

* AC abnormal, BC normal, Air-bone gap present – conductive deafness

* Downsloping/descending audiogram- higher frequencies affected first like in presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise induced hearing loss.

* Upsloping/ascending audiogram - lower frequencies are affected first like in early stages of Meniere's disease.

* U shaped/trough shaped/cookie bite shaped audiogram suggests midfrequency hearing loss and is seen in congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis.

* Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

* Carhartz notch - dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The radiograph shown below is done for better assessment of the sinuses. What is the common name of this view?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Towne's view

The radiograph shown above shows Towne's view.

Towne's view is taken with the patient in the supine position and lying on his back with the chin often depressed into the neck. The X-ray camera is angled at 30 degrees towards the feet so that the rays enter the head at the level of the hairline.

* This is usually taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

* Bilateral petrous pyramids are visible in this view and hence can be compared.

Structures seen are:

* Arcuate eminence and superior semicircular canal.

* Mastoid antrum.

* Internal auditory canal.

* Tympanic cavity.

* Cochlea.

* External auditory canal.

The image below shows Towne's view

Other options:

Option A: Waters' view (also known as the Occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view, where an X-ray beam is angled at 37° to the orbitomeatal line. The rays are passed from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate. It is commonly used to get a better view of the maxillary sinuses.

Option C: Caldwell's view (also known as the occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position) is a radiographic view of the skull, where the X-ray plate is angled at 15° to the orbito-meatal line. The rays pass from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate. It is commonly used to get a better view of frontal sinuses.

Option D: Submentovertical view/ Hirtz view/ basal view is taken with vertex near the film and X-ray beam projected at right angles to the film from the submental area. It is commonly used to get a better view of the sphenoid sinuses.

Pearl PF1596: Radiographic views of paranasal sinuses and mastoid

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about laryngomalacia?
options: Patient will present with an inspiratory stridor.
It is the most common congenital cause of stridor in children.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stridor improves in supine position.

In laryngomalacia, stridor improves in prone position.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of stridor. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis.  It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. Stridor is increased on crying but improves (decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal.

Direct laryngoscopy shows -

* Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself (omega-shaped)

* Floppy aryepiglottic folds, and

* Prominent arytenoids

A flexible laryngoscope is very useful to make the diagnosis. Laryngomalacia cannot be visualized in a paralyzed patient.

The below image shows the omega-shaped epiglottis:

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:

* Mostly, it self corrects by 2 years of age.

* Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.

* Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old child was eating peanuts when he suddenly developed respiratory distress, cough, and was unable to speak. What is the initial treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Perform Heimlich maneuver

In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts.

The rescuer should stand or kneel behind the patient and wrap his arms around the patient’s waist. A fist is made with one hand and using the other hand, the fist is driven into the patient’s abdomen with a rapid, forceful upward thrust so as to dislodge the foreign body. This is continued until the foreign body is expelled or if the patient becomes unresponsive.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

In a choking infant who is responsive, 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades and 5 downward thrusts on the chest are given in order to dislodge the foreign body.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

Other Options:

Option A: The blind finger sweep should be avoided in infants to avoid pushing the object further inside the airway. However, it can be done for unresponsive adults with complete FBAO. With the patient's face up, the mouth is opened by grasping both the tongue and lower jaw and lifting the mandible. The index finger is inserted along the inside of the cheek and using a hooking action, the foreign body is dislodged and removed.

Option B: Endoscopic removal is wrong as an initial treatment because it's not an immediate life-saving measure and requires time to set up and organize. It can be attempted once the airway is stabilized.

Option C: Immediate X-ray is wrong as initial treatment because it delays essential life-saving intervention. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque (especially peanuts) and the patient needs immediate intervention for respiratory distress.

questions.subject: ENT
