questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old boy complains of swelling and severe pain in his right ear associated with high-grade fever and profuse ear discharge. Clinical examination shows mastoid tenderness and perforation of the tympanic membrane. On examination, the swelling extends anteriorly to the right zygoma with a punctum over the right tragus, as shown below. Which type of abscess is most likely indicated in this area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Luc's abscess

Luc's abscess is most likely indicated in the given clinical vignette.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute mastoiditis that has occurred as a complication of acute infection of the middle ear. If the pus in this infection breaks through the bony wall between the antrum and external osseous meatus, it results in the formation of a Luc abscess (meatal abscess) and presents as a swelling in the deep part of the bony meatus.

Other abscesses related to mastoid infection:

* Postauricular abscess—the most common abscess that forms over the mastoid. In infants and children, this presents over MacEwen’s triangle.

* Zygomatic abscess—infection of the zygomatic air cells. It is situated at the posterior root of the zygoma

* Bezold abscess—In this case, the pus breaks through the medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck

* Citelli’s abscess—Here, the abscess is formed posterior to the mastoid, occupying a position more towards the occipital bone

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents with a long history of nasal obstruction, which is worse during inspiration. On anterior rhinoscopy, no obvious growth is noted. During examination, when the cheek is pulled laterally, the obstruction improves and the patient breathes comfortably through the affected nostril. Which of the following forms the lateral boundary of the site of obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper lateral cartilage

The above clinical scenario of a 32-year-old male, with nasal obstruction on normal anterior rhinoscopy, and a positive Cottle's Test (when the cheek is pulled laterally, the obstruction improves and the patient breathes comfortably through the affected nostril), which indicated that the site of obstruction was Internal nasal valve, the lateral boundary of this area is formed by the upper lateral cartilage.

The Internal Nasal valve is the narrowest portion of the nasal passage. It is bounded medially by the nasal septum, superiorly and laterally by the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage, and inferiorly by the floor of the piriform aperture. The nasal valve is the specific slit-like segment between the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage and the septum.

Conditions with a positive Cottle's test:

* Deviated nasal septum

* Collapsed nasal valve - causes snoring and sleep apnoea

* Valve stenosis

The image below depicts Cottle's test:

Pearl PF2211: Boundaries of the nasal valve

* Laterally: Lower border of upper lateral cartilage and fibrofatty tissue and anterior end of inferior turbinate

* Medially: Cartilaginous nasal septum

* Caudally: Floor of the pyriform aperture

The nasal valve is the narrowest part and offers maximum resistance to airflow

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the outpatient department by his mother with irritability, poor school performance, and a history of recurrent ear infections. Otoscopic examination shows a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid behind it. There is no blood clot present in the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Otitis media with effusion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient's history of recurrent ear infections and dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid and absent blood clots points to the diagnosis of otitis media with effusion (OME).

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, otitis media with effusion (OME), mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media:

* Rinne negative (BC>AC).

* Weber—lateralized towards the worse ear

* Audiogram—AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

* Impedance audiometry—flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side)

A B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media. Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve. This results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below:

Note: The tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear.

Other options:

Option B: Cartwheel appearance is seen in acute otitis media. It is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache, and hearing loss is seen in later stages.

Option C: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid that leads to bone destruction. It can be congenital or acquired, with acquired cases arising from tympanic membrane retraction or epithelial migration through a perforation. The expanding mass erodes nearby structures, potentially causing serious complications.

Option D: Tympanosclerosis involves calcification and fibrosis of the tympanic membrane, usually following chronic otitis media. It does not cause bone erosion or a retraction pocket.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD with a history of URTI and poor academic performance. He breathes through his mouth and has a high-arched palate. What type of hearing loss can be expected in this child? URTI- Upper respiratory tract infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conductive hearing loss

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing and a high-arched palate points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by conductive hearing loss.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterised by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of the tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably rhinolalia clausa (hyponasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, or tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild earaches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* A thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterised by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high-arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss, and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Primary auditory canal cholesteatoma is characterised by normal hearing.

Option C: Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic condition characterised by sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary abnormalities (such as two different coloured eyes or early graying of hair), and dystopia canthorum (widely spaced eyes).

Option D: A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought to the paediatric clinic by his parents, with complaints of difficulty breathing through the nose, frequent mouth breathing, and speech difficulties. The child has visible crowding of the upper front teeth and frequently complains of ear discomfort. On examination, the child has nasal obstruction and enlarged adenoids, as seen on nasopharyngoscopy. Otoscopic examination reveals bilateral dull tympanic membranes, as well as mild conductive hearing loss. Which type of tympanogram is most likely to appear in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type B Tympanogram

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, malocclusion of teeth, nasal obstruction and enlarged adenoids, along with bilateral dull tympanic membranes, points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by a type B curve on a tympanogram.

Pearl PF2005: Myringotomy

Indications:

* Acute suppurative otitis media:

* Severe earache with the bulging tympanic membrane.

* Incomplete resolution with opaque drum and persistent conductive deafness.

* Complications of acute otitis media,e.g.facialparalysis, labyrinthitis or meningitis with the bulging tympanic membrane.

* Serous otitis media.

* Aero-otitis media (to drain fluid and “unlock” the eustachian tube).

* Atelectatic ear (grommet is often inserted for long-term aeration).

Contraindication: Suspected intratympanic glomus tumor.

Incisions:

* In acute suppurative otitis media, a circumferential incision is made in the posteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane, midway between the handle of malleus and tympanic annulus, avoiding injury to the incudostapedial joint.

* In serous otitis media, a small radial incision is given in the anteroinferior quadrant and all the effusion is sucked out.

Complications:

* Injury to incudostapedial joint or stapes.

* Injury to jugular bulb with profuse bleeding, if jugular bulb is high and floor of the middle ear dehiscent.

* Middle ear infection.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old male diagnosed with maxillary sinus carcinoma undergoes surgery. The operative field is shown below. What is the name of the surgical procedure performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total maxillectomy

The given image shows a large post-surgical cavity following removal of the entire maxilla and palate, creating an oronasal defect with resection extending to the floor of the orbit, findings consistent with a total maxillectomy.

Maxillary sinus carinoma: The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma arising mainly from the maxillary antrum, which is more common in Males in their 6th decade, with extension outside the wall being very frequent.

Clinical features included unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and foul discharge. As it progresses, patients develop palatal swelling with loosening of teeth, facial swelling with infraorbital numbness, and orbital signs like proptosis and diplopia. In advanced disease, trismus and cranial nerve palsies.

Treatment involves, for the early stages, partial maxillectomy, with later stages, total maxillectomy can be done along with Chemoradiation.

Indications for Total Maxillectomy:

* T2 or T3 tumors of the maxilla without ethmoidal involvement.

* Radioresidual tumors of the maxilla.

Incision used for total Maxillectomy: Weber-Ferguson's incision (shown below)

Option A: A partial maxillectomy is performed for benign lesions or localised tumours, where only a part of the maxilla is excised, along with a small portion of the palate, resulting in a smaller post-surgical cavity with some surrounding structures intact.

Option C: Degloving is an approach used for scarless surgery via sub-nasal or intra-oral incisions, usually done for benign and localized lesions.

Option D: Ethmoidectomy is done via Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)- External approach and is used in ethmoidal tumors, chronic recurrent sinusitis, nasal polyposis, etc.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man reports gradual hearing loss over several years. He reports difficulty hearing conversations, particularly in noisy environments, and has difficulty perceiving high-pitched sounds. There is no vertigo, tinnitus, or ear fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presbycusis

This clinical vignette points towards a diagnosis of presbycusis.

It is a type of sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological ageing process in the ear.

The pathogenesis of presbycusis includes:

* Degeneration of the organ of Corti

* Degeneration of the spiral ganglion

* Degeneration of the stria vascularis

* Stiffening of the basilar membrane.

Clinically, it usually manifests in elderly adults over 65 years of age. It is gradually progressive and tends to affect the higher frequencies first. Characteristically, patients with presbycusis have significant difficulty hearing in the presence of background noise. Additionally, patients with presbycusis may also have a paradoxical hypersensitivity to loud sounds. This is due to the recruitment phenomenon. They may also have tinnitus. It significantly affects the quality of life, and patients tend to present with progressive social withdrawal.

On examination, tuning fork tests will show a picture of symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss with

* Positive Rinne's test in both ears, meaning the air conduction is better than bone conduction (AC>BC) in both ears

* Weber's test will show no lateralisation, meaning the sound is heard equally on both sides.

Diagnosis can be confirmed with audiometry. Treatment of presbycusis mainly includes using a hearing aid.

Other options:

Option A: Acoustic neuromas are noncancerous, usually slow-growing tumours that form along the vestibulocochlear nerve. They arise from Schwann cells. Schwannomas can occur on any cranial or peripheral nerve in the body, but in the brain, acoustic neuromas are the most common schwannomas.

Option B: Meniere's disease is usually unilateral. It is characterised by episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of ear fullness. Pure tone audiometry reveals a sensorineural type of hearing loss with lower frequencies affected first.

Option D: Otosclerosis is a disease of the otic capsule that usually presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss. Patients with otosclerosis characteristically hear better in noisy than in quiet surroundings (Paracusis Willisii). Tuning fork tests show negative Rinne's test, i.e., BC > AC. Weber's may be central, as this is typically symmetrical.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was brought to the hospital by his mother after being struck by a ball. In addition to double vision, he feels pain when opening his jaw. On examination, there was flattening of the malar eminence and periorbital emphysema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zygomatic fracture

In the given scenario, the child presenting with diplopia, flattening of the malar eminence and periorbital emphysema points to the diagnosis of zygomatic fracture.

Zygomatic fractures often result in facial asymmetry and visual disturbances due to involvement of the orbit.

After nasal bones, the zygoma is the second most frequently fractured bone. Usually, the cause is direct trauma. The lower segment of the zygoma is pushed medially and posteriorly, resulting in flattening of the malar prominence and a step deformity at the infraorbital margin.

Zygomatic bone following injury presents with:

* Flattening of the malar eminence

* Anaesthesia of the cheek in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve

* Periorbital emphysema

* Step deformity of infraorbital margins

* Restricted ocular movements

* Trismus

* Diplopia

It is diagnosed on the Waters’ or exaggerated Waters’ view, which shows the fracture and displacement the best.

Other options:

Option B: Maxillary bone fractures present with malocclusion of the teeth, elongation of the midface, mobility of the maxilla and CSF rhinorrhoea.

Option C: Nasal bone fractures usually result from direct trauma such as fights, falls, sports injuries, or road accidents. Clinical examination may show deformity, swelling, bruising, and nasal obstruction. Imaging may aid in the diagnosis, but the diagnosis is mainly made on the basis of physical examination.

Option D: Naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures are associated with CSF rhinorrhea, pug nose, telecanthus and displacement of eyeball.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was extubated after a surgical procedure that required prolonged ventilation. Shortly after the endotracheal tube is removed, the child exhibits stridor on auscultation. What part of the airway is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subglottic narrowing

This child presenting with stridor after prolonged intubation most likely has subglottic stenosis post-intubation.

The subglottis is the narrowest part of the paediatric airway, making it particularly prone to injury and stenosis following prolonged mechanical ventilation. The most common cause of subglottic stenosis in children is prolonged endotracheal intubation. Prolonged endotracheal intubation leads to ischemia and pressure necrosis of the subglottic mucosa. This results in a fibroinflammatory response, which progresses to wound contracture and airway narrowing. This explains the gradual onset of dyspnoea and stridor with preserved phonation. Pulmonary function tests reveal a fixed upper airway obstruction pattern.

Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy, which allows direct visualisation of the subglottic area to assess the degree of stenosis. CT or MRI may be used to evaluate the extent of narrowing and identify any underlying structural damage. Treatment can be via endoscopic balloon or mechanical dilation; laser therapy or surgical resection may be needed to remove the stenosis in severe cases. In severe cases, a tracheostomy may be required to bypass the obstructed segment and allow for breathing.

This condition is staged by the Cotton-Meyer grading.

Subglottic stenosis and laryngomalacia are the causes of stridor in neonates.

Stridor is a noisy form of respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. It may be heard during inspiration, expiration, or both.

* Inspiratory stridor is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g., laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g., laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea and primary and secondary bronchi, e.g., bronchial foreign body and tracheal stenosis.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female singer presents with difficulty producing high-pitched sounds following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness in her voice, but she is unable to elevate her pitch. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN)
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)

The nerve most likely injured in the given case is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN).

The affected muscle is likely the cricothyroid muscle, one of the paired intrinsic muscles of the larynx, which is responsible for elongating and tensing the vocal cords to produce higher pitches. This muscle's function is directly influenced by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which supplies it and facilitates the adjustment of pitch.

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve descends along the larynx, situated beneath the sternothyroid muscle, to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. By activating this muscle, the external branch enables the tension of the vocal cords to be increased, thereby contributing to the production of higher-pitched sounds. This intricate nerve-muscle interaction highlights the specialised role of the cricothyroid muscle in pitch modulation and vocal quality.

Other options:

Option A: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of the larynx up to the level of the vocal folds and no motor supply.

Option B: Injury to the right recurrent laryngeal nerve results in hoarseness and dysphonia due to paralysis of the right vocal cord, whereas paralysis of both vocal cords results in aphonia and inspiratory stridor. It supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx, except the cricothyroid.

Option C: Lesions of the glossopharyngeal nerve result in the loss of the gag reflex and other sensory loss like taste sensation and loss of pain on tongue, tonsil, pharynx and soft palate. It is motor to the stylopharyngeus, secretomotor to parotid glands, and gustatory to the posterior one-third of the tongue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged lady choked while eating fish and has associated symptoms of choking, hoarseness of voice, and foreign body sensation in the throat. On examination, the fishbone was lodged in the pyriform fossa. During its endoscopic removal, which of the following nerves is most susceptible to injury?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of Superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus. Foreign bodies may lodge in the piriform fossa and cause irritation. The nerve is easily accessible for local anesthesia, and it is through this nerve that pain is referred to the ear in carcinoma of the piriform sinus.

The pyriform fossa lies on either side of the larynx and extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold to the upper end of the esophagus and forms the lateral channel for food. It is bound medially by the aryepiglottic fold and the posterolateral surfaces of the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages. It is bound laterally by the thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage.

The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the larynx above the vocal cords.

The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone. It is pierced by the superior laryngeal vessels and internal laryngeal nerve.

Other options:

Option A: Tonsillectomy may damage the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Option B: The trachea of infants and children is soft and compressible, making it difficult to identify, and the surgeon may easily displace it and go deep or lateral to it, injuring the recurrent laryngeal nerve or even the carotid.

Option D: Thyroid surgery, tumours, neuritis, or diphtheria can also affect the external laryngeal nerve, resulting in paralysis of the cricothyroid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged male presents to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. Upon examination, the external auditory meatus has blood clots. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT Temporal bone

The clinical history of a road traffic accident causing bleeding through the ears is highly suggestive of a basilar skull fracture or ring fracture. Hence, the investigation of choice in the given clinical vignette is a CT scan of the temporal bone

Signs of basilar skull fractures:

* Haemotympanum: Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of a basilar fracture.

* Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa.

* Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle’s sign) refers to the collection of blood in the posterior aspect of the ear (mastoid region), indicating a middle cranial fossa fracture.

* CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: Double target sign, a double-ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen.

Following a head injury, the battle’s sign and raccoon eyes are usually delayed findings, developing between 6 hours to 3 days post-trauma.

The onset of CSF leaks following trauma may be delayed by several hours to days. Suspected fluid is confirmed as CSF by testing for β2-transferrin. Most CSF leaks are conservatively managed. Persistent leaks >7 days have a heightened risk of meningitis and are often surgically repaired.

Nasopharyngeal airways and nasogastric tube insertion are relatively contraindicated in basilar skull fractures due to the risk of intracranial placement. NIPPV is avoided due to the risk of pneumocephalus.

The image below shows raccoon eyes and a battle sign.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.

Pearl PF1160: NICE Guidelines for CT in Head Injury

National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Computed Tomography (CT) in Head Injury

Indications for CT imaging within 1 hour of following risk factors being identified:

* Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) <13 at any point

* GCS <15 at 2 hours after injury on assessment in emergency department

* Focal neurological deficit

* Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture

* More than one episode of vomiting

* Post-traumatic seizure

Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours

* Age >65 years

* Coagulopathy (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, or rivaroxaban use)

* Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., fall from a height, road traffic accident)

* Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room after an RTA with a history of diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. The radiological examination is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orbital floor fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Blowout fractures are isolated comminuted fractures caused by direct trauma to the orbit that result in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall, which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fractures is the medial wall of the orbit.

An isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called a blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum into the maxillary sinus, which may lead to enophthalmos and entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. The floor is made of zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones.

The patient with a blowout fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paraesthesia along the infraorbital nerve is also very common. Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis, and subconjunctival haemorrhage. Infraorbital hypoesthesia may be present because of entrapment of the infraorbital nerve.

Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called the "hanging drop sign" or "teardrop sign".

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics.

Le Fort fracture is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.

Investigations:

* X-ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity in the maxillary sinus.

* A CT scan is used to confirm the site and size of the fracture and entrapment of muscle.

* Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Large fracture involving at least half of the orbital floor

If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A tympanometry graph is displayed below. The arrow points to a sharp peak at pressure = 0 daPa. What type of tympanogram does the arrow represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type As

The given tympanograph is a type As tympanogram.

Tympanometry: It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear and the functioning of the eustachian tube. Results of tympanometry are plotted in the form of a tympanogram with:

* Compliance on the Y axis (ease of mobility of TM)

* Middle ear pressure on the X axis (regulated by eustachian tube)

Principle: When a sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, some of the sound energy is absorbed while the rest is reflected. A stiffer tympanic membrane would reflect more sound energy than a compliant one.

Tympanometry has also been used to evaluate the function of the eustachian tube in cases of intact or perforated tympanic membranes. A pressure of -200 or +200 mm H₂O is created in the middle ear, and the person is asked to swallow 5 times in 20 seconds. The ability to equilibrate the pressure indicates normal tubal function. It is also used in evaluating the patency of the grommet inserted in the tympanic membrane for treating serous otitis media.

By charting the compliance of the tympano-ossicular system against various pressure changes, different types of graphs called tympanograms are obtained. They are as follows:

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic male patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus oryzae. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised individuals.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus. The presenting features are facial pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, conjunctival swelling, congestion, and blurry vision. When the disease spreads to the orbit, proptosis can be present. It can later spread to the brain's frontal lobe and cavernous sinus.

The local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge is typically seen in invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discolouration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

A definitive diagnosis is done with a biopsy and histopathologic examination. It is the most sensitive and specific method. It reveals aseptate fungi with thick-walled, ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles. Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick, cottony, and fluffy surface.

Among the imaging techniques used for diagnosis, MRI is more sensitive to detecting orbital and nervous involvement than CT. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging technique of choice. The 1,3 beta D-glucan assay, which is helpful for the identification of most fungi, cannot be used for the diagnosis of mucormycosis.

Management: The underlying cause and risk factors should be addressed.

* Aggressive surgical debridement of involved tissues should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of any form of mucormycosis is suspected.

* Initial therapy with amphotericin B as the drug of choice.

* Posaconazole and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azoles that can be used as step-down therapy after response to amphotericin B.

The benefit of hyperbaric oxygen has not been proven yet and is not considered a standard treatment.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is characterized by complications such as cavernous sinus thrombosis when advanced cases are encountered. Clinical features suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis are bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and impairment of extraocular muscle function (ophthalmoplegia).

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial rhinosinusitis typically presents with purulent nasal discharge, pain, and fever, and the CT scan would show mucosal thickening without the characteristic hyperattenuation.

Option C: Allergic fungal sinusitis is an allergic reaction to the causative fungus. It is prevalent in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. There is no invasion of the sinus mucosa with fungus. It presents with sinonasal polyposis and mucin, which consists of eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and fungal hyphae. A CT scan shows mucosal thickening with centrally hyperdense areas. (Double density sign) There is an expansion of the sinus or bone erosion due to pressure, but no fungal invasion.

Option D: Invasive aspergillosis tends to affect immunocompromised individuals and cause more aggressive symptoms like facial swelling, necrosis, and a more destructive pattern on CT.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Three weeks ago, a patient underwent parotidectomy. He complains of excessive sweating, flushing, and redness over the parotid region, particularly during meals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Frey's syndrome

The symptom complex in this patient, coupled with a history of recent parotid surgery, is indicative of Frey's syndrome.

Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating/auriculotemporal syndrome) commonly develops after parotid surgery or other trauma that results in the opening of the parotid capsule. It results from damage to the autonomic innervation of the salivary gland.

There is a regeneration of the parasympathetic nerve fibres that stimulate the sweat glands of the overlying skin in response to salivary stimulation or mastication. It is thought to reflect abnormal innervation of sweat glands on the face by regrowing parasympathetic secretomotor axons that would previously have innervated the parotid gland.

Clinical features: Sweating, warmth, and erythema over the region of surgical excision of the parotid gland. This is due to the autonomic stimulation of salivation by the smell/taste of food

Diagnosis: The starch iodine will aid in diagnosis. The affected area painted with iodine will turn blue on exposure to sweat.

Management:

* Prevention: Sternomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascial flap, and insertion of an artificial membrane between the skin and the parotid bed will minimise the inappropriate regeneration of the autonomic nerve fibres

* Treatment:

*

* Antiperspirants with aluminium chloride

* Subcutaneous infiltration of purified botulinum toxin into the affected area

* Denervation by a tympanic neurectomy or auriculotemporal nerve avulsion has been advocated, but is often not curative

Other options:

Option A: Crocodile tear syndrome, or Bogard syndrome (gustatory lacrimation), is due to residual facial paralysis or faulty regeneration of the nervus intermedius of the facial nerve. It presents as unilateral lacrimation during eating and drinking.

Option B: First bite syndrome (FBS) is a condition that classically presents as severe pain in the preauricular region, initiated on the first bite of a meal.

Option D: Horner's syndrome is characterised by the classic triad of mild ptosis (due to Muller's muscle paralysis), miosis (due to dilator pupillae paralysis), and decreased ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the clinical presentation of Frey's syndrome?
options: Acute painful swelling in the submandibular region, aggravated with food intake.
Loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gustatory sweating

Frey's syndrome manifests as gustatory sweating and flushing while chewing food.

Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating/auriculotemporal syndrome) commonly develops after parotid surgery or other trauma that results in the opening of the parotid capsule. It results from damage to the autonomic innervation of the salivary gland. There is a regeneration of the parasympathetic nerve fibres that stimulate the sweat glands of the overlying skin in response to salivary stimulation or mastication. It is thought to reflect abnormal innervation of sweat glands on the face by regrowing parasympathetic secretomotor axons that would previously have innervated the parotid gland.

Clinical features: Sweating, warmth, and erythema over the region of surgical excision of the parotid gland. This is due to the autonomic stimulation of salivation by the smell/taste of food

Diagnosis: The starch iodine will aid in diagnosis. The affected area painted with iodine will turn blue on exposure to sweat.

Management:

* Prevention: Sternomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascial flap, and insertion of an artificial membrane between the skin and the parotid bed will minimise the inappropriate regeneration of the autonomic nerve fibres

* Treatment:

*

* Antiperspirants with aluminium chloride

* Subcutaneous infiltration of purified botulinum toxin into the affected area

* Denervation by a tympanic neurectomy or auriculotemporal nerve avulsion has been advocated, but is often not curative

Other options:

Option A: Crocodile tear syndrome, or Bogard syndrome (gustatory lacrimation), is due to residual facial paralysis or faulty regeneration of the nervus intermedius of the facial nerve. It presents as unilateral lacrimation during eating and drinking.

Option B: In sialolithiasis, the patient usually presents with acute, painful swelling in the submandibular region, which is aggravated with food intake. Symptoms resolve 1-2 hours after the meal is completed. On examination, a tender and enlarged submandibular gland can be noted on bimanual examination.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve, and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following head and neck cancers is most commonly associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oropharyngeal carcinoma

HPV infection is most commonly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma.

HPV 16 and 18 are considered high-risk subtypes and are associated with cervical cancer and precancerous cervical lesions. There is also evidence linking HPV 16 and 18 with cancers of the anus, vulva, vagina, penis, and oropharynx.

The E6 protein of high-risk types binds to the p53 gene, while the E7 protein inactivates the pRb gene. p53 and pRb are tumour suppressor genes that, when inactivated, result in uncontrolled cell proliferation. The presence of koilocytes is a histopathological marker of the virus. These cells have a perinuclear halo in the cytoplasm, and these cells disappear when dysplasia advances.

Laryngeal papillomas are benign tumours of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV types 6 and 11), which is most likely acquired at birth from mothers who had vaginal HPV disease. Juvenile papillomatosis, or respiratory papillomatosis, is the most common benign laryngeal neoplasm in children.

Important agents associated with malignant conditions:

* HHV-8 (mainly), cytomegalovirus - Kaposi’s sarcoma

* Epstein-Barr virus – Burkitt’s lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma

* HPV 16 and 18 – Cancer cervix

* HBV and HCV – Hepatocellular carcinoma

* Schistosoma – Bladder carcinoma

The head and neck cancers include cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands. Squamous cell cancer is the most common head and neck malignancy, often linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Non-squamous malignancies include thyroid cancer, salivary gland cancer, and sarcomas.

The risk factors for head and neck malignancies are listed below:

* Oral cavity cancer:

* Tobacco, smokeless tobacco like Bidi, Chutta, Paan (oral tobacco mixed with betel leaf, areca nut, and salted lime), Khaini, and marijuana

* Alcohol, poor oral hygiene, and intake of red meat and salted meat

* Infections with human papillomavirus and HIV

* Genetic conditions like Li-Fraumeni, ataxia telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, and Fanconi's anaemia

* Oropharyngeal cancer:

* Smoking and alcohol

* HPV 16 and 18

* Cancer of the larynx and hypopharynx (Option D):

* Tobacco and alcohol

* Nickel, mustard gas, and asbestos exposure

* Long-term exposure to sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid in battery plant workers.

* Postcricoid carcinoma is associated with previous radiation and sideropenic dysphagia

* HPV infection and immunosuppression

* Nasopharyngeal cancer: (Option A)

* Chinese population

* Epstein-Barr virus infection

* Nitrosamines in salted fish and meat

* Vitamin C deficiency

* Cancers of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinus:

* Tobacco

* Occupational exposure to dust from wood, textiles, and leather. Nickel and chromium dust and mustard gas exposure.

* HPV 16 and 18

Option B: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a known risk factor for post-cricoid hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following structures usually has the tip of the uncinate process attached to it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle turbinate

The tip of the uncinate process is attached to the middle turbinate.

The upper attachment of the uncinate process varies significantly and may connect to the lateral nasal wall, extend upward into the base of the skull, or medially attach to the middle turbinate. These variations influence the drainage patterns of the frontal sinus. The anteroinferior border of the uncinate process is connected to the lateral wall. The posteroinferior end of the uncinate process attaches to the inferior turbinate, dividing the membranous section of the lower middle meatus into an anterior and a posterior fontanelle.

The structures seen in the middle meatus are the uncinate process, a bony projection inferiorly stemming from the inferior turbinate and superiorly varying in attachment, and having an anterosuperior to posteroinferior curve mirroring the bulla ethmoidalis located above and lateral to it. The bulla ethmoidalis is a large ethmoidal air cell that projects into the middle meatus. The semilunar space between the bulla and uncinate is called hiatus semilunaris.

The area limited medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea is the infundibulum, in the inferior aspect of which the maxillary sinus ostium drains. The frontal sinus opening is usually near the anterosuperior attachment of the uncinate process (which is variable), while the middle ethmoidal air cells open at the bulla ethmoidalis.

The osteomeatal complex is the name given to the area containing the openings of these various sinuses in the middle meatus. Hypertrophy, pneumatization of the middle turbinate (concha bullosa), cancerous masses on the middle turbinate, etc., can cause the osteomeatal complex area to narrow considerably and result in sinusitis of the frontal, ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses.

The image below shows the computed tomography (CT) scan of the ostiomeatal complex

Important steps in FESS:

* Uncinectomy or Infundibulotomy

* Identification and enlargement of the maxillary ostium

* Bullectomy

* Penetration of basal lamella and posterior ethmoidal cells

* Clearance of frontal recess and frontal sinusotomy

* Sphenoidotomy

* Nasal packing

Indications of FESS:

* Chronic bacterial sinusitis refractory to medical treatment.

* Recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis.

* Polypoid rhinosinusitis.

* Fungal sinusitis with fungal ball.

* Antrochoanal polyp.

* Mucocele of frontoethmoid or sphenoid sinus.

* Endoscopic septoplasty.

* Epistaxis control by endoscopic cautery.

* Foreign body removal from the nose or sinus.

Other options:

Option B: The inferior turbinate is an independent bone, and the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus located below it.

Option C: The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized. The superior meatus is located below it, and the posterior ethmoid cells open into it.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea not responding to antibiotics. On examination, granulation tissue is seen in EAC, facial nerve palsy was present. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, and granulation tissue in EAC and facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease.

*

Treatment:

(i) Diabetic control.

(ii) Ear toileting

(iii) Antibiotic treatment against the causative organism(P. aeruginosa) for 6–8 weeks or more.

*

Antibiotics found effective are:

*

Gentamicin combined with ticarcillin. (intravenous)

*

Third-generation cephalosporins combined with an aminoglycoside. (intravenous)

*

Quinolones combined with rifampin. (oral)

If patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.

Prolonged antibiotic treatment has replaced radical surgery and resections done earlier for this condition.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child with B/L sensorineural hearing loss was given hearing aids, which have not been beneficial. Which of the following is the next treatment option for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cochlear implant

The next treatment option for this child is a cochlear implant.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from hearing aid.

The principle of the surgery is to place the electrode array within the Scala Tympani Of Cochlea. Intact 8th nerve and the higher auditory pathway is a prerequisite for surgery. The facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach is the preferred surgical approach. Auditory brainstem implant is placed in the lateral recess of 4th ventricle

Pearl PF1581: Cochlear implant

A cochlear implant replaces the organ of Corti i.e. when hair cells of the organ of Corti are severely damaged these implants bypass it and directly stimulate the auditory nerve.

Indication: Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss i.e. > 70 dB.

Components:

Preoperative investigation: Complete audiological evaluation and HRCT and MRI (to detect the structure of cochlea, cochlear nerve and CNS abnormalities).

Surgical approach: Two surgical techniques to approach the cochlea for implantation are the facial recess approach (via facial recess) and the pericanal technique (via EAC).

Postoperatively: Activation of the device after 3-4 weeks and evaluation is by HRCT (MRI is contraindicated).

Contraindications:

* Absence of cochlea (Michel aplasia)

* Deafness due to absent cochlear nerve, lesions of cochlear nerve or lesions of the central auditory pathway

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound while compressing the swelling. X-ray of the neck is seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given image along with the examination finding of Bryce's sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling in the neck due to dilatation of the saccule. It is more commonly seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to a raised transglottic air pressure in these people. It can be classified into internal, external, or combined types of laryngocele.

* Internal laryngocele is limited within the larynx and appears as a distension of the false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External laryngocele has a distended saccule that herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane and appears as a swelling in the neck.

* Combined or mixed laryngocele has both internal and external laryngoceles as its components where the air-filled sac extends both within the larynx and externally through the thyrohyoid membrane into the neck, and potentially into the mediastinum.

It presents with hoarseness of voice, cough, and airway obstruction (if large). External laryngocele presents as a reducible swelling in the neck that increases in size on coughing or performing the Valsalva maneuver. On pressing the neck swelling, a gurgling sound is heard, indicating a positive Bryce's sign. Adult laryngoceles can be associated with carcinoma.

Diagnosis is based on an indirect laryngoscopy and CT scan. Internal laryngocele is managed by marsupialization and external laryngocele is managed by a surgical excision through an external neck incision.

Other options:

Option A: The pharyngeal pouch(Zenker diverticulum) is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian's triangle is an area of muscular weakness between the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus and the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the oesophagus and the trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal oesophagal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: The tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female who was treated with steroids and remdevisir for COVID now presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is a non-contagious fungal disease most commonly caused by Rhizopus oryzae that is acquired through the inhalation of fungal spores from air. It may occur during COVID infection or after a few weeks (usually around the 3rd week) of recovery from it. Reasons for increase in mucormycosis cases in COVID patients are:

* Uncontrolled hyperglycemia due to any reason. COVID per se has a tendency to worsen diabetes and also precipitate diabetes in previously normal individuals.

* Misuse and irrational use of steroids. Steroid overuse can cause new-onset diabetes.

* Leucopenia associated with COVID

* Prolonged ICU stay, unhygienic humidifiers, and irrational use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

* Pre-existing comorbidities such as hematological malignancies, use of immunosuppressants, and solid organ transplantation.

A high index of suspicion is required for the early diagnosis of mucormycosis. Checklist of sentinel signs/ symptoms of mucormycosis to be monitored in patients admitted with COVID-19 are:

* Relatively early disease (Nose and sinuses):

* Headache and nasal obstruction (especially if severe or persistent and not responding to medications)

* Nasal crusting, brownish or blood-tinged nasal discharge

* Facial pain, pain over sinuses

* Paraesthesia/ loss of sensation over half of the face

* Discoloration of the skin or localized facial puffiness

* Loosening of teeth, discoloration, ulceration, or eschar over the palate

* Moderately advanced disease (Eye/orbital involvement):

* Eye swelling or redness, eye pain

* Double vision, drooping of the eyelid, blurring, and loss of vision.

* Very advanced disease (Intracranial involvement):

* Involvement of cranial nerves II-VI suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis

* Signs of MCA thrombosis

Diagnosis:

* KOH mount and microscopy

* Histopathology of debrided tissue shows presence of ribbon-like aseptate hyphae (5-15 µ thick) branching at right angles.

* Culture can be done but treatment should be started on clinical suspicion.

* CT of sinuses, CT chest for suspected pulmonary involvement ( presence of more than 10 nodules, reverse halo sign are highly suggestive of mucor), and MRI brain to look for the extent of intracranial involvement.

Management:

* Treatment of co-morbid illness and strict glycemic control.

* Anti-fungal therapy started early on high clinical suspicion even prior to microbiological confirmation can reduce mortality. Treatment involves a combination of surgical debridement and antifungal therapy.

* Liposomal Amphotericin B (5-10mg/kg) is the drug of choice and has to be continued for 3-6 weeks. It should be diluted in 5% dextrose and is incompatible with normal saline and Ringer lactate. Step-down therapy to be done with oral posaconazole or isavuconazole. Renal function must be monitored during the entire treatment period.

* Early surgical debridement after stabilization of systemic illness and ensuring facilities for post-surgical care and ventilation.

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of black or greyish membrane in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the sinus marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maxillary sinus

The sinus marked in the image is the maxillary sinus.

The sinuses seen in Water's view is marked in the Xray below:

Paranasal sinuses are air-containing cavities in that are present in the bones of the skull. These paranasal sinuses have been divided into two groups:

Anterior group: It includes,

* Maxillary sinus(Antrum of highmore)

* Frontal sinus

* Anterior ethmoidal.

All of the above sinuses open in the middle meatus and their ostia lie anterior to basal lamella of middle turbinate.

Posterior group: It includes,

* Posterior ethmoidal sinuses: Opens in the superior meatus

* Sphenoid sinus: Opens in sphenoethmoidal recess.

Note:

Maxillary and Ethmoid sinuses( including both anterior and posterior ethmoidal sinuses) are present at birth. The frontal and the sphenoid sinuses are not present at birth.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the B tympanogram seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serous otitis media

Type B tympanogram is seen with serous otitis media.

Pearl PF1067: Types of curves in tympanogram

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The image given below is from a chronic smoker's oral examination. Identify the lesion given.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leukoplakia

The given image with a white lesion of the tongue in a smoker is suggestive of oral leukoplakia

Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity. It is seen anywhere in the upper aerodigestive tract. It may represent squamous hyperplasia, dysplasia, and/or carcinoma with an associated risk of malignant transformation

It is defined as a clinical white patch that cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease. Risk factors include tobacco (including cigars, cigarettes, beedi, and pipes), alcohol consumption and chronic irritation.

A biopsy should be done to establish a diagnosis and an appropriate work-up is done if carcinoma is identified. Cessation of smoking, elimination of the areca nut/pan habit, and reduction in alcohol consumption should be encouraged. For lesions with moderate to severe dysplasia, surgical excision or laser surgery should be the treatment of choice.

Oral hairy leukoplakia is a different entity caused by the Epstein-Barr virus(EBV). It is due to the reactivation of EBV occurring in association with immunodeficiency commonly from HIV infection. It presents as white corrugated plaque over the lateral border of the tongue, which cannot be rubbed off.

Other white lesions of oral mucosa:

* Lichen planus

* Discoid lupus erythematosus

* White spongy nevus

* Candidiasis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the view in which the maxillary sinus is seen best?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water's view

Occipitomental view with an open mouth is also called the water’s view.

Water's view: The patient’s head is positioned such that the nose and the chin touch the film while the X-rays are projected from backwards. The mouth is usually kept open while taking the X-ray.

Structures seen in water’s view are:

* Maxillary sinuses (seen best)

* Frontal sinuses

* Sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with open mouth)

* Zygoma

* Zygomatic arch

* Nasal bone

* Frontal process of maxilla

* Superior orbital fissure

* Infratemporal fossa

Pearl PF1766: Radiographic views of temporal bone

Pearl PF1596: Radiographic views of paranasal sinuses and mastoid

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions does not form a grey-white membrane over the tonsils ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ludwig’s angina

Ludwig’s angina does not cause a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. It is the submandibular space infection.

D/D for membrane over tonsil:

* Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms

* Diphtheria

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Vincent’s angina

* Leukemia

* Candida

* Agranulocytosis

* Malignancy

* Aphthous ulcer

* Traumatic ulcer

Ludwig’s Angina is the infection of submandibular space.

One side of the submandibular space is the superficial layer of deep cervical fascia that extends between the hyoid bone and the mandible, while the other side is the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth and the tongue. The mylohyoid muscle separates it into two compartments:

* Sublingual compartment (above the mylohyoid).

* Submaxillary and submental compartments (below the mylohyoid).

Both compartments freely communicate in the midline with the opposite side. Therefore, infection rapidly becomes bilateral.

Dental infections are the most common cause and account for 80% of the cases.

Clinical features:

* Marked difficulty in swallowing (odynophagia) with varying degrees of trismus.

* When infection is localized to the sublingual space, structures in the floor of the mouth are swollen and tongue seems to be pushed up and back.

* When the infection spreads to the submaxillary space, submental and submandibular regions become swollen, tender and impart woody-hard feel.

* Usually, there is cellulitis of the tissues rather than frank abscess.

* The tongue is progressively pushed upwards and backward threatening the airway.

Treatment:

* Systemic antibiotics.

* Incision and drainage of an abscess.

* Tracheostomy, if there is severe obstruction of the airway.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the main arterial supply of palatine tonsils?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Descending palatine branch of maxillary artery
Ascending palatine branch of facial artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tonsillar branch of the facial artery

The main arterial supply of tonsil is by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

Five arteries supply the tonsil:

* Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (the main artery)

* Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery

* Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery

* Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery

* Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following laryngeal cartilages is least likely to be calcified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epiglottis

Epiglottis is unlikely to be calcified as it is made up of elastic cartilage.

Only hyaline cartilages can undergo ossification (calcifications on x-ray). It between the ages of 25-65y. These calcifications may be confused with foreign bodies of esophagus or larynx on x-rays.

The hyaline laryngeal cartilages are:

* Thyroid

* Cricoid

* Most of arytenoid.

The elastic laryngeal cartilages are:

* Epiglottis

* Corniculate

* Cuneiform

* Tip of arytenoid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is responsible for ear pain after a tonsillectomy surgery ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia after a tonsillectomy.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

Image below shows the anatomic relations of tonsil and tonsillar bed.

The ear receives an extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

Jacobson's nerve, along with branches from the sympathetic plexus forms the tympanic plexus. This plexus provides sensation to the middle ear, upper eustachian tube, and medial surface of the tympanic membrane. Referred otalgia transmitted by the glossopharyngeal nerve may be secondary to lesions and/or inflammatory processes of the nasopharynx, palatine tonsil, soft palate, or posterior one-third of the tongue.

Causes of referred otalgia via glossopharyngeal nerve:

* Acute pharyngitis

* Tonsillitis

* Peritonsillitis

* Peritonsillar abscess

* Post-tonsillectomy

* Foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area

* Elongated styloid process

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35 year old male presented to the clinic with complaints of episodic vertigo, sense of ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and a low-tone roaring tinnitus. What is the possible clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meniere's disease

The possible clinical diagnosis for a 35-year-old male presenting with episodic vertigo, ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and low-tone roaring tinnitus is Meniere's disease. It is also called endolymphatic hydrops.

The primary pathology in Ménière’s disease is the distension of the endolymphatic system due to an increased endolymph volume. This can result either from increased production of endolymph or its faulty absorption or both. Normally, endolymph secreted by stria vascularis fills the membranous labyrinth and is absorbed through the endolymphatic sac.

Meniere's disease is a chronic condition of the inner ear that affects balance and hearing. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, which are brief and intense episodes of spinning dizziness. Patients may also experience a sense of pressure or fullness in the affected ear, along with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear). The tinnitus associated with Meniere's disease is typically low-tone roaring in nature.

Other options:

* Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is another common cause of vertigo, marked by brief episodes of dizziness or vertigo that are brought on by particular head movements. Common triggers include actions such as rolling over in bed or looking upwards. BPPV does not typically cause ear pressure, hearing loss, or low-tone roaring tinnitus.

* Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the inner ear, usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. It can cause vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, but it is usually accompanied by other symptoms such as ear pain, fever, and a general feeling of illness.

* Syncope refers to a temporary loss of consciousness and muscle tone, often caused by a decrease in blood flow to the brain. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as vertigo, ear pressure, hearing loss, or tinnitus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and barking cough for the past 5 days. Examination reveals a hoarse voice, a moderately inflamed pharynx, and a slightly increased respiratory rate. His chest X-ray showed subglottic narrowing appearing like a steeple. Which among the following is not indicated in the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parenteral cefotaxime

The clinical scenario of a child with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever, and increased respiratory rate and an X-ray showing subglottic narrowing appearing like a steeple is suggestive of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). Parenteral cefotaxime is not indicated in its treatment.

The median age for laryngotracheobronchitis is 3 months to 5 years. It is caused due to viral infection of the glottic and subglottic regions. Patients present with low-grade fever,  barking cough, hoarseness of voice, and inspiratory stridor.

The image below shows a steeple sign, seen in croup.

Treatment of croup involves:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization - It constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption from the interstitial space and reduction of edema. The indications for the administration of nebulized epinephrine are:

* moderate to severe stridor at rest

* the possible need for intubation

* respiratory distress

* hypoxia

* Oral dexamethasone - Indicated in all the grades of croup. Corticosteroids reduce laryngeal edema through their anti-inflammatory action. IM dexamethasone and nebulized budesonide have an equal clinical effect. Corticosteroids should not be administered to children with varicella or tuberculosis as they may worsen the disease.

* A helium-oxygen mixture (heliox) may be considered for severe croup when intubation is being considered. Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

* Antibiotics are not indicated.

Most children that have croup can be managed safely at home. Indications for hospitalization:

* Progressive stridor

* Severe stridor at rest

* Respiratory distress

* Hypoxia

* Cyanosis

* Depressed mental status

* Poor oral intake

* Need for reliable observation

NOTE:

As the duration of action of racemic epinephrine is only less than 2 hours, it is mandatory to place the patient on observation for 2-3 hours to watch for the reappearance of symptoms. The patient can be discharged home if he has:

* No stridor at rest

* Normal air entry

* Normal O2 saturation

* Normal level of consciousness

* Received steroids

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, the right ear reveals conductive hearing loss with a dull tympanic membrane. A decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The given clinical condition is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking. The commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with the following symptoms:

* Cervical lymphadenopathy (most common)

* Nasal - obstruction, discharge, rhinolalia clausa, epistaxis

* Ear - eustachian tube obstruction leading to conductive hearing loss or recurrent otitis media.

* Ophthalmoneurologic - all the cranial nerves (CN) may be involved.

*

* CN VI - squint and diplopia, the most common cranial nerve involved

* CN III, IV, VI, - ophthalmoplegia

* CN V - reduced corneal reflex (Option B)

* CN II - exophthalmos (Option D)

* CN IX, X, XI - jugular foramen syndrome

* Horner’s syndrome

* Distant metastasis to the bone, liver, and lung.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone.

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

Pearl PF1696: Types of curves in tympanogram

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old child post-tonsillectomy comes to you with complaints of snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing and a slight decrease in hearing. On examination, you notice a high-arched palate. His school performance has deteriorated as well. His mother is worried. What is the next line of management for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The patient is suffering from serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy causing eustachian tube obstruction. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear is thought to happen due to either malfunctioning (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, palatal defects, tumors of nasopharynx) or increased secretory activity of the eustachian tube (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.

questions.text: A patient presented with surgical emphysema, after an emergency tracheostomy. What is the most likely reason?

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young boxer receives a blow near the eye during a boxing match. He presents to the ER with hematoma around eye, CT scan is shown below. Identify the radiological sign shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tear-drop sign

The given CT image dipicts 'tear-drop' sign and suggests a blowout fracture.

Tear-drop/ hanging drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water’s view.

An orbital blow-out fracture is an isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blow out fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum.
