Correct answer: D. Non-cultivable

Rhinosporidium seeberi is the causative agent of rhinosporidiosis, a chronic granulomatous disease characterized by friable, polypoidal masses involving the nose, nasopharynx, and conjunctiva. Despite extensive research, R. seeberi has not been successfully cultured on artificial media and is therefore considered non-cultivable. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination, which demonstrates large thick-walled sporangia containing numerous endospores.

Why not the other options?

• A. Blood agar: Used for many bacteria; Rhinosporidium does not grow on it.
• B. Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA): Used for most fungi, but Rhinosporidium seeberi is non-cultivable.
• C. Lowenstein–Jensen medium: Used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following signs is not typically seen in allergic rhinitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otto veraguth folds

Allergic rhinitis has characteristic facial signs due to chronic nasal obstruction and itching.

Typical signs:

• Allergic shiners → dark infraorbital discoloration (venous stasis)
• Allergic salute → upward rubbing of nose → transverse nasal crease
• Dennie–Morgan lines → infraorbital skin folds

Otto–Veraguth folds :

• Seen in psychiatric conditions (e.g., depression)
• Not associated with allergic rhinitis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Biopsy done under L/A

JNA is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor arising near the sphenopalatine foramen. It is classically seen in adolescent males due to androgen dependence.

·         Recurrent, profuse epistaxis due to high vascularity

·         Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction

·         May extend to pterygopalatine fossa, orbit, or intracranial cavity

Biopsy is not performed in suspected JNA because:

·         Tumor is highly vascular

·         Attempting biopsy can cause life-threatening hemorrhage

Diagnosis is made by:

·         Clinical presentation

·         Imaging (contrast CT/MRI)

·         Angiography showing feeding vessels

Management principle: Preoperative embolization followed by surgical excision is the standard treatment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 27-year-old man has an asymptomatic retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane without keratin debris. The TM is mobile on Valsalva. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wait and watch

• Mild retraction pockets without keratin accumulation are managed conservatively.
• Normal TM mobility indicates preserved Eustachian tube function.
• Observation with periodic otoscopic follow-up is recommended.
• Surgery is indicated if:

• Progressive retraction
• Keratin debris
• Cholesteatoma
• Hearing loss

• Ventilation tubes are reserved for persistent middle-ear effusion or dysfunction.
• Tympanoplasty is unnecessary in an asymptomatic mobile membrane.
• Retraction pockets can remain stable for years.
• Regular follow-up prevents delayed cholesteatoma.
• No keratin + mobile TM = Observe.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 32-year-old female presents with progressive hearing loss. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip in bone conduction at 2 kHz with relatively preserved air conduction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Otosclerosis

Carhart notch is a characteristic finding seen in otosclerosis, appearing as a dip in bone conduction threshold at 2000 Hz on audiometry.

• Otosclerosis causes fixation of the stapes footplate at the oval window
• This affects the resonance of the ossicular chain, especially around 2000 Hz
• Results in an artificial depression (notch) in bone conduction

Why other options are incorrect:

• Sudden SNHL: True sensorineural loss without specific notch
• Meniere’s disease: Fluctuating low-frequency SNHL
• Acoustic neuroma: Retrocochlear SNHL, no Carhart notch

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with headache and is evaluated for a brain tumor/cerebellopontine angle tumor. Histopathological examination reveals a tumor composed of Antoni A and Antoni B areas. Which of the following is the most sensitive immunohistochemical marker for this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. S-100 protein

Schwannoma (neurilemmoma) has its characteristic histopathological features of Antoni A (hypercellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular, myxoid) areas, often with Verocay bodies. Schwannomas arise from Schwann cells and show strong, diffuse S-100 protein positivity, making S-100 the most sensitive immunohistochemical marker.

Why not the other options?

• B. GFAP (Glial fibrillary acidic protein): Marker for astrocytes and glial tumors (e.g., astrocytoma, glioblastoma), not schwannoma.
• C. EMA (Epithelial membrane antigen): Characteristically positive in meningioma, helping differentiate it from schwannoma.
• D. c-KIT (CD117): Marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST), mast cells, and some seminomas; not a marker for schwannoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of recurrent ear infections. On otoscopic examination, the tympanic membrane is noted to be dull and retracted, with fluid visible in the middle ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Otitis media with effusion (OME)

Otitis media with effusion (OME) is characterized by non-purulent fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute infection, commonly seen in children with Eustachian tube dysfunction.\

•

Findings:

o    Dull, retracted tympanic membrane

o    Fluid level or air bubbles behind TM

o    Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy

•

Pathophysiology:

o    Poor Eustachian tube function → negative pressure → fluid accumulation

•

Symptoms:

o    Hearing loss, ear fullness

o    Usually no fever or acute pain

Why not other options:

• ASOM: Acute pain, fever, bulging congested TM
• CSOM: Chronic discharge with TM perforation
• Otitis externa: External canal inflammation, normal TM

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gradual progressive hearing loss. On examination, he has difficulty perceiving high frequency sounds, but other findings are normal. Which structure is primarily affected in this condition?
options: Inner hair cell of basal turn
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inner hair cell of basal turn

High-frequency hearing loss in elderly patients (presbycusis) primarily involves damage to the inner hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea.

• Base (basal turn) → detects high-frequency sounds
• Apex → detects low-frequency sounds

Pathophysiology:

• Age-related degeneration of hair cells (especially inner hair cells)
• Most pronounced at the basal turn → early loss of high-frequency hearing

Why other options are incorrect:

• Stria vascularis: Affects endolymph production (metabolic hearing loss)
• Tectorial membrane: Structural role, not primary site here
• Outer hair cells: Amplify sound, but inner hair cells are primary sensory receptors

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with long-standing diabetes presents with severe persistent otalgia and purulent otorrhea despite receiving appropriate antibiotics. Examination reveals granulation tissue in the external auditory canal. Imaging demonstrates erosion of the adjacent temporal bone, and the patient has developed facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malignant otitis externa

The clinical picture is characteristic of malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa, an aggressive infection of the external auditory canal that can progress to skull-base osteomyelitis.

It occurs classically in elderly patients with diabetes and immunocompromised individuals. The most common causative organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Important clinical clues include:

• Elderly patient with diabetes
• Severe, persistent otalgia, often disproportionate to examination findings
• Persistent otorrhea
• Granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, classically near the bony-cartilaginous junction
• Failure to respond to routine treatment for otitis externa
• Bony erosion/skull-base osteomyelitis
• Cranial nerve involvement, with facial nerve (CN VII) palsy being an important complication

Why not the other options?

• B. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Commonly presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, nasal symptoms, and unilateral middle-ear effusion due to Eustachian tube obstruction rather than painful external auditory canal granulation.
• C. Chronic suppurative otitis media: Characterized by chronic middle-ear infection with tympanic membrane perforation and persistent/recurrent otorrhea. Severe disproportionate pain in an elderly diabetic with EAC granulation strongly favors malignant otitis externa.
• D. Acute suppurative otitis media: An acute middle-ear infection typically presenting with fever, otalgia, and a bulging tympanic membrane. Skull-base erosion and persistent EAC granulation are not typical features.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient with hearing loss is examined and is found to be Rinne’s negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, while Rinne positive at 1024 Hz. What is the expected air conduction and bone conduction gap?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-45 dB

The Rinne test becomes negative only when the air–bone gap (ABG) exceeds a certain threshold, and this threshold varies with tuning fork frequency.

• Lower frequencies (256, 512 Hz): Rinne becomes negative earlier (smaller ABG needed)
• Higher frequency (1024 Hz): Requires a larger ABG to turn negative

Interpretation of the question:

• Rinne negative at 256 & 512 Hz → significant conductive hearing loss
• Rinne still positive at 1024 Hz → ABG not large enough to affect higher frequency

This pattern corresponds to an air–bone gap of \~30–45 dB

• ABG \~15–30 dB: Rinne may turn negative at 256 Hz only
• ABG \~30–45 dB: Negative at 256 & 512 Hz, positive at 1024 Hz
• ABG >45–60 dB: Negative at all frequencies

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with hearing impairment. On tuning fork testing, Rinne test is positive in both ears, and Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sensorineural loss in right ear

Recognize that Rinne test positive bilaterally (AC > BC) with Weber test lateralizing to the opposite ear indicates unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. In sensorineural hearing loss, the Weber test lateralizes to the better-hearing (normal) ear; therefore, lateralization to the left ear indicates sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conductive loss in left ear: In conductive hearing loss, Rinne is negative (BC > AC) in the affected ear, and Weber lateralizes to the affected ear.
• B. Conductive loss in right ear: Weber would lateralize to the right ear, not the left.
• C. Sensorineural loss in left ear: Weber would lateralize to the right (better) ear, not the left.

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Rinne positive (AC > BC) | Normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss

| Rinne negative (BC > AC) | Conductive hearing loss

| Weber lateralizes to affected ear | Conductive hearing loss

| Weber lateralizes to normal ear | Sensorineural hearing loss

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient has otitis media with effusion. Which of the following is wrong?
options: It undergoes spontaneous resolution after cold decreases
It shows Ad type of curve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It shows Ad type of curve

Otitis media with effusion (OME) is characterized by fluid in the middle ear without acute infection, leading to conductive hearing loss.

·         OME shows a Type B (flat) tympanogram

·         Indicates reduced tympanic membrane mobility due to fluid

Why option D is wrong (Ad curve):

·     Type Ad curve = hypermobile tympanic membrane (e.g., ossicular discontinuity)

·     Not seen in OME

Clinical features:

·       Commonly bilateral (especially in children)

·       Associated with upper respiratory infections (cold)

·       Often resolves spontaneously after resolution of infection

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL). Which of the following regimens is the most effective?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral prednisolone

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an otologic emergency defined as a sensorineural hearing loss of ≥30 dB affecting at least three consecutive frequencies within 72 hours. Early initiation of corticosteroid therapy (preferably within 2 weeks of symptom onset) offers the best chance of hearing recovery. Oral prednisolone is the first-line treatment for most patients.

Why not the other options?

• B. Steroid + high-dose aspirin: Aspirin is ototoxic at high doses and can worsen hearing loss.
• C. Gentamicin + steroid: Gentamicin is ototoxic and is used for conditions such as Ménière disease, not SSNHL.
• D. Intratympanic steroid injection: Primarily used as salvage therapy when oral steroids are contraindicated or when there is incomplete recovery after systemic corticosteroids.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with bilateral hearing loss with worsened right ear hearing loss. On examination, the doctor recommends stapedectomy as a final resort to the problem. What would be the findings of tuning fork tests based on which the doctor has recommended stapedectomy?
options: Rinne’s test positive , Weber’s test lateralized to left ear
Rinne’s test positive , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear
Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to left ear
Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear

Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation, leading to characteristic findings on tuning fork tests.

·         Rinne test: Negative (Bone conduction > Air conduction)

·         Weber test: Lateralizes to the affected ear (right ear in this case)

Why stapedectomy is advised:

·         Fixation of stapes footplate

·         Surgery restores ossicular chain mobility

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Rinne positive: Seen in normal or SNHL

·  Weber to opposite ear: Seen in SNHL

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of hearing loss and can understand only shouted or amplified speech. What would be the degree of impairment according to the WHO classification of ability to understand speech ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe hearing loss

The WHO classification of hearing loss is based on the ability to understand speech and hearing thresholds (dB).

Key concept:

| WHOGrade | dBHL | Description | Performance

| -------- | ---- | ----------- | -----------

| 0 | ≤25 | No impairment | No/very slight problem; able to hear whisper at 1 m

| 1 | 26–40 | Slight impairment | Able to hear and repeat words in normal voice at 1 m

| 2 | 41–60 | Moderate impairment | Able to hear and repeat words using raised voice at 1 m

| 3 | 61–80 | Severe impairment | Able to hear some words when shouted into better ear

| 4 | ≥81 | Profound impairment including deafness | Unable to hear and understand even shouted voice

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a perforation in the tympanic membrane. During the evaluation, a Rinne test is performed. What is the expected outcome of the Rinne test in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Negative

A tympanic membrane perforation causes conductive hearing loss (CHL), and the Rinne test becomes negative on the affected side.

• Rinne test compares Air Conduction (AC) vs Bone Conduction (BC)
• Normal: AC > BC (Rinne positive)
• Conductive hearing loss: BC > AC (Rinne negative)

Pathophysiology in TM perforation:

• TM perforation → impaired sound transmission through middle ear
• Air conduction is reduced → bone conduction becomes relatively better

Clinical interpretation:

•

Rinne negative = conductive hearing loss

•

Seen in:

• TM perforation
• Otitis media
• Otosclerosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with high-frequency hearing loss that worsens in noisy surroundings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Presbycusis

Presbycusis is an age-related sensorineural hearing loss characterized by bilateral high-frequency loss with difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments.

·     Pathology: Degeneration of hair cells in the basal turn of cochlea

·    Hearing loss:

o    High frequency first

o    Gradually progressive, bilateral and symmetric

·   Hallmark complaint:

o    “I can hear but cannot understand,” especially in noisy settings (poor speech discrimination)

Why not other options:

·     Meniere disease: Fluctuating low-frequency loss, vertigo, tinnitus

·     Acoustic neuroma: Unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus

·    Otosclerosis: Conductive hearing loss, not high-frequency SNHL

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with vertigo and vomiting that is consistently triggered by turning in bed or changing head position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BPPV

BPPV is caused by displaced otoliths (canaliths) in the semicircular canals, most commonly the posterior canal. These particles move with head position changes, stimulating the vestibular system and causing vertigo.

·         Vertigo triggered by turning in bed or head movement

·         Brief episodes (seconds)

·         Associated nausea/vomiting

·         No hearing loss

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Vestibular neuritis

·         Causes sudden severe continuous vertigo lasting days

·         Not triggered by position

·         Often follows viral infection

C. Ménière’s disease

·         Episodic vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness

D. Labyrinthitis

·         Vertigo with hearing loss (due to involvement of cochlea)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male with a history of occupational loud sound exposure presents with hardness of hearing. On examination: • Rinne test is negative on the left and positive on the right. • Weber’s test lateralizes to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left conductive hearing loss

Tuning fork tests (Rinne and Weber) are used to differentiate conductive and sensorineural hearing loss and to localize the lesion.

·         Rinne test:

o    Left ear → Negative (bone conduction > air conduction) → indicates conductive hearing loss

o    Right ear → Positive → normal or sensorineural

·         Weber test:

o    Sound lateralizes to the left ear → either conductive loss in left ear or sensorineural loss in right ear

Since Rinne is negative on the left, the diagnosis is left-sided conductive hearing loss

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Right conductive hearing loss: Weber would lateralize to right

·         Right sensorineural hearing loss: Weber would lateralize to left, but Rinne would remain positive bilaterally

·         Left sensorineural hearing loss: Weber would lateralize to right

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are features of central nystagmus except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fatigability

Central nystagmus results from lesions involving the brainstem or cerebellum. Unlike peripheral vestibular nystagmus, it is non-fatigable, has no latency, may persist for more than 2 minutes, and its direction may change with gaze or head position.

• Fatigability is a feature of peripheral vestibular nystagmus, not central nystagmus.
• Therefore, absence of fatigability (non-fatigable nystagmus) suggests a central lesion.

| Feature | Central Nystagmus | Peripheral Nystagmus

| ------- | ----------------- | --------------------

| Latency | Absent | Present (few seconds)

| Fatigability | Absent (non-fatigable) | Present

| Duration | Persistent (>2 min) | Brief (<1 min)

| Direction | May change with gaze/position | Fixed direction

| Visual fixation | Not suppressed | Suppressed

| Associated symptoms | Neurological deficits common | Prominent vertigo ± tinnitus/hearing loss

Why not the other options?

• A. No latency ✓: Central nystagmus begins immediately after the provoking maneuver.
• C. Lasts for more than 2 minutes ✓: Central nystagmus is persistent and does not fatigue.
• D. Direction changes in different positions ✓: Direction-changing (gaze-evoked) nystagmus is characteristic of central pathology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Cochlear implantation is not indicated in which of the following conditions? 1. Otosclerosis 2. Congenital hearing loss 3. Fixed malleus 4. Ototoxicity induced hearing loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 & 3

Cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells in the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve. Therefore, it is useful only when the problem lies in the cochlea (sensorineural loss), not in sound conduction.

Indicated conditions:

·         Congenital sensorineural hearing loss

·         Ototoxicity-induced sensorineural hearing loss

Not indicated conditions:

1.      Otosclerosis

Primarily causes conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation. Managed with stapedotomy or hearing aids, not cochlear implant (unless advanced with cochlear involvement, which is rare).

2.      Fixed malleus

A conductive pathology affecting ossicular chain mobility. Treated with ossiculoplasty, not cochlear implant.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a child aged 3½ years with an ear problem, which one of these situations merits urgent referral to hospital?
options: Pus seen draining from the ear, and discharge reported for less than 14 days
Pus seen draining from the ear, and discharge reported for more than or equal to 14 days
Pus seen draining from both ears, irrespective of duration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tender swelling behind the ear

According to the IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) guidelines, a tender swelling behind the ear suggests mastoiditis, a serious complication of acute otitis media. It requires urgent referral to a hospital for intravenous antibiotics and possible surgical intervention.

Why is C correct?

• Tender swelling behind the ear is a sign of mastoiditis, which is an IMNCI urgent referral indication.
• Mastoiditis can progress to:

• Meningitis
• Brain abscess
• Lateral sinus thrombosis
• Facial nerve palsy

Why not the other options?

• A. Ear discharge <14 days ✘

• Classified as Acute Ear Infection.
• Managed with oral antibiotics and local ear care; referral is not routinely required.

• B. Ear discharge ≥14 days ✘

• Classified as Chronic Ear Infection.
• Managed with dry mopping and topical antibiotic ear drops; referral is not urgent.

• D. Bilateral ear discharge irrespective of duration ✘

• Bilateral involvement alone is not an indication for urgent referral unless there are signs of mastoiditis or other danger signs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In the case of ototoxicity induced by diuretics, which specific structure within the cochlea is most susceptible to damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stria vascularis

Loop diuretic-induced ototoxicity (e.g., furosemide, ethacrynic acid) primarily affects the stria vascularis of the cochlea, disrupting endolymph production and the endocochlear potential, leading to sensorineural hearing loss, which is often reversible but may become permanent with high doses or concomitant aminoglycoside use.

Why not the other options?

• A. Outer hair cells: Primarily damaged by aminoglycosides and noise-induced hearing loss, not loop diuretics.
• C. Inner hair cells: Less commonly affected; not the primary target of diuretic ototoxicity.
• D. Macula and crista: Vestibular sensory organs involved in balance, not the principal site of diuretic-induced cochlear toxicity.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: On Head impulse test, for a Left vestibular neuritis patient, Saccade will be in which direction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right on left head rotation

The Head Impulse Test (HIT) assesses the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). In unilateral vestibular loss (e.g., left vestibular neuritis), the VOR is impaired on the affected side.

• When the head is rapidly turned towards the affected side (left):

→ Eyes fail to stay fixed on the target

→ A corrective (catch-up) saccade occurs

• The saccade is directed towards the target (opposite to head movement)

Application to question:

• Left vestibular neuritis → defective left VOR
• Head turned to left → eyes move with head (cannot fix gaze)
• Corrective saccade occurs to the right

Hence: Right saccade on left head rotation

Why not other options:

• Saccades occur only when turning toward the affected side
• Direction of saccade is opposite to head movement, not same side

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The commonest organism causing Suppurative Otitis Media is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Streptococcus pneumoniae

Acute Suppurative Otitis Media (ASOM) is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Other common pathogens include Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Staphylococcus aureus: More commonly associated with chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).
• C. Acinetobacter spp.: Uncommon cause.
• D. Escherichia coli: Rare cause.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the limit of daily exposure of noise that people can tolerate without substantial damage to their hearing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 85 dB

Noise pollution is an important environmental health hazard. For occupational exposure, 85 dB(A) for 8 hours/day is considered the maximum permissible daily exposure without significant risk of hearing damage. Prolonged exposure above this level can cause Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL).

High-Yield Pearls

• Safe daily occupational noise exposure: 85 dB for 8 hours/day.
• >85 dB: Increased risk of permanent hearing loss with prolonged exposure.
• Pain threshold: Approximately 120–130 dB.
• 140 dB: May cause immediate acoustic trauma and tympanic membrane rupture.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not typically associated with conductive hearing loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endolymphatic hydrops

Endolymphatic hydrops refers to excessive accumulation of endolymph within the membranous labyrinth and is the characteristic pathological correlate of Ménière disease.

Because it involves the inner ear, particularly cochlear function, it produces sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) rather than conductive hearing loss.

The hearing loss in Ménière disease is characteristically:

• Fluctuating
• Sensorineural
• Often affects low frequencies initially
• Associated with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and aural fullness

Why not the other options?

• A. Otosclerosis: Fixation of the stapes footplate at the oval window interferes with transmission of sound and classically produces conductive hearing loss. A mixed loss may occur with cochlear involvement.
• B. Otitis media with effusion: Fluid in the middle ear impairs movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles, producing conductive hearing loss.
• D. Suppurative otitis media: Middle-ear infection, tympanic membrane perforation, and/or ossicular damage can interfere with mechanical sound transmission and produce conductive hearing loss.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not preferred in a child with bilateral SNHL?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

In bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), management focuses on amplification and auditory rehabilitation, not middle ear procedures.

·         SNHL involves inner ear (cochlea) or auditory nerve damage

·         Therefore, treatment should bypass or compensate for cochlear dysfunction

Appropriate management options:

·         Hearing aids → first-line in mild to moderate SNHL

·         Cochlear implant → severe to profound SNHL

·         Educational support → e.g., front-row seating, speech therapy

Why adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is NOT preferred:

·         Grommets treat conductive hearing loss (e.g., otitis media with effusion)

·         They act on the middle ear, not the cochlea

·         Hence, no benefit in SNHL

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the first investigation in newborn for audiological assessment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions)

Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the first-line screening test for hearing assessment in newborns.

·  Measures sound waves generated by outer hair cells of cochlea

·  A small probe in the ear canal records these emissions

Screening protocol:

·   Step 1: OAE screening

·   Step 2 (if abnormal): BERA/ABR for confirmation

Why other options are incorrect:

·    BERA: Confirmatory test, not initial screening

·    PTA: Requires cooperation (not suitable for newborns)

·    Impedance audiometry: Assesses middle ear, not primary screening

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the least likely risk factor for falls in an elderly person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hearing impairment

Falls in older adults are multifactorial and are most commonly associated with impaired vision, muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, arthritis, cognitive impairment, and medications. Although hearing impairment may contribute indirectly to reduced environmental awareness, it is not considered a major independent risk factor for falls compared with the others.

Why not the other options?

• B. Visual deficit ✓: Major risk factor due to impaired depth perception, reduced contrast sensitivity, and poor hazard detection.
• C. Arthritis ✓: Causes pain, joint stiffness, and impaired mobility, increasing fall risk.
• D. Muscle weakness ✓: One of the strongest modifiable risk factors, particularly weakness of the lower limbs.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following modalities is not used for hearing assessment in an infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pure tone audiometry

Assessment of hearing in infants requires objective or behavioral methods because they are unable to cooperate with subjective tests. Early detection of hearing loss is essential for speech and language development.

Methods used in infants:

• Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA/ABR): Objective, evaluates auditory pathway up to brainstem
• Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE): Screens cochlear (outer hair cell) function
• Free-field audiometry (Behavioral observation audiometry): Uses sound stimuli and observes infant response

Why pure tone audiometry is not used:

• Requires active participation and subjective response from the patient
• Infants cannot understand or respond reliably to tones

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which type of tympanogram is typically seen in patients with adenoid hypertrophy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type B

Adenoid hypertrophy commonly leads to Eustachian tube dysfunction → middle ear effusion (OME), producing a Type B (flat) tympanogram.

·     Enlarged adenoids obstruct the Eustachian tube opening in the nasopharynx

·     This causes negative middle ear pressure → fluid accumulation

·     Fluid dampens tympanic membrane movement → no peak on tympanometry

Tympanogram interpretation:

• Type B (flat curve): Seen in

o    Otitis media with effusion (OME)

o    TM perforation (with large ear canal volume)
